JANUARY, 1907.
PRICE TWOPENCE.
OLD STUDENTS' CLUB SUPPER.
HE thirtieth annual Supper of the Old Students'
Club, commonly known as The College Supper,
was held in the Maurice Hall on Saturday, 15th
December. Mr. R. H. MARKS, the President of the
Old Students' Club, took the chair as usual, and
although there were present about twenty less than last year, the
Hall was comfortably filled. The portrait of Maurice, by Mr.
Lowes Dickinson, was mounted on an easel on the platform,
and of the other Founders, Dr. Furnivall and Mr. Westlake were
present. The guests also included the Principal and Vice-
Principal, Major General Sir Frederick Maurice, Messrs. Arthur
and Goldsworthy Lowes Dickinson, Mr. G. P. Gooch, M.P.,
Mr. Caröe, the architect, and Mr. Douglas Forster, the clerk of
the works of the new building, Mr. Cornford, Dr. C. W.
Kimmins, Mr. P. J. Hartog, Mr. C. T. Millis, and Mr. A. A.
Jack. The letters of regret from absent friends referred to by
Mr. Marks as chairman included those from the Rev. J.
Llewelyn Davies, Rev. B. H. Alford, Sir R. Mowbray, M.P.,
the Hon. Alfred Lyttelton, K.C., M.P., Dr. W. Garnett, L.C.C.,
Prof. Osler, Prof. M. E. Sadler, and Messrs. C. E. Maurice,
George A. Macmillan, Arthur B. Shaw, Harold Spender,
R. W. R. Stokes, Sidney Webb, and Richard Whiteing. The
supper was well served, and the punch excellent, as usual,
although Jones had not this year the customary assistance of
Castell in the making thereof. The speeches were characterized
by the usual freedom of thought and expression, and absence
of any kind of restraint. We like to think that in probably no
other place could such contrary opinions be stated and
listened to with such good humour as those which were
expressed by Professor Dicey and Dr. Furnivall respectively on
the subject of our hereditary Upper Chamber.
There were 179 present at the Supper, namely, Messrs. G. M. Atkins,
E. C. Atkinson, F. Atterbury, Thomas Austin, T. M. Balson, George Beavis,
James Benny, W. H. Berry, Berry, B. Black, S. Bradgate, H. de Brent, E. A. Brett,
A. J. Bride, J. Bromhall, J. Bromhall, junr., junr., F. E. Brooks, G. Buckland,
S. W. Burns, G. T. Butler, Auguste Canivet, W. D. Caröe, C. G. Cash,
J. R. Chandler, Tom Coan, E. R. Cole, A. Coleman, E. T. Colesby, William

After the Supper, the customary toasts to "The Memory of FREDERICK
DENISON MAURICE, Founder and First Principal of the College," and
"The Memory of GEORGE TANSLEY, Founder and First President of the
Old Students' Club," were given by the Chairman, and honoured, upstanding,
and in silence. Smoking was then allowed, and Mr. MARKS again rose to
propose the toast of "The College," in the following words: -Mr. Principal
and gentlemen, it is a matter for sincere congratulation that the College at
the present moment is in a better position, from the point of view of numbers,
of finance, and of teaching power, than it has ever been at any time in its
history. Thanks to the Building and Equipment Committee-Messrs. Dent,
Bradgate, Mure, Forster, and the Vice-Principal-since we last met in this
hall the building has been completed, and the equipment of it is nearing
completion. You probably have noticed that within the last week we have
had affixed tablets showing the Maurice Hall, the Ruskin Art Room, the
Tom Hughes Gymnasium, the Litchfield Room, and the Tansley Room, in
memory of the men who had so large a share in the making of the College.
Something yet remains to be done in the way of decorating the walls of the
hall, and the rooms and corridors of the building, and of fitting the rooms with
picture rails. It will also be desirable, in the near future, when our funds
permit, to substitute light iron work for the substantial but ugly brick wall

to-night. (Cheers.) The efficiency and enthusiasm of our teaching staff are
maintained at as high a level as ever, one and all being animated by the
desire to give of their best to the College. In examinations this year, our
friend Torrington, who has done much good work for the College, especially
on the advertising committee, has gained the mark of distinction in the
London Chamber of Commerce Senior Examination in oral French, and the
Society of Arts highest grade in written French and oral German. (Cheers.)
Mr. Torrington gives the College the benefit of his knowledge by teaching
the Foreigners' Class. The Tansley Scholarship was awarded to A. J.
Wildey, and the three Tansley prizes, of £2 worth of books each, were
awarded to A. J. Wildey, J. C. Castell, an old friend and fellow-worker, and
J. S. Tutte. H. Bacher gained the mark of distinction in the London
Chamber of Commerce Senior Examination in Spanish. With regard to the
Clubs, it is to be be regretted that the Cricket Club has not realized the hopes
expressed for its success. One reason suggested for its failure is that sculls
and oars, plus something else, prove a more powerful attraction than bats and
stumps (Oh, oh!); the Swimming Club, on the other hand, is increasing in
numbers and activity; the Field Club continues to scour the country round
London once every month, and the Furnivall Cycling Club to tour it as often as
they can; the Sketching Club, an offshoot of the Art Class, which flourishes
under Mr. Wilkinson's care, is strong in numbers and in work; like the
Field and the Cycling Club, it is an outdoor one, which, in town or country,
appropriates any nice bit of scenery it comes across; the Chess and Draughts
Club was disorganized for a short time, but it is now again in good working
order. It has played played 16 matches, won 10, drawn 4, lost 2, and has 43 matches
on hand; the Debating Society during its past session has, as usual, by its votes
and speeches, solved most of the knotty problems which were in the air,
and what the Debating Society left undone, the College Parliament speedily
finished in its recent session. The College Parliament found a dignified
speaker in C. D. Robertson, and a courteous and able premier in W. J.
Torrington. While each party emulated another place in giving candid
opinions on the shortcomings of the other party, it is said that this particular
Parliament differed from that in the other place by doing a large amount of
business in an incredibly short space of time. Among the functions that have
taken place during the present year were the Poor Children's treat on the first
Saturday in January; the formal opening of the College in the same month
by Sir William Anson, when between 400 and 500 members and friends were
present, 234 of whom sat down to tea in the Common and Coffee Rooms;
and a Garden Party to Ruislip, which was well attended and most successful, in
July, organized and carried through by the Common Room Committee. Early
in May the Annual Excursion to Cambridge took place, when forty members
of the College enjoyed the well-known Cambridge hospitality, under
the fostering care of our good friend Cornford. (Cheers.) To show the
degree of importance that attaches to this visit, I may point out that the
Editor of the COLLEGE JOURNAL has devoted no less than seven pages of his
valuable space in the June number to a description of this visit, two pages
consisting of a tabulated statement showing all the different places where each
man was entertained during his stay, and proving at the same time the vast
amount of trouble taken in organizing the visit. Seven members of the Chess
Club went to Cambridge on November 17th, to play the Trinity College Club,
and these were again entertained by Cornford and his friends. One of the
many chroniclers of the May visit wrote, "There is not, in all the Colleges,
a Court like Neville's, nor a man like Cornford." (Hear, hear.) College
parties have also been hospitably entertained during the year by Mr. J. С.
Denmead, at South Mimms, Mr. C. E. Maurice, at Hampstead; and Mr.
John Fotheringham, at Fawkham. To each and all the College is grateful for
the kindness shown to its members. During the year the College has had
many valuable gifts from its members, which have been acknowledged in the
JOURNAL, and of these the last in order but not least in importance is the
splendid gift of Mr. J. A. Forster in panelling and decorating the Common
Room in the handsome manner in which it is now to be seen. (Cheers.) It
is a satisfaction to recognize that in all cases but one (that of Miss Horner)

all recent gifts come from our own members. A word as to our staff. The
Superintendent and his Assistant are entirely devoted to the College.
(Cheers.) The Assistant-Superintendent is l'ami de tout le monde, ready to
do anything for anybody; and the Superintendent is the man whose courage
and temper never fail him under the most trying circumstances, not even
when he has to interview a lady on business who insists on doing all the
talking for three quarters of an hour. (Laughter.) Our Vice-Principal gives
his constant attention to our business and to the College; he is mostly to be
found here two or three nights a week, sometimes four, and he takes a
deep personal interest in all the details of the work of the College, which is
always in his thoughts. (Cheers.) Our Principal is farther away from us,
and cannot in the nature of things, spend so much time among us, but we
know he is always ready to come to us whenever the need arises, in spite of
the distance. During the year he has given us several lectures and the
Opening address, besides attending Council meetings. He not only serves
us himself, but he requisitions his friends to help us with our teaching and
with our funds. Recently he brought Prof. Osler from Oxford to lecture to
us, and a short time ago the Superintendent received a letter which ran thus :-
"Dear Sir, I beg to enclose herewith £10 for the Maintenance Fund, as
requested by the Principal." It is his pleasure to serve the College, and his
heart is always in it. Gentlemen, I ask you to drink to the College, and with
it, I beg to couple the names of our Principal and our Bursar. (Loud cheers.)
PROFESSOR DICEY said, there were some occasions in life when modesty
was certainly not a virtue, and he thought this was one, when he had to
speak, not of himself, but of an institution of which he had the honour to be
the head, although he did not labour in it as much as others. He had ob-
served that the higher one got in a profession, the easier were the duties to be
discharged; and, although this did not apply pply to himself, he had found that
the salary got higher compared with the amount of the work. The reason
was that, as one was raised up to perform the duties at the head, it was
certain that the greater part of them were already performed by other persons.
There was no other institution which he so profoundly respected as the
House of Lords, and no members he so much respected as the legal members
thereof, but he had noticed that, whereas County Court judges, and even
High Court judges, had many difficult cases and possibly knew little about
the law applicable to them, yet when a case reached the House of Lords,
the Lords had the advantage of the question having been argued before at
least two courts below, and the facts ably stated by competent lawyers. All
the drudgery having been done, all that remained for them to do was to say
judicious "dittos" to those who had spoken before. The higher up you are
the less you have to do. Of this he was quite sure, as regarded himself in
the College. He often had flattering remarks made to him about the merits
of the College, to which he assented. It was his duty to assent. He did
not disclaim the credit. In speaking about the College he considered it his
duty, whilst keeping within the limits of the truth, to make his statements
impressive. We were not like some institutions, asking for a hundred, or
two hundred thousand, and hoping to get twenty or forty. We did not in
fact ask any longer-or, at all events, not obtrusively for more than we
already had. We were not in debt, and that was to our credit. Secondly,
we felt that, although we took the step with great hesitation, we did the right
thing in selling our old houses at a very good price, and in using the money
in erecting the best building our means allowed. The result was that we
bulked much more largely before the public. We looked important, and he
was proud of the fact. Then, as Mr. Marks had quite properly pointed out,
certain gifts had been made to us by old members of the College. In addition
to this encouraging feature, we had rendered to us by or through old students
an amount of service and zealous help which could be equalled in few
institutions. The younger Mr. Forster, as clerk of the works, had given us
an amount of pain and trouble and skill which could not be got for money.
(Hear, hear.) The Common Room, of which any college in Oxford or
Cambridge might be proud, with its panelling, filled us all with a feeling of
affection, and he believed there was no one present who did not feel a personal

zeal and attachment for this place of a very rare kind. (Cheers.) It was

Mr. MURE contrasted the unfinished state of the College a year ago
with our present happy condition, and reminded us of the work of the Building
Committee established in 1901, first to alter the old buildings in Great
Ormond Street, and afterwards to rebuild the College here. He took that
opportunity to publicly thank its members, Mr. J. A. Forster, the Vice-

Mr. Leon and Mr. W. C. Marshall, for the practical and valuable assistance
they had rendered. (Cheers.) He then referred to the work of the Appeal
Committee, whose efforts had resulted in a useful addition to the Building
Funds. We were indebted to the London County Council for the handsome
grant of £500 a year they had made to the College. (Cheers.) Fortunately
we had two friends on the Council, Dr. Garnett and Dr. Kimmins, well
acquainted with our work, and the grant had been made as free from
harassing restrictions as could be desired.
(Cheers.)

THE MUSEUM.
THE College Museum has just been enriched by the very handsome gift
of Miss Horner of her collection of recent and fossil shells. Miss Horner
being a near relative of the late distinguished geologist, Sir Charles Lyell,
and enjoying the friendship of many other eminent geologists and naturalists,
had unique opportunities of pursuing her favourite studies. During her
many sojourns on the continent, the cabinet, made in sections for convenience,
always accompanied her, and shells, both recent and fossil, from many
localities, and geological formations, go to swell the collection. Some of the
specimens are from Sir Charles Lyell; others are from Prof. Edward Forbes
and Sir Frederick Banbury. The whole are arranged on the system of
S. P. Woodward, and are housed in a very handsome cabinet, which of itself
is a considerable addition to the Museum fittings.
J. WARREN.
FURNIVALL SCULLING CLUB.
SUNDAY, December 2nd, was a nice day for the river, and the club sent
twenty-three members up to Richmond in divers boats. The sculling eight
crew were Jackman 8, Ethel Lidington, 7, Peckham, 6, Lizzie Skinner, 5,
Sammons 4, Kate Lock 3, Nellie Duxbury 2, Furnivall 1, Len Ingram cox.
The four, Hugh, Owen, West and Nye, with Castell cox. The two sliding-
seat doubles were Driver, Hagerty, MacWilliams and Lock, and his two
daughters. Jack Munro was in a gig, and Mowberry and Smart in rumtums.
All dined at the New Inn, Ham Common, as usual. At the club a large party
had gathered, and our new vice-president, Dr. Arthur Koebling, entertained
all the members to tea.
On the 9th, several scullers preferred to join the Lubbock Field Clubmen,
so the only boats out were two doubles and a light four, with Owen stroke,
Sammons 3, West 2, Furnivall bow, and Jack Sewell cox.
The sculling eight turned out on the 16th, with a crew of Munro stroke,
Castell, Peckham, Sammons, Reglar, Nye, Driver, Furnivall bow, and Nellie
Duxbury cox, and had the tide all the way up. On starting from Biffen's
they turned the boat too soon, and bashed her stern into the edge of the raft
box, making a nine inch rent in her stern, which nearly filled the end of the
boat with water by the time they reached Messum's. The rents were filled
with soap and white lead to make her watertight on the journey home.
The cold weather did not deter the sculling eight (6 men and 2 girls) from turn-
ing out on the 23rd. Two fours were also out on Christmas Day, Dr. Furnivall
sculling as usual on both these occasions. J. B. WEST, Hon. Secretary.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
OLD STUDENTS' CLUB.
PESSIMISM IN LITERATURE.
At the second meeting of this club for the present session held
in the Common Room, on Saturday, December 1st, at 7.45 p.m.,
Mr. E. M. FORSTER, B.A., opened for discussion the question,
"Is the Pessimism in Modern Literature to be deplored?" The
chair was taken by Mr. R. H. MARKS, President of the club, and
there were 48 other members present, namely :-
Thomas Austin, T. M. Balson, Tom Barnard, Sydney Bradgate, F. S.
Brooks. Charles Castle, E. R. Cole, Stephen J. Coombs, W. C. Cutts, John
Dale, W. J. Davis, H. O. Driver, E. Č. Duchesne, H. C. Dumbrill, E. С.
Englehart, F. S. Flint, Herbert Gallaher, C. Godfrey Gümpel, W. P. Harley,
E. A. Harrison, A. Hepburn, S. J. Hertford, James Holloway, C. P. King,
E. S. Landells, J. D. Macnair, C. F. Marshall, C. F. W. Mead. J. J. Munro,
E. Murphy, T. A. Paterson, G. C. Peckham, Leonard Pocock, C. W. Rapley,
E. J. H. Reglar, J. Gerald Ritchie, J. W. Roberts, F. C. Roper, E. W.
Rowntree, W. J. Spray, M. Staal, Sidney Stagg, M. W. Starling, E. Tissier,
J. Warren, C. R. Williams, G. E. Winter, and A. Wilshaw.
MR. FORSTER'S PAPER.
In every subject for discussion there are two questions, which
must be kept carefully apart--the question of opinion and the
question of fact. And of these questions, the question of fact must
be discussed first, for if the fact has not taken place, we can have
no opinion about it, favourable or unfavourable. Before we discuss
the recent appearance of the sea-serpent, we must be sure that the
sea-serpent has appeared. Before we discuss the policy of the
government, we must be sure that the government has a policy.
Before we discuss the German emperor's perfidious declaration of
war, the annihilation of the British fleet, and the landing of a
German army corps in East Anglia-well, before we get excited,
we had better buy The Tribune as well as the Daily Mail. And so
this evening, before we discuss the pessimism in Modern Literature,
let us be sure that Modern Literature is, to an appreciable extent,
pessimistic. To an appreciable extent. Not entirely. That we
cannot and do not want to prove. The pessimism in literature, not
the pessimism of literature, is the question of fact before us, and
having decided that, we can pass to the question of opinion, and
discuss how far this pessimism is good, how far bad.
Now the question of fact is surely not very difficult to decide.
However we define pessimism, we can easily find something in
modern literature that will illustrate our definition. Not once but
many times may we read in modern books that time flies, that man
deteriorates, that virtue is not rewarded, that innocent actions have
appalling consequences, that there is nothing new, nothing true
under the sun. Literature, thank goodness, also tells us other
things. But it most certainly tells us these things. I would even
go further and say that its general tendency is pessimistic, and that
optimism is the exception.
Consider those three men who have, for good or for evil, obtained
a European reputation, and who are imitated, not only in their own
countries, but all over the continent.
I refer to the Frenchman
Zola, the Norwegian Ibsen, and the Russian, Tolstoy.
Zola is the most cheerful of the three. By the side of his com-
panions, he appears almost hilarious. He finds the world horrible,
but he does believe that it can be made better. Pessimists have called


## p. 7 (#15) ###############################################

OLD STUDENTS' CLUB.
7
him an optimist. No one has applied this epithet to Ibsen, who finds
the world horrible, and believes that it will remain horrible. Ibsen has
no panacea for society. People call him a teacher, but I should like
to know what he teaches. Not that we should love one another; he
thinks that disastrous. Not that we should have ideals that is even
worse. If we tell the truth, he scolds us; if we don't tell the truth,
he scolds us. Whether we walk or talk or work or play, Ibsen gets
his knife into us. He finds us all diseased, all incurable, and his
interest in humanity is that of a vivisectionist in a mangy dog.
Of Tolstoy, the third of this gloomy trio, one must speak in a
different tone. Perhaps there is not a man alive who loves humanity
more. But he too finds the world horrible, and believes that it will
remain horrible. His cure is simple but alarming: annihilation.
Let the human race cease to propagate itself. Let it die out, by
its own desire. Then-according to Tolstoy-the Will of God will
be accomplished, and Humanity, having solved the problem allotted
to it, will enter upon its spiritual reward. Tolstoy is a far more
interesting man than either Ibsen or Zola. He is a great artist, with
a feeling for beauty, and even with a sense of humour. But at the
back of it all lies a profound pessimism-a belief that our life on
earth is a hopeless tangle, and that all who transmit life are guilty of
a crime.
Such are the three men who have obtained European reputation-
at all events in the region of the novel and the drama-the region
in which I am most interested and from which most of my examples
will this evening be drawn. They are men of diverse temperaments,
but they all have this belief, that the world, as it now exists, is a
perfectly horrible place. Their enormous sale and their enormous
reputation are sufficient proof that there is pessimism in literature,
at all events in continental literature. Let us turn to the literature
of England.
In politics, and in practical matters, England has generally been
the teacher of Europe. We have given her the example of
Parliamentary Government. We have given her the revolution of
1688. More recently, we have given her the Encyclopædia Britannica.
But in the domain of literature-from which I exclude The Times
and all its works-the case is exactly reversed. Europe teaches
England. For good or for evil, we lag behind the continent. We
-get most of our ideas second hand. We make splendid use of them
when we do get them, but they are imported: occasionally they
are dumped. Shakespeare may be the highest product of the
Renaissance, but the Renaissance was made in Italy. Shelley may
be a prophet of revolution, but the ideas that inspired him were
made in France. And so the ideas that inspire or worry us to-day
are made, some of them in Germany, but nearly all of them out
of England. One might compare Europe to a ship and England to
a little boat, tugged in its wake. It is a very splendid little boat,
but it does not come first. It follows the ship through all weathers
and into all seas. The ship to-day has sailed into the grey waters
of pessimism, and the little boat follows it.
We have in England no one great man whose name rises naturally
to our lips, as Tolstoy rises to the lips of a Russian. We have no
leader of acknowledged superiority, and it is more difficult to
generalize about our literature, and to decide whether it leans towards
optimism or pessimism. Yet, if we compare the novelists of to-day
with the novelists of fifty years ago, we can surely make a generaliza-
tion of a kind. The older generation had a lightness of spirit, a


## p. 8 (#16) ###############################################

8
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
robustness of outlook, that is apparently denied to the younger.
Compare Charles Dickens, Charles Reade, Tom Hughes, and
Anthony Trollope, with R. L. Stevenson, George Gissing, Thomas
Hardy, Henry James. The latter writers have a quality in them
that may be called morbid. They are quicker to register discomfort
than joy. They are obsessed with the sadness of life-Gissing with
the sadness of social conditions, Stevenson with the sadness of ill
health, Henry James with the sadness of personal relations, Thomas
Hardy, with the general sadness of everything. In some way
or another, nearly every modern writer lets us hear the note of
sorrow. Take such a writer as Bernard Shaw. We call him a
humourist, and no doubt he does make us laugh at the time. But
when we come away, we don't know why we were laughing. We
feel terribly depressed. There is none of the radiant afterglow that
we feel when we have finished a novel of Dickens or seen a comedy
of Shakespeare.
In our literature there sounds that undernote, like
the toll of a subterranean bell, "The world is a horrible place! The
world is a horrible place!" As I said before, we hear other things.
But we do hear this thing. We do hear pessimism. The question
of fact that pessimism exists, and to an appreciable degree-is
surely not to be disputed. Let us turn from it to the question of
opinion. Is this pessimism to be deplored?
And now I must come into the open. Hitherto I have concealed
my own opinion. I have been proving what no one is likely
to dispute an agreeable task, and one on which the orator gladly
lingers. Indeed, I have known orators who linger on nothing else
and prove by overwhelming arguments that the earth is round and
that the sun never sets on the British possessions. Amidst deafening
applause, they resume their seats, and a vote of confidence in Mr.
Chamberlain's Fiscal policy is proposed, seconded, and carried
unanimously. I have nothing to do with these crafty politicians. I
am concerned with literature, a comparatively straightforward
subject, and I will come into the open and say boldly that this
pessimism is not to be deplored. There is something to be said for it.
There are reasons, and noble reasons, for the output of unhappy
books. To call them insane, or diseased, or continental rubbish, is
in my opinion pernicious as well as inaccurate. They are not to
be dismissed with a shrug of the shoulders.
Now, at the first glance, the case against pessimism seems over-
whelming. Do we not all sympathize with the old lady who
exclaimed "Buy a modern novel? No thank you. If I want to cry,
I can do it without spending 4s. 6d." Why should we spend money
on the chance of being made unhappy? Nor is the old lady the
only spokesman. People who think, people who love beauty, people
who have wide knowledge of the world, join in her protest. They
are angry with all these unhappy books. They are angry with the
noisy author who tells them that it cannot be helped and that they
ought to be unhappy. Is there not happiness in daily life, happiness
sure and certain? Then why should the author neglect it? Why,
when we ask him for wine, or at all events for fresh water, should he
hand us a cup of bitter tears, and declare that these are the results
of his chemistry, these the quintessence of life--that the many-
flavoured world distills at last into no sweeter drink than this? How
tempting it is to say "The author is worse than a public nuisance.
He is a liar. For we know for certain that life is full of the most
glorious things."
And so it is. We are perfectly right about life.
But between


## p. 9 (#17) ###############################################

OLD STUDENTS CLUB.
9
life and books there is one great difference-a difference that is too
often neglected--a difference on which my chief argument will be
based. It is simply this. The end is of supreme importance in a
book. The end is not of supreme importance in life. We do not
judge a man by the words that he gasps on his death bed. But we
do judge a book by the words that are written on the last page.
The popular criticisms of a book, "It was so sad the last page
nearly made me cry," or "It is so nice: they all get married in the
end," are very good criticisms, as far as they go. The instinct to
peep at the last page and see whether the hero gets her or not, is a
good instinct in a way. A book that ends feebly, leaves a bad taste
in the mouth, or to put the point in choicer language-a book that
ends feebly has failed as an artistic whole. A book with a strong
ending leaves a good taste behind.
We forgive it many previous
faults. I think one cannot be too emphatic over this question of
the end.
This being so, let us ask ourselves-A man to-day, if he writes a
novel, how will he end it ? "Happily, of course," the optimist
replies. Very well. In what kind of happiness? What happy
incident will he select from life? The optimist hums and haws.
He says, "Why, my dear man-life's full of happy incidents." We
answer, "Exactly. Now choose one that will do for the end of a
book." He hums and haws again. He is fond of a hundred things
-of music, of football, of his friends-yet none of these things quite
do for the end of a book. And sooner or later, he will give the old,
old answer, marriage. Let the book end with a happy marriage.
Let the lovers be united, to the sound of wedding bells.
A hundred years ago, or fifty years ago, this would have seemed
a very good answer. But our social feelings are altering very
rapidly. We of to-day know that whatever marriage is, it is not an
end. We know that it is rather a beginning, and that the lovers
enter upon life's real problems when those wedding bells are silent.
Our better education, and the better education of women has taught
us this. The early Victorian woman was regarded as a bundle of
goods. She passed from the possession of her father to that of her
husband. Marriage was a final event for her: beyond it, she was
expected to find no new development, no new emotion. And so the
early Victorian novelist might reasonably end his book with a
marriage. The social feeling of the period approved him. But the
woman of to-day is quite another person. She is by no means a
bundle of goods. She may throw herself flat on the floor of the
House of Commons and resemble a bundle, but she only does it to
give more trouble to the police. She may marry, but her marriage
is most certainly not an end, either for herself or for her husband.
Their courtship was but a prelude: their wedding is but the raising
of the curtain for the play. The drama of their problems, their
developments, their mutual interaction, is all to come. And how can
the novelist of to-day, knowing this, end his novel with a marriage?
We have thus driven the optimist from a most important strong-
hold. We have proved to him-not that marriage is unhappy, but
that marriage will not do for the ending of a book. We have not
attacked his view of life, but we have attacked his view of literature.
He goes back to his music and his football and his friends, and
thither we follow him. But as a literary critic we do not follow him.
Instead, we turn to that despised creature the pessimist, and say
"How would you end a book?" And the pessimist replies, quite
simply and satisfactorily, "By some scene of separation."


## p. 10 (#18) ##############################################

10
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
It seems to me that the modern author, if he is conscientious and
artistic, is bound to listen to this advice. He may not be a pessimist
himself. But he wants to end his book on a note of permanence, and
where shall he find it? Remember that he is a modern author, and
therefore saturated with the idea of evolution. He has not merely
been taught that all things change. He has breathed it in, as men
have breathed it in at no other age. He may be neither scientist
nor philosopher. He may even protest. But he has breathed it in
and he must breathe it out again. Where shall such a man find rest
with honour? Scarcely in a happy ending.
It is useless to tell him that happiness exists. That is not the
point. Of course it exists, frequent and intense. He would be the
last to deny it. But is it permanent? Is there any happy situation
on earth that does not contain the seeds of decay, or at all events of
transformation? The modern mind is, in this respect, horribly
acute, and perceives that the glorious, happy things are not the things
that last. And therefore, for an ending, the modern author must go
elsewhere, or leave his work unfinished. Separation-that is the end
that really satisfies him-not simply the separation that comes
through death, but the more tragic separation of people who part
before they need, or who part because they have seen each other too
closely. Here is something that does last-the note of permanence
on which his soul was set. He has laboured sincerely; he has told
a story not untrue to life; he has said the last word about his
characters, for he leaves them in a situation where they can never
meet each other any more. Such a book as "The Wings of the
Dove" has, for all its obscurity, a clear and most artistic ending.
The man and woman in it, after many tests, attain to perfect know-
ledge of each other, and that knowledge entails eternal separation.
Whether they marry or not-perhaps they do; it is left doubtful-
they are divided by a chasm which no tenderness can ever bridge.
Were there a bridge-there was no ending. For if you once admit
that these people can meet again, you admit the possibility, from
Henry James's point of view, the certainty of a change in their
relations. The living change continually. Only those who are dead,
or dead to each other, are unalterable.

won 10, drawn 2, lost 2; but badly in the League-won 1, drawn 2, lost 2.
All particulars may be seen on the notice board in the Coffee Room.
The most interesting match up to the present has been against Trinity
College, at Cambridge, where we made a draw; undoubtedly both teams

We all enjoyed

coming twelve new Cambridge men to our College. May they all become
teachers in the College and vice-presidents of our Chess Club!
There is a certain Club down East where we regularly lose, twice a year.
It is an uncanny spot-this East-puts one in mind of Jerusalem! It is
uncanny because something always happens to prevent us getting a strong
team there.
Smith and Melzer are always willing to accept subscriptions to the club.
The minimum subscription is 1s.; but there is nothing at present in the rules
to prevent anyone giving more.

SKETCHING CLUB SUPPER.
W. M. C. SKETCHING CLUB SUPPER.
11
THE W. MC. Sketching Club's first supper was held on Saturday,
8th December, in Room No. 16, which was very kindly placed at the disposal.
of the club by the Executive Committee. Twenty-eight sat down, which
means that nearly the whole of the members of the club were present,
Mr. A. W. Matthews, an old member of the Art class, coming up from Luton
for the occasion. The price charged for the tickets, 1s. 6d., was not intended
to cover the cost of the supper, the balance being provided from the club
funds, and consequently only members were invited to attend. At the close
of the feast, Mr. R. H. MARKS arose and said how much pleasure it gave
him to take the chair on such an occasion. Meetings of this kind did good
by bringing men together, and helped to do away with anything in the nature
of cliquism. Suppers and meetings like this were not so frequent now as they
were at one time he remembered when the science classes used to meet once
a month for tea The Sketching Club was doing good, because it took men
out into the open air on Saturday afternoons. He asked them to join him
in drinking the health of Mr. Wilkinson, the vice-president of the club, and
of Mr. Silk, the secretary. Mr. Wilkinson replied, and was followed by
Mr. Silk, who proposed the health of Mr. Lowes Dickinson, the president of
the club. After this toast had been honoured, Mr. Marks said he had
recently seen Mr. Lowes Dickinson, who was now much better after his
illness; he had recently celebrated his eighty-seventh birthday, and was
still keenly interested in the welfare of the College. Mr. Silk then proposed
the health of the two guests, Mr. Marks and Mr. Duchesne, and the latter
responded.
A move was then made to the Ruskin Art Room, where a concert and
a lantern display by some of the members of the Photographic Section, were
given. Slides made from photographs by Messrs. A. E. and W. J. Homewood,
A. T. Hurt, C. H. Marks, F. Riley, E. W. Silk, and R. W. Wilkinson, and
humorous slides by Messrs. T. E. Pickles and J. James, in all nearly 120 were
shown. These were principally from photographs made on Sketching Club
outings and summer holidays, and included views up and down the Thames,
the Lake District, and on the continent. The musical portion of the enter-
tainment consisted of a couple of glees. "A Canadian Boat Song," and
"Oh, Who will o'er the downs," by the Sketching Club Glee Party-
Messrs. Barnett, Pickles, Hurt, and Seeley; song, "Queen of the Earth," by
Mr. W. N. Routh; "Drinking Song," Mr. E. C. Seeley; song, "A Jovial
Monk," Mr. H. Devey; song, "Yeomen of England," d," Mr. T. E. Pickles:
song, "Maid of Athens," Mr. R. W. Wilkinson; song, "The Little Hero,"
Mr. W. H. Barnett; "The Land Lubbers lying down below, below, below,"
Mr. E. C. Duchesne; comic songs, "The story of a tintack," Mr. W. N.
Routh, and "When father goes to work again," Mr. W. A. Jutting; and a
recitation by Mr. A. E. Homewood, "The Burial of Dundee." The songs
and a batch of slides were given alternately. It was a great success, many of
the pictures recalling to memory some very pleasantly spent afternoons.
One little surprise was in store for us, Mr. Wilkinson saying he had a
picture to throw on the screen of something we should set great store by, be
very careful how we treated, and value as something exceedingly difficult to
replace, and that was-Mr. Marks, whose portrait then appeared; the piano
started, and the club sang "For he's a jolly good fellow." Mr. Marks, in
response, said he was extremely surprised, he did not know what he had done
that he should be treated in this manner, but he was grateful for the kindness
shown him; he could not think how the portrait had been procured.
It was a surprise for everyone, except Mr. Wilkinson himself.
The time to stop came all too soon. So very interesting had the
evening's entertainment been, that from 7 o'clock to 11.30 was not long
enough. A flash light photograph was taken of those present. The club is
indebted to Messrs. A. E. and W. J. Homewood, who supplied and worked
the lantern, and also to another member of the same family who played the
piano. The secretary wishes to thank the club for the way in which it
responded to his call for slides and music, and to express his gratitude to
Barnett for arranging details of the supper. E. W. SILK, Hon. Secretary.

On Thursdays February, 14th and March 14th, at the same

Besides the above, on Monday evenings, at 8 o'clock,
Mr. A. Guthkelch, M.A., will deliver a course of lectures on

On Tuesdays, at 8 o'clock, Mr. H. Travis Mills, M.A., will

leon," on "Europe after Napoleon, with special reference to
England in the Nineteenth Century as illustrated by a study
of the leading statesmen of the century." And on Fridays, at
8 o'clock, Mr. Banister Fletcher, F.R.I.BA., will continue his
course of lectures on "Architecture."
On Saturday, 24th November, Sir John A. Cockburn,
KC.M.G., lectured in the Maurice Hall, on "Australian Ideals."
While admitting that methods which were successful in Australia
might not answer so well in England, he gave much interesting
information about practical Australian experiments in many
matters which to us are unsolved problems. In Australia, for
instance, Woman Suffrage, Protection, Graduated Income Tax,
Graduated Death Duties, and Conscription, are actual and
successful facts. The speaker entirely captivated his audience
by his personal charm and power of speech, and evidently
aroused a keen interest in our great Colony. Sir John Cockburn
was the first Premier of South Australia.
On the following Saturday Canon Glazebrook gave us a
lecture on "Rome," illustrated by dissolving views. And on
December 8th, W. J. Fitzmaurice-Kelly addressed us on "Don
Quixote." His lecture was in reality an extremely interesting

Student and Class Entries. -The experience of the second
and third terms of last session had warranted the hope that, with
the completion of the building and of the equipment, a large
increase of students might be expected. Your Committee did
not however think it wise to leave any stone unturned whereby

this result might be secured, and consequently authorised the
Advertisement Committee to spend a larger amount than
formerly upon advertising. Mr. Torrington, the chairman of
that sub committee, and his colleagues spent much time
considering the most effective method of making the College
known. The result was most satisfactory, as every record for the
October term has been broken. Previously to this term, the
largest number of new students joining in the October Term was
410, in 1892; this term 562 new members have been enrolled.
The record for a whole term stood at 875, in 1889; the number
at present on the College books is 938. The demand for term

stock, and had it not happily been decided to try an innovation
in the shape of an "enrolment" week previous to the opening of
term, the office staff would have been quite unable to cope with
the press of enquirers and of those desirous to join the College.
For every subject but two there has been an increased entry.

class. Probably, too, in Botany, the alteration which necessitates
a student coming for practical work on one night, and for
theoretical on another, has caused this subject to be less
attractive than had been anticipated. The comparative entries

COLLEGE NOTES.

W. J. Torrington again proved his knowledge of French and
German by gaining the mark of distinction in the London
Chamber of Commerce Senior Examination in oral French, and
by passing the Society of Arts highest grade in written French
and oral German; W. F. Frost and Julius Jacob passed the
Board of Education Advanced Stage Examination in Botany, the
former taking a second and the latter a first class; H. Bacher
gained the mark of distinction in the London Chamber of
Commerce Senior Examination in Spanish ; and J. D. Challen,
E. W. Jones, and P. A. Milner all passed the advanced stage
examination in Latin.
The award of the Tansley Scholarship and prizes was made
this year in the same manner as last. The Studies Committee
appointed a small sub-committee to examine the records
exhaustively, and then after consideration of their report made a
recommendation to the Executive Committee. Acting upon
this recommendation, the Executive awarded the Tansley
Scholarship to A. J. Wildey, and Tansley prizes of £2 in books
to A. J. Wildey, J. C. Castell, and J. S. Tutte. It is proposed
in future years to widen the area of enquiry by asking the help of
the class teachers in suggesting students who in their opinion
may be deserving of this honour.
Lectures. The College has been very fortunate this session
in securing an exceptionally attractive list of lecturers for both
the Thursday and Saturday evening lectures. The attendance
at both classes has been on the whole good, but probably would
have been better, especially on Thursdays, if the time of com-
mencement had not been changed. The list for the January
Term is not yet completed, but Sir Patrick Manson, Surgeon
General Evatt, Miss G. Lowthian Bell, Mr. A. J. Ashton,
Mr. G. P. Gooch, Mr. Sidney Olivier, Mr. H. M. Baynes, and
Mr. J. Raphael have been kind enough to promise Saturday
evening lectures, whilst the Principal and Professor Kirkaldy
have promised Thursday evening lectures. In addition to these
series, two courses of University Extension lectures have been
arranged in conjunction with the London County Council and
London University. On Tuesdays, Mr. Trevelyan lectures on
History, and on Fridays, Mr. Banister Fletcher on Architecture.
Both these courses have proved fairly attractive, but the short
notice at which these lectures were arranged did not give quite
sufficient time for adequate advertisement.

Mr. Alford's lectures will be resumed this month, on Sundays,
at 6 p.m.
The oldest of our founders, our dear old friend Mr. Lowes
Dickinson, attained the age of 87 years on the 27th November.
We congratulate him and ourselves upon his being still with
us, and helping us still, in many ways.
Mr. Felix Oswald, son of Dr. Eugene Oswald, has, according
to the Daily Chronicle of December 3rd, in which issue a whole
column is devoted to him, done a most noteworthy and coura-
geous piece of work, by which he has earned the degree of
Doctor of Science of the University of London. Eight years
ago, while still a civil servant in Somerset House, Mr. Oswald
obtained leave of absence, and went as geologist of an expedition
to Armenia, in company with Mr. H. F. B. Lynch, M.P., for
whose volume on Armenia Mr. Oswald made maps and plans,
and he also determined to write the results of his own investiga-
tions. Not only has he written the book, but in the course
of three years he set up the type of over 500 pages, and printed
104 copies, two pages at a time, at an initial outlay of about
£21. A book written and produced under such extraordinary
conditions well merited the distinction its author has gained.
Dr. Felix Oswald is now in charge of the District Probate
Registry, Nottingham.
Mr. George Allen having, as above mentioned, presented a
set of six portraits of John Ruskin to Dr. Furnivall, for the
Working Men's College, they have been mounted and framed,
at his own expense, by Mr. C. H. Perry, who cut the mount
himself, and they can now be seen in the Coffee Room. The
portraits bear the following descriptions:-(i.) The Author of
"Modern Painters," 1843, by G. Richmond. (ii.) John Ruskin,
1853, by J. E. Millais, from the picture in the possession of
Rear-Admiral Sir Wm. A. Dyke Acland, Bart. (iii.) John Ruskin,
by himself. (iv.) John Ruskin, engraving by W. Roffe. (v.) Prof.
Ruskin, and Sir Henry Acland, Bart., from a photo taken by Miss
Acland, at Brantwood, Aug. 1st, 1893. (vi.) John Ruskin, born
February 8th, 1819. The last portrait is a fine side view photo-
graph taken towards the end of his life. Under it are the
following lines in the handwriting of, and signed by, Canon
Scott Holland, taken from his "Life of Ruskin":-
He lifted his voice in praise of high and noble things, through an evil
and dark day; and now he sits there silent and in peace, waiting for the word
that will release him, and open to him a world where he may gaze on the
vision of perfect Beauty, unhindered and unashamed.
HENRY SCOTT HOLLAND.
Dr. Furnivall had expressed a wish that a quotation from
one of Canon Scott Holland's writings should be written
beneath the picture, so that it should form a memento of two
great friends of the College, so Perry wrote to the Canon, who
gladly fell in with the suggestion.

Heat 3
THE event of the month has been our 80 yards scratch race, held on the
19th December, in which 8 members competed out of 12 present at the Baths.
The object of the race was to test the pace of our men, with a view to
future handicap races. The times and results were as follows:- Heat 1
-R. Hagerty, 70 secs.; E. C. Seeley, 90 secs., T. J. Bush, 100 secs. Heat 2-
E. Hagerty, 70 secs., R. Wedderburn, 72 secs., A. T. Hurt, 105 secs.
-J. Hagerty, 70 secs., V. Herick, did not finish. The final was therefore in
the hands of the brothers Hagerty, and ended thus, R. Hagerty, 67 secs.;
J. Hagerty, 70 secs.; E. Hagerty, 75 secs. Mr. T. Hopkins kindly officiated
as starter and judge. New members continue to join us, and at no meeting
during the month has the attendance fallen below 8. It is intended to hold
a handicap race towards the end of January.

W.M.C. DEBATING SOCIETY.
W.M.C. DEBATING SOCIETY.
19
ON Tuesday, November 20th, Mr. A. E. HOMEWOOD moved that "Modern
Civilization is based on wrong Principles." The room was well filled, and the
debating was of a high order. Mr. Homewood denounced the sordidness and
commercialism of modern life, and contrasted our conditions and aspirations
unfavourably with those of other civilizations. He pleaded for nobler ideals,
for plainer living, and for higher thinking. Mr. GRUGEON, in opposing, argued
chiefly that modern civilization was based on Christian ethics, and that as the
latter were good, the former was good also. The motion was eventually
carried by 22 votes to 3.
On November 27th, Mr. E. J. TURNER, B.A., moved "That English
spelling should be reformed." Mr. Turner evidenced the extreme difficulty
experienced by the young in consequence of the needless irregularity of our
spelling; said this was the chief source of discouragement to the foreign
student of English, and an enormous amount of time was wasted all round,
which might be saved by introducing some sort of uniformity into the spelling
and dispensing with superfluous letters. While not in sympathy with pure
phonetic writing, because of the enormous number of sounds which would
have to be represented, he urged the importance of appointing a Committee,
to be composed of learned men from the principal English-speaking countries,
to meet and make suggestions with a view to arriving at some modification
of the existing irregularities in the spelling of the language. Mr. G. M.
TREVELYAN, M.A., in opposing the motion, called attention to the difficulties
such a scheme would involve, and feared that, once our spelling were tam-
pered with, much confusion would result, and many different sorts of literary
English produced.
The motion evoked many excellent speeches, but was ultimately lost by
23 votes to 19.
On December 4th, Mr. SYDNEY PRESBURG had arranged to move "That
Progressive confusion and Socialistic methods were the main factors in the
routing of the Progressives at the London Borough Councils (1906) Elections,"
but at the last moment he was unfortunately prevented, through illness, from
attending. As no one could be found to support the affirmative, Mr. C. G.
CASH opened the discussion by moving the negative. With almost over-
powering eloquence he subjected the reactionaries and their tactics to a severe
criticism. He eulogized the splendid work accomplished during the Pro-
gressive term of office, and with much rhetorical force proclaimed his
admiration for those who devoted themselves to raising the level of the poor,
and to helping those who could not help themselves. A spirited debate
followed, and the motion was ultimately rejected by 26 votes to 3.
On December 11th, Mr. A. S. LUPTON, M.A., moved "That County
Councils in future should be formed out of the Parliamentary Opposition for
the time being." With much scholarly ingenuity, Mr. Lupton directed his
argument to show that existing government was an unmitigated evil, which
it was necessary should be met, either by some such scheme as was suggested
in the motion, by which the minority for the time being was in some way
represented, or in the alternative by an anarchial state, and no government at
all. Mr. C. F. W. MEAD Opposed, and the motion was lost by 15 votes to 6.
The next Debate will take place on Tuesday, 8th January, when Mr.
Geo. F. Shee, M.A., Secretary of the National Service League, will move
"That the adoption of Universal Military Training for National Defence is a
just and necessary measure."
C. F. W. MEAD, Hon. Secretary.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
CORRESPONDENCE.
[Under this heading the Editor will be glad to publish letters of interest to
past and present members, but he declines all responsibility for the views
therein expressed.]
Re JOINT CLUBS' SUPPER.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
MY DEAR POocock, -I got your letter re Joint Clubs' Supper, but
delayed answering it until I had had an opportunity of putting the points
raised by you before a representative gathering of younger College men of
the present day. The opportunity came on Wednesday last, when the
details of this year's supper were carefully considered by the following:-
Balson, Barnett, Castell, Colesby, Driver, Gray, Hopkins, Landells, Melzer,
Munro, Nield, Nye, Offer, Peckham, Randall, Reglar, Starling, West,
Wildey, and myself. I think you will admit that this score of names represents
a gathering of men of all shades of opinions, and men who have the welfare
of the College and their fellow-members closely at heart. By no stretch of
the imagination could this body of students and teachers be described as a
clique. It seems to me, therefore, that you will be the first to admit that
you have had a fair hearing.
The chief point under discussion was, of course, the question of price.
Last year the price of the tickets was fixed at 2s. 6d. per head, and a supper
was put on which was equal in every respect to the supper for which the Old
Students' Club charges 3s. It was equal in quality, was quite as well served,
and there was more of it. But this price of 2s. 6d. was harshly criticized by
you, both in the speech which you made in reply to the vote of thanks
accorded to you as chairman of last year's Joint Clubs' Supper, and also in
the JOURNAL. You said the price of the tickets kept many men away from
the Supper, and your letter of the 30th ult. shows that the same idea still
exists in your mind. Your letter reads as follows:- "I feel very strongly
that an attempt should be made to place it (the Supper) within the reach of
the poorer members. I should like to see revived the boiled leg of mutton
soirée, with Christmas pudding and apple pie, that we had in the very early
days at Is. 6d., cooked on the premises-and bring your own knife and fork.
I should not mind bringing my own plates and glasses as well. Drinks
extra, of course. I don't think you want any jellies, butter, cheese, celery, or
other kickshaws, if you have joint and two vegetables, bread, and pudding or
pie, and that ought to be done for Is. 6d., and profitably too." I have
quoted pretty fully from your letter, for I don't want it said that I have
burked" any of your arguments.
Now, let us just consider this question on its merits, without making
comparisons with the Old Students' Club Supper. It seems to me, even
at the first glance, that you have given away your case. You say, quite
rightly, that those early suppers were cooked on the premises. But the
muster at those early suppers was, it must be remembered, only about thirty,
whereas we hope to get at least a hundred at the next Joint Clubs' Supper.
Can our kitchen staff cope with a supper of this size? Assistance can be
procured, of course; but assistance must also be paid for.
Then with regard to crockery and cutlery. You know as well as I do
that the kitchen equipment is insufficient to meet the requirements of such an
occasion. Your answer is that the men can bring their own knives, forks, and
plates. Are you serious in this? Would you be willing to ask a man to pay
Is. 6d. for a supper ticket, and tell him that he must come provided with a
meat plate, a pudding plate, a bread plate, two knives, two forks, a spoon,
and a couple of glasses; and that it would be a praiseworthy deed if he
could also smuggle into his pocket a salt-cellar, pepper-box, meat dish, and
similar unconsidered trifles? Would you also tell him to bring his own
dish-clouts, bowl, and tea cloths, for washing up, and that the College would
supply the hot water? Or must the poor wight take the plates home dirty,
and spend weary moments in his bachelor den scrubbing off cold mutton fat?


## p. 21 (#31) ##############################################

CORRESPONDENCE.
21
Ugh! The thing is quite unthinkable. I am sure many men would marry
their landladies' nieces rather than do that. Besides, awful thought! if the
men are too poor to pay 2s. 6d., they may not possess the table utensils
enumerated above, and in their desire to attend the supper might even be
tempted to purloin them at their pet restaurant. I knew one man who was
always finding grog rummers in his pockets; but that's another story.
To return to our (boiled) muttons. My memory also goes back to those
very early Joint Clubs' Suppers; but I never remember being called upon to
bring my own cutlery, etc. Neither do I recollect the price of the tickets, so
I will pin my faith to your figures. What I do know, however, is that the
expenses of those suppers were partly met by donations. I have before me
the figures of all the Joint Clubs' Suppers since 1896, and in this matter I am
not speaking from memory. Let us take the 1899 Supper as an example.
The tickets were Is. 9d. each, and 60 students were present. The fare was
very plain, and nearly everybody was dissatisfied. Yet that year the Supper
expenses were only just met by the help of donations from Mr. Tansley and
the Clubs, these donations amounting to £4 5s., or Is. 5d. per head! You
can inspect the figures whenever you like.
A similar thing occurred every year. The price charged for the tickets
did not nearly cover the cost of the supper, even when the fare was plain and
the supper cooked on the premises, and the deficit was met by means of
donations. This meant that the clubmen paid more than their fair share, for
they were mulcted through the clubs to which they subscribed, and in addition
they paid as much for their tickets as the men who were not supporters of any
clubs. Besides, the men who did not go to the suppers had to pay for those
who went. Yet, in spite of the fact that the tickets were cheaper, the suppers
were no better attended in those days than they are to-day.
Now, with regard to the fare provided. In this matter you have walked
into a curious bog from which you will find it hard to extricate yourself. You
surely must know that "kickshaws," although they help to make a dinner
enjoyable, cost little, or nothing. It is the joints which run up the expenses.
You advocate one joint; we intend having two. But please don't blink the
fact that one joint costs as much per head as two. Also, please remember
that soups, jellies, cheese, and inexpensive "kickshaws" reduce the quantity
of meat required. The man who dines off nine courses doesn't eat nine times
as much as the man who is limited to one course. Other things being equal,
he eats about the same quantity as his (perhaps) less favoured fellow, and
unless the viands are expensive (and the "kickshaws" mentioned by you
cannot be so regarded), a dinner of many courses costs very little more than
a simpler meal. To put it plainer, a supper composed of half-a-pound of
meat and half-a-pound of vegetables, costs quite as much, if not more than a
pound of food composed of equal weights of meat, vegetables, pie, and
"kickshaws."
Look at the matter from another standpoint. The cheapest supper we
can put on, as we have to get supplies from an outside caterer, and do not
want to cut out the punch, necessitates a charge for tickets of 2s 6d. per head.
The Old Students' Club Supper costs 3s. per head, although the caterer
should charge less since the numbers at that supper are double those at the
Joint Clubs' Supper. Are we to assume then, that the Old Students' Club
makes a handsome profit, and puts a high price upon its supper tickets in
order to keep the company select ? And are all old students so much
wealthier than present students that price doesn't matter so far as they are
concerned? Of course not. You and I know quite well that the Old
Students' Club Supper tickets are put at 3s. because they cannot be sold at a
lower price without making a loss, and we are enabled to put our Supper
tickets at 2s. 6d. because we spend less on printing, postages, etc. We are
not so unfair as to say that you prescribe "plain living and high thinking"
for the students, while you and the Old Students' Club wallow in luxury.
Then why not be fair to us, and give us credit for doing our best?
I could write a good deal more upon this subject, but feel that I have
written too much already. Let me just say in conclusion that all the points
upon which I have touched, and many others, were fully discussed by the

the Joint Clubs' Supper "as a protest," were invited to run the Supper at a
lower price if they thought it possible; but they declined to step into the
breach! The meeting then agreed that the price of tickets for this year's
Supper should be 2s. 6d., that punch should be provided as usual, and that a
fresh chairman should be elected every year. This last resolution is, of
course, an innovation; it comes into operation at once, but as it is not
retrospective it was decided that you should be asked to preside at this year's
Supper. I hope you will honour us by doing so.
Please don't think there is any ill-feeling on our part on account of your
criticisms, because there isn't. If we could put the price of tickets at Is. 6d.,
we should be only too pleased to do so; but we do not see how we can do so
without the aid of charity. If there is any College man who really cannot
afford to join our festive gathering because 2s. 6d. is beyond his means, and
he is too proud to accept a ticket, I hope he'll look in during the songs and
speeches. We shall be glad of his company, I know he'll find a swig of
punch and a pipe of baccy at the table of whichever sport he indulges in, and
I am certain that he'll value these and good fellowship more than a charity
meal of boiled mutton at Is. 6d. - Sincerely yours, W. C. JONES,
December 7th, 1906.
Hon. Secretary, Joint Clubs' Supper Committee.
[This letter clearly illustrates the advantage of a meeting, over
correspondence. At meetings, men of various minds and clashing ideas can
jangle them together and produce harmony, whereas in correspondence there
is the danger of being misunderstood, from the inability to see the effect of a
letter upon its recipient or to furnish any necessary explanations. Tom
Hughes once told the writer, on his being introduced to him as the editor of
the COLLEGE JOURNAL, that he did not believe in journalism--he believed in
personal contact. By personal contact with other men at the meetings and
debates at the College, a man learns his place and also to value other men
at their proper worth. If, however, my unlucky letter quoted above has
done nothing else, it has probably helped to settle the question of price. -ED.]
DR. FURNIVALL writes:-One note of the "Good Old Times" might
have been cited by Munro in his opening speech in the late debate on the
subject, contending that we were well rid of those ancient days; and this is
that for the country working-man of the time, education was forbidden,
unless the leave of the lord or lady of the manor in which the parent worked
was obtained. Dr. Andrew Clark, in his paper on "Serfdom on an Essex
manor" (Chatham Hall, in the parish of Great Waltham), 1308-1378, in
the Historical Review, July, 1905, cites a case, on page 483: - "In September,
1344, Andrew Samar was mulcted 3d. [5s. now], because posuit filium suum
ad scholas sine licencia domina," he sent his son to school without leave of
the lady of the manor. Our plan of mulcting a man for not sending his boy
to school is surely an improvement on this old one.
THE REFORMERS' YEAR Book for 1907, just published, contains a
great deal of information on labour matters which is not to be had from any
other source. In addition to a number of articles dealing with the reform
movements of the day in this country and abroad, there is special reference
matter relating to the Labour Party, and also directories of reformers, reform
societies, trades councils, etc., giving several thousand addresses in all. There
is also a complete list of Members of Parliament, with their private addresses,
constituencies, and majorities. Among new features is a section of some
urgent reforms, in which such subjects as Graduated Income Tax, Municipal
Milk Supply, Old Age Pensions, Payment of Members, Poor Law Reform,
are dealt with concisely and to the point, whilst the Woman's Movement
during 1906 receives special treatment.
Messrs. F. W. Pethick Lawrence and Joseph Edwards are the joint
editors of the book, the full index to which enables the principal facts to be
readily utilized, Published at 4, Clement's Inn, Strand, price Is. nett.

THE LIBRARY.
THE SHAKESPEARE READINGS.
23
DECEMBER 2nd. -" A Midsummer Night's Dream." On this occasion
the Readers, forsaking their accustomed haunt, journeyed to Adelaide Road.
Mrs. Tansley had kindly invited them to read at her house.
Behold them, then, sixteen in number, almost filling the room, sitting at
ease in cosy corners and on comfortable lounges. In front of them a cheerful
fire. Behind and around, an array of shaded lights to help in reading the
text, and incidentally giving picturesque effects in facial expression. At the
piano, Mrs. Tansley herself, ready to strike the keynote of the play with a
selection from Mendelssohn's overture.
Our spirits attuned to the mood, we settled down to a delightful time,
and dreamed for two hours of many strange and familiar things; of a violent
quarrel between a Fairy King and Queen, more passionate quarrels of two
ill-starred couples, and a spirited discussion of some workmen. The latter
was reminiscent of an annual Club meeting. Barnett, as secretary, did his
best to please everybody, and Peck, in the character of a member of some
importance, sat on everybody, undertook all the speaking, and in the end
pronounced the whole affair a great success. Paterson, Wallace Davis,
Krauss, and Staal chimed in now and then with great effect. It was all so
probable, very silly, but vastly amusing. The two loving couples were
ridiculous. They made one another miserable, but in the end they were
happy. A little imp of mischief was at the bottom of it all. He came on at
the end and said it was only his fun.
When we woke up, we thanked Mrs. Tansley for her kind thought in
asking us to come, and for her valuable help in ensuring our pleasure and
comfort. And then we adjourned for refreshments and gossip.
December 16th. -" Henry V." Back to our old places. Scene: the newly
decorated Common Room. Outside, a drizzling rain which had depressed
our spirits all day.. Inside, a goodly company of eighteen men, very cheerful,
considering that nearly every reader had several parts allotted to him. The
illusion of much work was speedily dispelled when it was found that, owing
to the courtesy and "cutting" of the Committee, Barnard as Henry did
nearly all the talking and made a speech on the slightest provocation. A
most striking linguistic display was given by several readers. Wallace Davis
spoke in French, in a Welsh style of English, and in his mother tongue.
Balson, as befitted a princess, spoke in polite polite French And even Paterson,
as Pistol, indulged in some outlandish lingo ngo distinctly foreign. We ought to
have had more of the humour on't, nevertheless the play was worth doing.
We elected A. E. Homewood, Wallace Davis, and T. M. Balson, to cast the
plays, and the president drew attention to our new notice-placard, the work
and gift of one of our readers.
"Twelfth Night" on January 6th, when ladies will assist us in our revels.
The Ladies Nights" are open to members and their lady friends.
THE LIBRARY.
TOM BARNARD.
A GREAT number of books have been presented to the Library this
month, viz.-A parcel of about 80 books from Mr. Percy Bunting, comprising
works on Philosophy, Politics, Religion, and History, in French, German,
and English; about 30 books, chiefly general literature and fiction, from
Mr. Langdon Everard; several from Mr. Godfrey C. Gümpel, an old College
student, including a work of his own on "Common Salt"; 29 volumes of the
"Quarterly Review" from Mr. G. W. Prothero; and three from Dr. Furnivall,
one of which is the "Golden Calendar," containing some verses on rowing by
Tom Hughes and his brother George. An English dial clock has been given
by Mr. H. R. Levinsohn, the late librarian. The show case, the octagon table,
and the armchairs given by Mrs. Litchfield are now in the Library and are
handsome additions to its furniture. Two more cosy armchairs given by
Mr. Julius Jacob have arrived, and the bay in front of the fireplace has now
quite the homelike air which was so characteristic of our old Library in Great
Ormond Street.
J. C. CASTELL,

​LUBBOCK FIELD CLUB.
On December 9th the club was favoured with perfect weather. The blue
sky remained unclouded all day, the air was gloriously transparent, and the
sun pleasantly warm. On the other hand, the wind was keen, and as soon
as the sun grew low, a frost made itself evident. Had it set in earlier, the
roads and paths would have been considerably improved, and the boots of the
party would have excited less attention on our return to town. We met at
Finchley Station at 9.45, and crossing the golf-links, made our way to Totte-
ridge across the fields. From there we continued by road to Highwood Hill,
whence a series of pleasant paths led us to the Elstree Road. Following this
across the Edgeware Road, we kept to the right of the Aldenham Reservoir
until Aldenham House was reached. We then made a detour through the
pleasant grounds of Hillfield, and found a track which brought us to
Letchmore Heath. Here we halted for lunch, and having disposed of that,
resumed our route to Aldenham. After visiting the church and woods, we
took a bye road to Bushey Heath, and made an unsuccessful attempt to find
a certain right-of-way through Bentley Priory. We then crossed the heath
and made for Stanmore, whence a still unspoiled path across Canon's Park
led us to Whitchurch and Edgeware. From here the majority of the party
returned by electric tram, while the remnant, after a short stroll, caught the
5.17 train home. The distance walked was something over twenty miles,
which is considerably above the average. Little was done in the collecting
way, the only records being in the direction of pond life. An immense
gathering of rooks at High Canons interested us considerably, large tracks of
ground being quite black with them. We were also struck by the fact that
we came across two farms where Shetland ponies formed the greater part of
the live stock. Some very youthful lambs we encountered seemed to have
lost their frolicsome habits owing to the cold.
The next walk will be across the Surrey Downs to Leith Hill, starting
from Effingham and returning either to Bookham or Leatherhead. Take
excursion ticket to Effingham, 2s. Train leaves Waterloo (South Station) at
10.5, on Sunday, January 13th, 1907. J. HOLLOWAY, Hon. Secretary.
THE LINGUISTS.
THIS society, which has been inactive for the past two years, has been
reformed. At a general meeting held on December 12th, Mr. W. J.
Torrington was appointed president, Mr. A. Hepburn, vice-president, and
Messrs. T. M. Balson, E. W. Jones, and J. J. Munro were elected as a com-
mittee. It has been decided to hold meetings every Wednesday from 9.30
to 10.30 p.m., the first evening in French, the second in German, and so on
alternately. Foreigners and all members interested in foreign languages are
invited to attend the meeting. The life subscription is one shilling, and I
shall be pleased to hear from any member willing to open conversation on any
subject in either French or German. To induce foreigners to attend it was
decided to devote the last twenty minutes of each evening to English.
Mr. Torrington will give an address in French on Wednesday, January 9th,
at 9.30 p.m., in the Club Room. IIis subject will be announced later.
W. MELZER, Hon. Secretary.
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL is supported partly by
Annual Subscribers living in different parts of the World, and
partly by circulation among the Students and Members. Its success
depends upon a regular demand, and to ensure this, the Editor
would be glad if as many readers as can will become Subscribers.
Subscription 2s. 6d. per annum, post free.

MARCH, 1907.
THE COFFEE ROOM.
PRICE TWOPENCE.
APPEAL FOR DECORATION FUND.
N extremely enthusiastic and well-attended meeting of
students and teachers was that, convened by the
Common Room Committee, which was held in the
Common Room on Monday, February 11th, to dis-
cuss "What are the best ways and means of raising
a fund large enough to decorate the Coffee Room, carrying
out as far as possible the scheme of decoration of the
Common Room?" Mr. B. P. MOORE presided, and after
referring to the munificence of our friend Mr. J. A. Forster in
decorating the Common Room so splendidly and luxuriously as
it was, explained that we wished to raise the necessary funds to
embellish the adjoining room in the same way, amongst
ourselves. He called upon Mr. W. C. JONES, who said it was
Mr. Reglar who first gave voice to the idea that had occurred to
several of the members, that the students themselves should take
advantage of the opportunity to make the Coffee Room as cosy
and comfortable as its neighbour. He had asked Mr. Duchesne
to get from Mr. Caröe, our architect, an estimate of the cost,
and Mr. Caröe had put it at about £100, and had very kindly
sent a detailed scheme and plans showing the decorations which
he would propose, and which included not only panelling
and wall decoration, but also a very handsome ceiling
advocated the formation of a committee to carry out this scheme
of decoration and to collect the necessary funds for the purpose.
Mr. E. J. H. Reglar referred to the generous gifts of the
founders of the College, and the unselfish work and many
benefactions which they and their successors had for upwards of
fifty years bestowed upon the College. It had occurred to a
good many men, since Mr. Forster had made the Common Room
what it was, that they would like to do something in return for
and in recognition of all the benefits which the members had
received. The opportunity had now arisen, and he suggested
the names of a dozen representative men amongst the students
who should form a committee to carry out the scheme proposed,
with Mr. H. K. Randall as secretary. He thought the students
would come forward and support this appeal, and that if all
gave in accordance with their means, £150 would soon be
He


## p. 50 (#40) ##############################################

50
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
realized. He hoped the Common Room Committee would give
their assistance and make a grant towards the fund, and also
that some of the clubs would do likewise. Mr. TORRINGTON
supported the proposals. Mr. SYDNEY GRUGEON followed on the
same lines, and recalled the work done in the old College by
Messrs. Davenport, Eason, Muliett, Murphy, and others, when
it was discovered that the panelling of the old Coffee Room had
in past years been canvassed and papered over, in restoring and
decorating it, labouring late night after night for that purpose.
Mr. MUNRO, in an eloquent speech, set before us the College
traditions, the generosity of its early founders, their love of their
fellow men, and their wide humanity.
These features were
perpetuated in this present building, and now arose the
opportunity for the students, in their turn, to leave some tangible
memorial of their personalities, by decorating the Coffee Room
in the manner suggested. Every student, seeing what he
received here, in culture, in education, and in social intercourse,
ought to take an active part in adding to the comfort of and
preserving the fabric of the College. He should give the
proposal his most hearty support.
Mr. A. E. HOMEWOOD, usually in the opposition, in College
discussions, could not bring himself to oppose on this occasion.
Mr. HEPBURN, the well-known wit of the College debating
circle, whose opinions, to put it mildly, do not as a rule exactly
coincide with those of Mr. Homewood, begged leave to be
allowed to "climb down" off the committee suggested, and let
Mr. Homewood take his place, but this request was greeted with
loud cries of "No, no."
Mr. R. H. MARKS said we should put in practice the French
saying, " payer de sa personne," and then became reminiscent, as
Sydney Grugeon had been, calling to mind the time when the.
members worked hard at the task of removing the whole of the
Museum from "down the yard "at 46, Great Ormond Street, to
the second floor.
Mr. Lupton having suggested three methods of collection-
(i.) arming the committee with revolvers, (ii.) a placard outside
announcing our impending bankruptcy and that £2,000,000 was
urgently required, and (iii.) the formation of the committee into
a company, limited by guarantee of one shilling each, which
should give the order and forthwith fully subscribe its capital-
none of which were received seriously, Mr. Pocock cordially
supported the proposition. It would be for the committee to
devise methods of collection, but the meeting could make
suggestions. It was not every man who could afford to put his
hand in his pocket for a lump sum donation of the amount he
was willing to give. In many cases, however, it would no doubt
be found that members would be willing and able to subscribe
sixpence or a shilling a week for a certain number of weeks, and
he suggested that part of the collection should be made in this
way, and that six of the committee should be told off, one to

Mr. RANDALL said that when a scheme like this was proposed,
and he personally was on the committee, he made up his mind
that "This thing has got to go through," and the best thing to
do was to set about it, hard and fast, in the best way possible.
As the last report of the Common Room Committee showed,
they devoted £26 IOS. towards furnishing and decorating
College rooms, out of last year's balance; and with the even
better promise of the current year, he thought they would
willingly vote a substantial amount towards this fund. As a
comparatively new member, he had been struck with the amount
of self-sacrifice amongst both students and teachers here, working
unselfishly for the good of other men, in the spirit which had
dominated this College for the fifty years of its existence. He
felt that the younger students ought to put their backs into this
thing, and show their gratitude for all that had been done for
them in the past, and raise a memorial in the shape of the de-
coration of the Coffee Room. During the meeting a list had
been circulated amongst those present, which had just been
handed back to him, and it contained promises to the extent
of £25 from those present in the room. He saw no reason why
the Common Room Committee should not vote £25 or £30;
and with the help of the JOURNAL, he saw no reason why the
necessary funds should not be forthcoming in a month.
elected as secretary, he would do his very best in the matter.

carried unanimously.

treasurers of the fund, and a circular letter, drawn up by Mr.
Marks, was directed to be printed and issued to College members,
old and new, inviting them to contribute donations or weekly
subscriptions to the fund.
