OBITUARY.
SIR GODFREY LUSHINGTON.
WE much regret to have to record the death of Sir Godfrey
Lushington, KC.B., G.C.M.G, who died on February 5th, at
the age of 74. Sir Godfrey, after sixteen years' service in the
Home Office, became its Permanent Under-Secretary of State
in 1885, and continued in that office until his resignation in
1895. As Mr. Godfrey Lushington, he came to the College at the
end of the fifties with his twin brother Vernon (afterwards Judge
Lushington), and was a power in it so long as he was able to
give his time to it; and when no longer able to do this, his
influence remained, and is acknowledged to this day by the men
who knew him best in the College. Endowed by nature with
an attractive and cheery personality and a pleasing voice, he was
at that time embued with the doctrines of Carlyle, and he
heartily believed in his doctrine of work, which he not only
preached, but sought to make a living force in those with
whom he came into contact in the College. He did not content
himself with advocating Carlyle's views as to work, but he put
them into vigorous practice by his constant activity. He was
wont to warn us that we were more ready to be mindful of our
rights than of our duties. At different times he taught Arithmetic,
English Literature, Latin, and German. He not only taught
his students German, but he provided them with books. He
was a delightful teacher, and study under his guidance was a
pleasure. It was no uncommon thing in the sixties to see
Godfrey and Vernon Lushington, Arthur Cohen, and Litchfield
in the Common Room of the old College of an evening. So
much did the two brothers resemble one another, that on the
occasion of the marriage of Mr. Vernon Lushington, when we
had a tea and music to celebrate the event-in those days we
could be happy on tea and music-our then secretary, Mr.
Thomas Shorter, offered his congratulations to the wrong brother.
Sir Godfrey was present with his brother at Tansley's funeral in
1902, and he was also present at some of the Principal's lectures
on trades unions two or three years ago in Great Ormond Street.


## p. 54 (#44) ##############################################

54
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
As a member of the Old Students' Club, and a subscriber to the
JOURNAL, Sir Godfrey kept up his connection with the College
to the time of his death. Mr. H. J. Hartley, one of Sir Godfrey's
early students, and a member of the old Nineteenth Middlesex
Rifle Corps, then a printer's reader, working from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.,
Saturdays included, says-
"As an old student of the College, I was very sorry to hear of the
death of Sir Godfrey Lushington. About the year 1860, he took
the advanced Latin class, in succession to Mr. Brodribb. As myself
and Hurst, "the brushmaker" mentioned in the College History,
who died in 1862, were the only students entering, Mr.
Lushington suggested that instead of going to Great Ormond
Street, we should come to his father's house in Doctors' Commons.
Accordingly, for a couple of terms we met there twice a week, from
eight till nine o'clock in the morning, and read the 'Germania' and
'Agricola' of Tacitus, and part of the Second Book of Virgil's
'Æneid.' An excellent Latin scholar, Mr. Godfrey Lushington as
a teacher was kind and considerate; but he could not tolerate any
want of care in the preparation of exercises, and was quick to notice
any looseness of thought or inexactitude of expression. His was a
personality that ensured respect, and I think no one could come in
contact with him without being impressed with the conviction that
he was a man of strong mind and exceptional ability."
Mr. Richard Taylor says of his old teacher: “I have recollections
good and pleasant for me, and refreshing to recall now and again in
quiet moments. If any present student should wish to know how
this particular teacher struck me when I was an erratic young man,
let me say that three teachers were specially labelled by me at first
sight, Maurice was the prophet, Ruskin the poet, and Lushington the
gentleman. 'He is gentle who doeth gentle deeds.' Each was a
gentleman, but these were my labels for them at first sight; and now,
while writing this, at over three score years and ten, they are
unchanged."
Mr. J. Rigby Smith, an old student, writes: "I have a very
grateful memory of an interview he once granted me at the Home
Office. His attitude in a difficult matter was perfect, both in point
of justice and of courtesy."
In an appreciation of Sir Godfrey which appeared in the Times
of February 12th, the writer said: "It rejoiced him to call the
attention of the Secretary of State to a piece of work well done by
a junior clerk, for he seemed to feel a personal responsibility for the
younger members of the office. He loved good work and genuine
zeal; his contempt for pretentious writing and parade was complete.
He was a delightful companion, and a sound classical scholar, with an
accurate and extensive knowledge of English literature. His record
of loyalty and devotion to the public interest is one which will never
suffer by any comparison."
A poet once said that nothing endures so much as personal
qualities, and it is the personal qualities of such men as Godfrey
Lushington that have helped to make the College what it is
to-day. We owe much to him and to his brother for all their
cheerful work in helping to build up the College, for which its
members are deeply grateful, and for which they will always
reverence his memory.

JANUARY 13th, was a mild, sunny, summerlike day, and the result was
that the small party that started from Effingham Junction at 11.15, with
Leith Hill Tower as its destination and Jones's dog as its leader, had a very
enjoyable walk. We started south at a good pace across the common,
through the village, and were soon negotiating the northern slopes of White
and Effingham Hills. By this route the open is not reached until some
way down the Southern slope of White Downs, on reaching which point it
became evident that there was but little chance of a glimpse of the sea from
our destined view point. Before starting the descent, Britton left us,
proclaiming aloud his opinion that the programme would not be carried out,
but, as will be seen, he proved to be a false prophet. We descended the hill by
Leaser's Barn, past the end of Deerleap Wood, and took the road to Abinger
Church, opposite which the "Abinger Hatch" Inn proved a convenient
halting place for lunch. From this point we continued by road across the
Common, but took to the woods when safely past Parkhurst Cottages, and
reached the top of the hill at 2.30. Shoreham Gap, Lancing College, and
Chanctonbury Ring were easily made out, but the glint of the sun on the
sea, which should complete the picture, was missing. After a short halt we
struck down to the Broadmoor track, and continued through Tillingbourne
Park and the Rookery, to Westcott. Keeping to the right of the Millpond,
we then struck up the hill and found the climb exceptionally trying. By
the time we were on top, facing Ranmore Common, the light, which, owing
to the accumulating clouds, had been rapidly fading, failed us altogether,
just when we needed it most. We attempted, however, to strike across the
woods, but soon found ourselves in private grounds, in a land of notice boards
and pheasants. We accordingly beat a retreat, but so much time had been
wasted, that when we finally extricated ourselves and reached the road at
Bagden Farm, it was evident that it would be necessary to put our best pace
. on. Accordingly through the darkness we went in two parties, the dog
keeping up communications between the pacemakers and the rearguard, and
a final spurt across Bookham Common brought us to the station just in time
for the 6.14 train home. On this occasion the walk was "the thing," and
little collecting was done except by the canine member of the party. The
distance covered turned out to be something over twenty miles.
February 10th was spent in a walk to Burnham Beeches. See next
month's JOURNAL.

return ticket to Purley (S. E. R.), 18. 9d.

Woldingham, and district. Take

Cannon Street. Provide lunch.
J. HOLLOWAY, Hon. Secretary.
THE COLLEGIANS' DANCE.
ON 5th January, the "Collegians" celebrated their 21st dance, the first
that has been held in the new College. The Committee, owing to the limited
accommodation afforded by the Maurice Hall, were compelled to refuse a
large number of applicants, and for the next dance, on the 23rd of March, it
will be necessary to still further reduce the numbers, in order to ensure the
comfort of those attending.
Mr. Mellish, our College Music Teacher, supplied the band, and a very
satisfactory one it proved. The decorations were carried out under the
direction of the Misses F. and R. Reglar, with Reglar, Duchesne, and others
as assistants. Everybody who saw the hall must have felt gratified at the
artistic arrangement of bunting, Japanese fans, umbrellas, etc., and the
Committee tender their sincere thanks to all for their kindly assistance.
Mrs. Robbie surpassed herself and catered in a most able manner.
As regards the actual dance, I would refer readers to the report of the
Special Correspondent of the W.M.C. JOURNAL, in the February number.
H. K. RANDALL, Hon. Secretary of Dance Committee.

56 THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
THE JOINT CLUBS' SUPPER.
It must be a glorious thing to be a poet-to be able to take one's stand
on that exalted eminence whereon are set Tennyson, Shelley, Browning,
"Spring Onions," Homewood, and the gentle author of "Mary had a little
lamb," and give artistic verisimilitude to a bald and unconvincing narrative
by expressing one's thoughts in cadenced rhyme. I should like to be a poet;
but, alas, Nature has dealt hardly with me in that respect. A poet should be
long and lank, with hair in hyacinthine curls, and eyes that look a trifle
blank, except when gazing at the girls! But I'm a chubby little wight,
inclined to be a trifle stout, with jacket suit that fits me tight, and scrubby hair
just thinning out; and so the Muse to me is coy, and frenzy never rends my
soul (which, though not quite an unmixed joy, is rather pleasant on the
whole). I never pipe exalted strains, or into dithyrambus lapse. My friends
may say I lack the brains; my foes will say they're right, perhaps! [How's
that, Laureate ?]
But, there it is, I don't write verse, so, gentle reader, you must be
content with an account of the sixteenth annual Joint Clubs' Supper in
solemn, sombre prose. It's hard on you. I know it is, for when I wrote an
account of last year's supper in tabloid form, Tom Barnard told me it was
the best thing of mine he had ever read-it was so nice and terse. But it's
harder still on me, for the task of recalling a supper, many weeks after the
event, makes me into a kind of ruminating animal.
There are suppers and suppers. There are cosy little spreads restricted
to particular persons, and there are big official suppers where both body
and brain are refreshed. But the supper of the year, so far as the clubmen
are concerned, is the Joint Clubs' Supper, and that which took place on
December 29th, 1906, was a worthy successor to a long line of jolly
junketings. Seventy sat round the festive board, and had a right good time.
It was pleasant to see so many old faces gathered round, and seemed to
suggest the phrase, "Once a College man, always a College man." There
was Dr. Furnivall, cheery and young as ever; Perry, whiskered and witty;
Harley, momentarily oblivious to infants' foods; Hopkins, perky as in his
bachelor days; Martin-may his shadow never grow less; Tarr, returned to
the flesh-pots of Egypt, after his sojourn in the land flowing with moon and
honey; R. H. and C. H. Marks, two marks which only amount to one
Bob"; Nield, Paterson, Torrington, Barnett, Balson, Barnard, and heaps
of others. It was good also to see many a comparatively new face, and to
find oneself surrounded by vigorous, unselfish fellows, to whom the social life
of the College may be safely entrusted when the old brigade shall have shot
its bolt. The tables were laid in the Coffee Room, as it was felt that the Hall
would be rather cheerless, and Nye, Melzer, and others had succeeded in
relieving the barrenness of the walls by hanging them with holly and
evergreens. The fare was plain but pleasant; but the menu was a veritable
triumph, set out in most gorgeous French which alone was worth the money
paid for the tickets. It was a liberal education in itself, and gave such a
zest to the meal that one passed from "Consommé Crowndale" and "Bœuf
rôti à la Duchesne," to "Fromage et pain du Dent" (which sounds
suspiciously like "cheese and toothache") as in a dream. Each course was
a riddle, a mystery, a delicious dive into the unknown which made one
wonder what was coming next; but which found a substantial solution in
boiled mutton or some similar kickshaw.
Mary had some "Bœuf Duchesne,"
And then, the little glutton,
She called for "Jambe de mouton," and
They brought her boiled mutton.
After the tables had been cleared, the "Punch à la Jones-Castell" was
brought in, briars were speedily got into full blast, and then the real business
of the evening commenced. There is one perennial joy at the Joint Clubs'
Supper, and that is the toast list. Year after year some of our best men
have kinked up the grey matter in their brains in an effort to evolve an
original series of excuses for a drink. This year was no exception to the
rule. Most of the toasts put up were as searching as ever, and as mystifying
as the menu, while the victims who responded were quite as quaint and


## p. 57 (#47) ##############################################

THE JOINT CLUBS SUPPER.
57
erratic as usual-even though Gray was not present. This feature of the
proceedings is one which I would commend to the notice of students of the
theory of evolution, for it is undoubtedly an interesting example of the
survival of a barbarous custom. When primitive man sat down to a
prehistoric joint clubs' supper, his victims probably lent a relish to the
proceedings by forming the bill of fare; nowadays we sup off kickshaws, and
afterwards serve up our victims on toast.
As Pocock was not allowed to take his plate, he took the chair, and took
it in his customary good style. He had laboured hard all the afternoon,
writing out toast lists, and doing other work of a like nature; but was game
for a good speech in spite of it all. He proposed "The College," a toast
which elicited a stirring speech from our G. O. M., Dr. Furnivall. Tyler
then sang "The Toreador's Song" in fine style, after which Mead showed
that auld acquaintances were not forgotten by proposing the toast of
"Absent Friends," to which Duchesne suitably responded. The foundations
being thus laid, Perry stuck on a stratum of melody, descriptive of the doings
of "The Undergraduate" before he arrives at years of discretion and teaches
at the College, and then we had one of the puzzle toasts, "The Wet Bobs
and Bobettes," which is by interpretation the Furnivall Sculling Club.
Alternative titles were, I hear, "West's Weans" and "Paradise Regained."
Randall proposed this toast, and gave as his reason for leaving the club in
question that he had found something better to do. Landells responded
with a speech full to the brim of mysterious humour, which hugely delighted
his audience, after which E. W. Davis, having a Welsh name, naturally sang
a song about "The Old Green Isle." The toast next honoured was "This
Year's Tansley Scholar," proposed by Torrington, responded to by Wildey
(let us hope the order will be reversed next year), after which Castell urged
the holder of the honour in question to forsake his teetotal habits by putting
before him the classic doings of "The Student of Bonn."
Now, I must be careful how I handle the next few toasts, for owing to
their complex character, and the fact that speakers were warned, by means
of a footnote on the toast-list, not to exceed 9.140627 minutes, I am a bit
hazy with regard to their actual meanings. There was first of all a toast
which sounded like a geography lesson, "The Clubs-Militant and Pacific,"
with which Nield and Melzer played battledore and shuttlecock; then
Barnard gave us a little poem all about a pleasant sort of person named
"Fuzzy-Wuzzy," who is "all 'ot sand and ginger when alive," and drank
imaginary quarts out of a pint pot. [Mind how you go, Mr. Printer, this
paragraph is thickening up already!"] Then Reglar cooed of "Wooers
and Wooed-Wooed Actually and Would Be"; we understood, or thought
we could, who wooed and who wooed should be; but when Nye stood, sans
interlude, and sang "I would, I would," he, though never rude, in merry
mood, tabooed could, should and would be. [Dear, dear, we're fairly "dans le
consommé," as they say in the French class; those long vowel sounds, Mr.
Scott, have quite lost me in the wood.]
Nye was followed by Skegg, who propounded "The Riddle of the
Universe-the Ladies," and found a worthy Edipus in Cash, whose bronzed
face, silver tongue, and golden utterances added yet another cheery note to
the chequered experiences of the evening. Exigencies of space forbid me to
pursue this fascinating theme or coin fresh adjectives, so I will pass on to
say that Jones next sang "The Trumpeter," and then scooped the Cycling
Club's attendance prize. Munro then proposed a toast, much to his
amazement and our amusement, and gave us "Hymen's Haul," coupled with
the name of Tarr, our untiring pianist, who rose nobly to the bait-occasion,
I mean. Songs by Perry and Randall, “Solomon Levi" and "Who carries
the Gun" (a somewhat incongruous sequence of titles), served as a prelude
to the toast of "The Chairman," proposed by Jones, and after Pocock bad
confessed all his misdeeds and had been duly cheered, the meeting ended
with "Auld Lang Syne," sung with customary College fire.
It was a most successful evening, and, tell it not in Gath, little economies
effected by the committee resulted in a balance in hand of 15s. This I purpose
handing over to the Coffee Room Decoration Committee, if my colleagues
agree, so all will benefit by the battle of the half-crown ticket.
W. C. J.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
THE LITERARY SOCIETY.
SEVERAL College men suggested last year the foundation of an Early
English Society, and at first the idea seemed feasible enough. But Early
English is a highly technical subject, and one not likely to interest many
fellows such a Society would, therefore, be necessarily very limited, and
few papers could be obtained without outside assistance. The proposal did
not seem, then, on second thoughts, to be worth following up.
But it seemed that a College like our own ought not to be without a
permanent Literary Society. ty. We are particularly rich in literary associations:
many great names of the Victorian era are linked with our early history; and
the College possesses to-day many friends, teachers, and students who are
particularly connected with the literary world, or greatly interested in it.
The Reading Circles of the past were ephemeralities; they did good work,
but were not lasting.
In order therefore to start such a society, I called a meeting of students
on Thursday, January 24th, at 9.30 p.m., in the Clubroom. About thirty men
attended. The chair was taken by Alexander Hepburn, who improved the
shining hour by recounting drolleries to the amusement of the meeting. The
following resolution was put and unanimously carried : "That in the opinion
of this meeting a society should be formed in the College for the purpose of
discussing and reading papers on general literary subjects."
Officers were then elected. Dr. Furnivall, was unanimously chosen
President. Lionel Jacob, B.A, our Vice-Principal, A. S. Lupton, M.А.,
and H. R. Levinsohn, B.A., were similarly elected Vice-Presidents. A
ballot was held for the election of the Committee, and Hepburn, A. E.
Homewood, Landells, Reglar, Starling, and Winter, were ultimately chosen.
Munro was elected Honorary Secretary.
On Thursday, January 31st, a Committee meeting was held in the
Clubroom, Mr. Lupton presided, and Hepburn, Homewood, Landells,
Munro, and Starling were present. It was decided that the Society should
meet on alternate Thursdays during the same months as the Debating
Society, that the time of commencing should be 9.30 p.m., and that the Hon.
Secretary should arrange for a paper to be read, or an address to be given,
at each meeting, sufficient in length to occupy at least half-an-hour, when a
general discussion would follow. The Society should require no subscription,
so that any member of the College might be at once a member. The Hon.
Secretary and Committee should be annually elected.
The first meeting of the Society was held in the Coffee Room on
Thursday, February 7th, when our President, Dr. Furnivall, gave us an
address on Browning.
Dr. Furnivall, as one of the founders of the Browning Society and a
friend of the poet, was able to give us valuable reminiscences of the man, and
to tell us in particular of his manner of working and of the greatness of his
personality. Our lecturer pointed out the chief characteristics of Browning's
poetry, and the man's aspirations, ideals, love, and above all, his sterling,
invincible manliness, illustrating each point by readings from the better
known pieces of the master.
About sixty students were present, and a discussion followed, in which
our chairman, Mr. Lupton, and Dr. Jernegan, Homewood, Barnard, and
Munro took part. A hearty expression of thanks was rendered to Dr.
Furnivall for his address, and the hope was expressed that we should all open
our Brownings with renewed interest, and learn to love more the man and
his work, and see better the deep significance of his words.
On Thursday, February 21st, A. E. Homewood gave a paper on
Wordsworth.
On Thursday, March 7th, Professor Ker will read
a
paper on
Jane Austen.
On Thursday, March 21st, Mr. Levinsohn will give us a paper.
May I express the hope that all College men who are interested in
Literature will give us their assistance, and will take part in the discussions
which follow each paper?
JOHN MUNRO, Hon. Secretary.

TANSLEY SWIMMING CLUB.
THE annual general meeting of the club was held in the Club Room on
February 13th, with Mr. R. H. Marks in the chair. The secretary presented a
report of the year's work, in which he stated that the club had an active
membership of 19, and spoke of the interest taken in the club by new
members of the College. The balance sheet showed a sum of £3 4s. 8d. in
hand. Of this sum it was the unanimous wish of the meeting that £1 1s.
should be handed to the Committee for the Decoration of the Coffee Room.
It was decided to change the night of meeting to Thursday at 7.30, and to
meet in future at the Whitfield Street Baths. The president, on behalf of
the club, presented medals to R. and J. Hagerty, the winners of the scratch
race held in December last. Mr. Marks was re-elected as president;
Mr. H. R Levinsohn, vice-president; and Mr. Thos. Hopkins, handicapper and
judge. As to the captain and vice-captain, it was thought that these officers
should be elected by a race amongst the members to be held on the first
night of meeting, the first and second men respectively taking the positions
for the year. Eight members turned up at Whitfield Street on 21st February,
and all were of opinion that these baths were an improvement on those at
King Street. No one, however, seemed inclined to compete for the two
vacant offices, and the race was therefore postponed to the following week.
We shall be glad to see any swimming members of the College who can
conveniently meet us on Thursday evening, and special attention will
be given to those desiring to learn this very useful art.
H. O. DRIVER, Hon. Secretary,

SECOND-HAND BOOKS.
Every College student desirous of picking up bargains in Second Hand
Books should visit the College Library on Monday the 11th March, or the
Tuesday and Wednesday following. A considerable number of old Library
books will be on sale on those evenings. Several of the books are standard
works, and the only reason for parting with them is that they are in what the
TIMES BOOK CLUB would describe as "a condition indicating more than
six months' use."
No reasonable offer will be refused, and even unreasonable offers will
receive respectful consideration.

for kitchen utensils, £3 towards furnishing the Serving Room, and 10s. to the
Furnivall Children's Treat. This proposition was adopted.

Professor Dicey will give the concluding lecture of his course
on "The Scottish Parliament and The Union," on Thursday,
March 14th, at 8 o'clock.
We heartily congratulate our Economics teacher, Mr.
Theodore Morison, M.A., upon his having been appointed to
the Council of the Secretary of State for India, an appointment
which we understand is the highest prize to which the retired
Anglo-Indian official can aspire. Mr. Morison retired from the
Principalship of the Mahomedan Anglo-Oriental College,
Aligarh, United Provinces of India, two years ago; and he will
no doubt be able to render the Secretary of State (Mr. Morley)
much assistance in all questions of Education in India, to which
it is understood special attention is to be given in the near
future. The India Council consists of the Secretary of State
and ten members; the latter are appointed for ten years, and
receive £1200 a year each, and a pension of £500 a year at
the end of their term of office. The Council meets weekly,
and reviews the whole of the work of the administration in
India. The Times of India thus refers to Mr. Morison's
appointment:-
The appointment of Mr. Theodore Morison to the India Office Council
brings to that body an element of buoyant optimism that is not usually
supplied by its recruits. The inevitable tendency of a body composed as the
Council is, must be towards Conservatism, and towards an excessive admira-
tion for things as they are. It would be unnatural to expect men who have
passed the best years of their life in the Indian Services not to regard the
state of affairs which they left as the embodiment of human wisdom.
Mr. Theodore Morison has no such limitations. He takes the most liberal
view of the employment of Indians in the Services. He is a staunch friend of

but his pet nostrum, the manning of a province like the Berars by Indian

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
OLD STUDENTS' CLUB.
THE TAXATION OF LAND VALUES.
Mr.
AT the third meeting of this Club for the session, held at the College on
Saturday, February 2nd, a subject of present importance was discussed. Mr.
Michael Cababé, M.A., opened upon the proposition "That a special rate or
tax on Land Values is unjust, as being confiscatory in its operation."
R. H. Marks, president, took the chair and 69 members were present,
namely, Messrs. T. Barnard, B. Black, E. A. Brett, P. J. Brett, Sydney
Bradgate, J. T. Baker, G. T. Butler, G. Beavis, G. Buckland, T. M. Balson,
Michael Cababé, S. J. Coombs, A. W. Coombs, A. E. Coombs, C. G. Cash,
C. Castle, J. R. Chandler, W. J. Davis, H. C. Dumbrill, J. J. Dent, R. Eason,
H. Eyers, J. F. Frewer, Herbert Gallaher, S. B. W. Gay, Alfred Grugeon,
Godfrey C. Gümpel, E. A. Harrison, W. Hart, A. E. Homewood, E. Е.
Homewood, J. S. Homewood, W. J. Homewood, Wm. Hudson, W. R. J.
Hickman, A. Hepburn, Julius Jacob, J. W. Jenkins, W. F. Jennings,
K. Johnson, C. P. Lucas, C.B., T. Martin, W. Melzer, B. P. Moore,
E. Murphy, R. H. Marks, G. S. Offer, G. J. Offer, G. Peckham, Leonard
Pocock, Sydney Presburg, F. C. Roper, IH. K. Randall, E. J. H. Reglar,
J. Gerald Ritchie, W. A. Robinson, B. J. Rose, J. W. Roberts, Arthur B.
Shaw, E. W. Silk, M. Staal, W. J. Spray, R. E. Taylor, T. Waterhouse,
A. J. White, C. R. Williams, A. Wilshaw, Charles Wright, and G. Wanklin.
Mr. CABABE put his case so clearly and with such lucidity and exactitude,
that we are able to summarize his remarks somewhat briefly. He said the
subject of the taxation of land values had been before the public now for
some twenty years, and probably Henry George's book, on "Progress and
Poverty," first drew specific attention to it. He asked us to put aside all
party views, and come to a rational conclusion upon the economic effect of
such proposals as this. The proposal he was about to deal with was, that
there was something about land which warranted a special tax or rate being
placed on the land value. By the "land value" was meant the "site value."
Of all land which was not merely barren waste, there was a site value, apart
from the capital expenditure upon it. The capital expended might take
either the form of farming-draining, ditching, fertilizing, etc.; or putting
bricks and mortar on it-dwellings, shops, or factories for business purposes.
And the proposal was, not to put a tax on the value given by reason of the
capital expenditure, but that the site value should be taxed by a special tax,
because, it was said, the site at present escaped either altogether or partially
taxation or contribution to purposes of either imperial or local government.
He proposed to controvert that proposition, and to say that it would be
unfair, as being confiscatory, to put any such rate or tax on sites throughout
the country, apart from capital expenditure. He was not discussing the
question whether land nationalization was a good thing or not, either by
taxing up to 20s. in the pound, or otherwise, or by buying out the owners,
which would appear to be the proper plan, if such a thing were decided upon.
If it would lead to that earthly paradise all of us desired, it would be a cheap
method; but whether it would do so, was another matter. That was not,
however, before us for discussion. The point of view from which, as practical
men, we must approach the question before us was this all countries seemed
to have found that for their economic development, it was necessary to
recognize private property, not only in capital and the other instruments of
production, but also in land. Having private property in land, it was but
right that it should be subject to taxation, and should contribute its proper
share to public expenditure. But all owners of property should contribute
their fair share or quota to the public expenditure of the country. That was
the object of taxation. It was not the object of taxation to raise funds not
required for public purposes, in order to rectify what any person might think
to be errors in the distribution of wealth. Now, the question, Did land so
contribute? lay on the threshold of our enquiry. It was expedient to
consider what might be the site value of the United Kingdom. Taking the
existing land with all its buildings, etc., upon it, we found, from income tax


## p. 63 (#53) ##############################################

OLD STUDENTS CLUB.
63
returns and other sources, what its annual value was. We then took the cost
of building the houses, etc., and ascertained what annual sum represented
that expenditure, and deducting this from the annual value, arrived at the
site value. With the help of Mr. Money's figures, he placed upon all urban
property the site value of fifty millions a year, of which London represented
about fifteen millions, and the rest of the towns thirty-five or thirty-six
millions, as the annual value of the sites. That site value was really centred
in the small area of less than one million acres. We might eliminate entirely
agricultural land, the enormous bulk of the land of the country. In the case
of ricultural land, there was no unearned increment, but a very considerable
decrement. And economists seemed agreed that in its case, the ultimate
incidence of the rates was pretty obviously on the landlord, and not on the
farmer. Now, a rate of 2s. in the pound on fifty millions would be five
millions a year. Taking that as a suggestion, merely for the purposes of
argument, would it be fair to put a special tax on site values by which that
fifty millions would be reduced to forty-five millions, or not? At the very
threshold of the problem lay the question, Did the sites now contribute to the
public burdens as they should? And what would be the effect of such a
special tax as was proposed? Could you put on such a tax at all, so as to
make the owner for the time being pay it, or not? If you could not, and if
it transcended the wit of man to devise a means by which you could make
the site-owner for the time pay that special tax, and if the levying of such
a tax amounted merely to a deduction from the capital value of the present
owner's property-if he (the opener) could establish that, he should have
gone some way to establish his proposition. So far as imperial taxation was
concerned, we need not trouble ourselves. All property-rents, dividends,
profits of business, or what not-was already taxed in the same way, fairly and
equitably, for imperial purposes.
So far as the owners of site values and
ground rents were concerned, imperial taxation, whether by income tax,
death duties, or any other mode of contribution, dealt with them in the
same way as other kinds of property. Passing to local taxation, and
considering how rates were made, and what their incidence really was-we
found about forty millions a year levied as rates, the greater bulk of it coming
from the central town districts, where the wealth of the country arose.
The view as to their incidence generally adopted was that of Lord Goschen,
that all rates ultimately fell upon the land-owner. But he, Mr. Cababé,
thought that must be wrong; and that Lord Goschen omitted to appreciate
the distinction between the site value and the house value. The house was
a shelter built for the benefit of the occupier. A great many, though of
course not all, of the purposes for which rates were levied, were for the
distinct benefit of the occupier. The person catered for, in sanitary work,
paving, lighting, etc., was the occupier, and upon him necessarily fell the
expense. It was quite otherwise with regard to the site. There was no
local capital expenditure for it. The landlord was extremely anxious to have
his land built upon. There was constant competition between land-owners
to have their land covered. (No, no.) As soon as they saw their chance to
make ground rents, they did, in twenty cases out of twenty-one. He could
not see any means by which to shift a rate on to the site. It could not be
done otherwise than by creating a rent-charge, subject to which the land
would be sold. There was the increase of capital value due to the building
of the house; and the rates upon that naturally fell upon the consumer or
person catered for. But the rate upon the site would be a deduction from
the ground rent which the landlord could otherwise have claimed. The
land owner would be obliged to take, even for the most choice and picked
sites, such a sum as he could obtain, in competition, less the amount of the
rate to impinge upon the site value. If we put such a tax as was suggested,
upon the ground rent or site value, all we should do would be to take so
much of the capital value of the present owner's property, and nothing else.
Mr. Cababé put the case of a house, on which the ground rent was £24 a
year. If a tax of 2s. in the pound were put on it, the ground rent, instead
of being worth £24, would be worth £21 125. a year, and if then sold,
would fetch a less price than before the tax. The whole loss would fall on


## p. 64 (#54) ##############################################

64
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
the present owner; the purchaser would not feel it, and would not, although
owner for the time being, bear the burden of the tax at all. If a special
tax were put on any other kind of property, such as bank shares, for example,
they would fall in value in the same way. The holder for the time being
would suffer, but subsequent owners would not.
The result of such a tax
would be simply to confiscate part of the capital interest of the present
owners. That would be unfair. (Cheers.)
The usual adjournment for refreshments took place.
Mr. S. J. CoOMBS, who opened the debate, thought that Mr. Cababé
had proved himself an excellent advocate for the ground landlord, whom
Providence had placed in an unjustifiably fortunate position, but that he
had forgotten to take into consideration the occupiers' point of view.
Mr. Coombs objected to the word "confiscation." It had been applied to
every measure aiming at the profits of what he called gambling. When
Mr. Goschen got a measure passed reducing Consols from 3 ultimately to
2, that was "confiscation by Act of Parliament, and Mr. Coombs
proposed to go to Parliament in order to get at site values. One of our
difficulties was the numerous systems of land tenure. All legislation with
regard to land had been introduced by landowners from the agricultural
point of view. Since we had become a manufacturing and commercial
country, we had got an urban and a suburban tenure, and the present difficulty
was that we were governed by the suburban method. Those gentlemen who
happened to have large urban sites were the lucky people. Work which was
necessary to make property tenantable, or which enormously improved its
value, was done for them by the occupiers, yet it had been admitted that they
did not pay local rates. It was a fiction to say that landowners did not
hold their land for a rise, and were only too anxious to lease it. Ground
rents, like everything else, were subject to supply and demand. If an owner
built on his land prematurely, the property was likely to become derelict.
In this question of the taxation of ground rents, it was an absolute necessity
that something should be given to the occupier. Why should he be forced
to live in a certain class of house, and pay every penny of the cost of services
which added to the value of the land in every form? Wherever a park was
opened, for instance, the value of the land around was increased; and
though the benefit of it was deferred, immediately the lease fell in, up went
the ground rent. It was time that the people of this country made up their
minds that they would not be taxed out of existence; and that they should
try to saddle the right horse, which was the gentleman who had had the luck
to enjoy site values created by the people themselves.
Mr. HART said that with regard to "confiscation," the boot was on
the other leg; that the land was the people's; that they should tax the land-
lord, instead of letting the landlord tax them in the shape of rent; and that
they should ultimately get back their own. He pointed out how others
besides ground landlords got incomes out of the existing system, and instanced
a case in which a lessee at £600 a year sublet a portion only of his holding
for £1,200.
Mr. WRIGHT thought Mr. Cababé might now have arrived at the
conclusion that it was unwise to use the word "confiscation." Confiscation
had been defined as appropriation of private property to the sovereign or
public treasury. If that was confiscation, it seemed to him that all taxation
was confiscation, and that what Mr. Cababé meant was that the particular
form of taxation in question was inequitable. If the word "inequitable" were
used in all such discussions, it would help matters, because "confiscation"
was a question-begging word, indicating a grievance at the outset. He was
in agreement with the opener, that a tax specially aimed at land would be
inequitable. The whole question of taxation was one of immense difficulty,
and he hoped he would not be considered transgressing if he trenched upon
it in general. The opener had laid down what was to Mr. Wright a very
provocative proposition, when he said that it was not the object of taxation
to redress inequalities. He (Mr. Wright) thought that the great problem before
the community was how to reduce the frightful inequalities which existed, with-
out reducing the totality of wealth. Any proposal to reduce inequalities which

would stand the test he suggested, he should consider a good one. He was
of opinion that the whole problem of rating wanted overhauling. The
present system was a haphazard and highly unsatisfactory method of raising
funds for the necessary expenses of the community. To put the same tax on
a man in connection with his business as upon a man keeping up a merely

be found which would press equally upon the community in proportion to

without sympathy for ground landlords, great or small. He had no particular
sympathy with the owners of any kind of property, and he claimed no

would only be plundering in the sense of one class being singled out from
the others. We had in the Income Tax and Death Duties an admirable
method of getting hold of every property-owner in existence. If money was
wanted, that was the way to get it. People would never be convinced that
they were being subjected to injustice, if taxation was in proportion to

Mr. RANDALL said Mr. Cababé had been careful to explain what site
value was, and had instanced a house rented at £200 a year, £50 of which
he had put down as site value; but he had not told us how that site value
was created. Mr. Randall thought it was created by the competitive needs
of the people, and the improvements effected by the rates they paid. He
could not see therefore that it would be confiscation to put say a 5 per cent.
tax on that £50. He thought Henry George's views of land nationalization
were out of date. It was impracticable to tax the landlord out of existence;
we must buy him out. It was the only just way, and it would be a cheap
way for the country. Municipal authorities should have power to buy land
where they could in town areas. Professor Kirkaldy had been lecturing on
Political Economy at the College, and shared the view that the landlord did
pay the rates. He had supported his view by instancing the case of his own
house in Birmingham. A tramway had been run down his street, and as it
decreased his enjoyment of the house, whilst the rates were going up, he was
going to demand from his landlord a reduction of rent, which he would
probably think it wise to grant, owing to the decreased competition for the
premises.
Mr. EASON pointed out that previous speakers had overlooked the
important fact that the municipalities were spending huge sums of money on
public undertakings, which would have to be paid off by the people through
the rates within sixty years, when they would naturally expect the rates to
fall. But the lower the rates the higher the ground-rent; and under existing
conditions the landlord, when his leases fell in, would reap the whole of the
benefit of the immense asset which the municipalities were building up.
Mr. A. B. SHAW agreed with nearly all Mr. Cababé's arguments, but
differed from his conclusions. Mr. Shaw thought that the existing owner
did pay the existing rate, but that a special tax ought to be laid upon him
because the expenditure which made towns habitable and attracted popula-
tion, increased the competition for and consequently the value of the land;
and it was not confiscation for the State to take out of the land what it had
temporarily put into it. He thought we had a complete analogy in what
happened at the beginning of last century, when Mr. Pitt raised money for
the expenses of the European wars by a land tax of 4s., rising to 6s.,
redeemable at 20 years' purchase. This question of site values was not
merely one of dukes and earls. He himself was enjoying a large part of the
site value of his house, because he paid to an earl a much lower ground rent

than the site was worth. Such a tax as was suggested should fall on all
who were lucky enough to be enjoying the increased value of sites, which
was brought about by rate expenditure; diture; and the fact that it had been so long

Mr. RITCHIE said we were on the very threshold of municipal improve.
ment, and infinitely behind what we ought to be. We were doing something
to make our cities habitable and worthy of Englishmen. It was notorious
that occupiers could not pay any more towards this end, and he thought the
ground landlords would not regard it as confiscatory, if they were asked to
share. (Laughter.) He would refer Mr. Cababé to Berlin, where they taxed
site values with excellent results. Anybody who had travelled in Germany
knew the contrast that German towns presented to ours. In New Zealand
they were taxing site values, and he considered them a proper subject for
taxation, because municipal improvements like parks, drainage, etc., went to
raise site values; and as these went up, it was most equitable that they should
pay for the increased profits which accrued. It seemed to him that it was
impossible to dispute the equity of that. The fact that the rates at present
fell upon the occupiers was a mere accident. The rate laws were introduced
before the great industrial development of this country, and circumstances
having changed, it was right that there should be a redistribution of this
burden. The hard part of the case would be that of the small investors who
paid heavy occupancy rates, but the tax might be made a progressive one.
He believed that the area of London owned by the great landlords was very
much greater than had been suggested. Enormous profits must accrue to
Lord Cadogan, for instance, from Chelsea, owing to the construction of a
magnificent embankment; and it was not only what the municipalities did,
but every form of industry, tubes, railways, motor busses, etc., went to raise
site values enormously. He really did not think that the fortunate gentlemen
who were in the position of owning such site values would complain, if they
had to bear a slight increase of taxation. (Laughter.) He held a small site
value himself, and he would not complain, and he did not think his neigh-
bours would complain, if they had to bear a larger share of taxation.
(Applause.)
Mr. CASH was strongly in favour of the taxation of site values. If
there was confiscation, it was on the part of the ground landlord. He reaped
the benefit of municipal improvements, and the occupiers paid for them.
Landowners, large or small, should be made liable for a part of the local
rates. The occupier groaned under his burdens, and not only so, but on the
expiration of a lease which might previously have been comparatively
valueless, the landlord might decline to renew it except at an enormously
increased rental, in respect of a value which he had done nothing to enhance.
The London ratepayer had now to meet expenses which were greater than he
could bear. New sources of revenue must be found, and this one of site
values was easy to work. In view of the great municipal struggle that was
impending in London, it was imperative to advocate every means of resisting
the men who would tighten our burdens upon us, and deliver us over to trusts
and monopolies.
Mr. GUMPEL said the essential point was, Why was the site value of
London so high? What was the difference between a house, say, in the
middle of Camden Town, and a piece of ground in the suburbs? The sole
difference was that in the one place people had come to live, and in the other
they had not. It followed, then, that the site value was created by the people,
and he thought he might fairly say that Henry George's position was logical.
What was created by the people belonged to the people, and all the confisca-
tion was on the side of the landlord. Therefore, a tax even to extinction was
perfectly logical and perfectly just.
Mr. S. BRADGATE agreed with Mr. Shaw that Mr. Cababé's arguments
were fairly good, but that his conclusions did not commend themselves.
Mr. Bradgate thought that such a tax as was proposed would not be
inequitable, but he doubted whether after all it would enable us to enter into
our inheritance. If we put a tax on the owners of site values, would not

they get it back in the rent? How were we to prevent them from raising
their rents, if we put a tax on them? Then again, the proposal was on all
fours with the question of betterment. The argument that a man should pay
a site tax, because the value of his land had been increased by improvements
in his neighbourhood, was on all fours with the argument that where

Mr. MOORE said he had not been able to come in time to hear the
greater part of Mr. Cababé's opening, but he had heard the conclusion, in
which it was pointed out that the taxation of a site value involved the
deprivation of the present holder of a certain amount of the capital value
of his property. [Mr. Cababé interposed that it fell wholly upon the present
holder, and not at all upon subsequent purchasers and investors.] Mr.
Moore continued that he would just like to point out that on a smaller scale
that had already been done in the last few years. We had a small property
tax at the present moment. For years that tax had stood at 8d. in the pound.
A few years ago our Park Lane friends had plunged us into an absurd war,
and the Income Tax shot up to Is. Surely, all subsequent transactions in
property had been based on the assumption that a shilling property tax was
about what was to be taken into account in making a transaction; and it
seemed to him that on a very small scale we had in that case the
circumstances which the opener so deplored. [Mr. Cababé again interposed
that his argument was against a special tax on one form of property, in contra-
distinction to others.] In regard to that, Mr. Moore wished to point out,
in reply to the gentleman who had maintained that it was wrong to tax one
type of rich men and not another, that other rich men in almost all cases
did a good deal for the community-our great manufacturers and so on.
They were of course allowed to absorb a quite undue share of the profits of
their concerns, but it seemed to him that while they did a great deal for the
community, the great ground landlord did nothing at all; he was purely a
leech. He simply sat sucking millions out of the pockets of London, without
contributing a single shred to the value of the land on which the city stood;
and that seemed to him to differentiate the rich ground landlord from every
other class of rich man in the community, and to justify his being singled out
for exceptional treatment.
Mr. CABABE, in closing the debate, thanked the meeting very sincerely
for the interesting discussion. It was a great satisfaction to him to find that
it had been quite unnecessary for him at the commencement to ask those
present to enter upon it free from class bias. In the observations that had
been made in support of the view that there was ground for exceptional treat-
ment of site values, there lurked a certain fallacy. It had been admitted that
they contributed, and contributed largely, to existing rates; but it was said
that site values themselves were created by the rates. He thought that was
nonsense. How could it be said that the poor rate and education rate
increased ground rents? Certain rates, sanitary rates for instance, were for
services which the householder could not do without. It had been said that
he ought not to be liable for them, because they were necessary to make the
landlord's property tenantable. But they were on the same footing as the
service which was rendered for the tenant in the protection of his dwelling.
What was it, then, that enhanced the value of landed property? Many
things might bring that about. It might suddenly be found that there was
an opening for a good harbour in connection with the property; or coal
might be found near it; or a railway might come through it; or it might
become a convenient centre, through the normal play of industrial forces.
And the benefit that accrued from these was in no way confined to the
ground landlord; it went chiefly to the lucky people who found that it paid
them to give high rents out of the profits and interest on the capital they
invested there. Mr. Cababé emphasized his conviction that to single out for
taxation one form of private property from another was not the way to real
reform.

PROPOSED CLUB RULES.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR MR. POCOCK, -Annexed is a copy of some proposed rules drawn
up by the Common Room Committee, which are intended to apply to all
College Clubs in the future, provided they receive the sanction of the Clubs
and Executive Committee.
The rules were drawn by my Committee after correspondence with the
Executive Committee, who proposed that we should consult the College Clubs
upon them. We are in consequence calling a general meeting of the Clubs,
to be held in the Common Room on Monday, March 11th, at 9.30 p.m.,
when Mr. Sydney Bradgate will take the chair, and the rules will be
submitted for discussion, and will I hope be accepted by the members of the
different College Clubs unanimously.
A perusal of the draft will, I am sure, convince you that the manner in
which they are framed is an honest attempt to bring all the Clubs into line,
and to give them a much stronger attachment to the College as a whole.
Then again we have provided for the safeguarding of Club finances. This
of course is a most delicate subject to handle, but I trust that all Clubites will
view the proposition in the spirit in which it is proposed, namely, to relieve
private members of the College of the responsibility for the safety of their
Club funds. Lest some Clubites should think that these proposed rules are
an attempt to lower their prestige, I may say at once that this is farthest
from our thoughts, our one and sole idea being to centralize Club finance and
make one common banker for all Clubs.
There is no rule which in any other way attempts to interfere with or
control Club privileges, and I trust the meeting will see we only wish to
prevent "regrettable incidents" in Club life, for it is no use regretting after
the incidents have arisen, and the responsibility for any "incidents" which
may occur in the future will rest on the shoulders of anybody who attempts
to reject or wreck the rules. -Yours sincerely, H. K. RANDALL,
Hon. Secretary, Common Room Committee.
PROPOSED RULES AS TO COLLEGE CLUBS.
1. The Superintendent of the College and the Common Room
Committee shall be notified of any meeting at which it is intended to
commence a Club or Society in the College.
2. Every Club shall hold a General Meeting at least once in each year,
and in the event of such general meeting not being held, the Common Room
Committee shall call a general meeting.
3. A report of every annual general meeting shall be sent to the
Secretary of the Common Room Committee, and shall also be forwarded to
the Editor of the COLLEGE JOURNAL for publication within one week.
4. All officers of a Club shall be elected by ballot by the members of
the Club at a general meeting of the Club, but in the event of a vacancy
afterwards occurring, the Committee shall have power to co-opt a member of
their Club to fill such vacancy.
5. Every Club shall have a Committee, Secretary, and Treasurer,
elected annually at the annual general meeting.
6. The Superintendent of the College shall be an ex-officio member of
the Committee of every College Club, but shall not be entitled to vote
thereon.
7. No person who has not been a member of the College for two
consecutive terms shall be eligible to hold office in any Club.
8. Every valuable asset belonging to any Club shall be lodged with the
Superintendent of the College, unless otherwise provided for by the
Superintendent.


## p. 69 (#59) ##############################################

CORRESPONDENCE.
69
9. The funds of each Club shall be lodged with the Superintendent of
the College as Banker, except so much thereof for immediate use and petty
expenses as is permitted by the Committee of each Club.
10. The Secretary of each Club shall keep proper minutes of all
Committee and General meetings; and shall present a balance sheet at each
annual general meeting of the Club, which shall be presented to the meeting
for adoption.
11. Two independent Auditors shall be selected by the Committee of
each Club to audit each account presented at the annual general meeting of
the Club.
12. If the majority of the Committee of any Club shall decide that
an extraordinary general meeting of their Club is necessary, they shall
appoint one of their number to call such an extraordinary general meeting
on an agreed date, in the event of the Secretary refusing or neglecting to call
such meeting within seven days after notification from his Committee so
to do.
13. The Common Room Committee shall see that these rules are duly
carried out, and shall report any defaulting Club to the Executive Committee.
SUNDRY GRIEVANCES AND SUGGESTIONS.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR MR. EDITOR, -Will you allow a student of the College room in the
JOURNAL for a short ventilation of one or two of his grievances? A few
nights ago our Instructor made earnest appeal to the students in the Book-
keeping class to subscribe towards the fund for the Decoration of the Coffee
Room. One of the students promptly stood up, and after a short speech in
favour of the College, subscribed 5s. It was at once taken up by the other
students, and I believe that a sum of about £2 2s. was subscribed in all.
But in his few remarks this student mentioned a difficulty which I think
might be obviated. He said that although our Instructor had on many
occasions alluded to the good fellowship which existed between students and
teachers in the College, yet nevertheless he had been attending the College
for about four months, and had often been in the Common Room, but no one
had yet spoken to him, or appeared desirous to make his acquaintance. This
is not only his experience, but that of other students as well as myself. We
can hardly expect during the class time to become much acquainted with one
another. We want to personally know our Instructor, and he wants to
personally know us, but we have very little opportunity of doing so.
Could it not be arranged that our class should close up at 8.15, re-open
again at 8.30, and go on to a quarter to ten? Then it would give us an
opportunity of a quarter of an hour's meeting in the Common Room. It
would be a welcome break to the students, and also a very welcome break to
our Instructor. He must often feel very tired after two and a half hours'
continuous teaching.
Then, too, it would be an advantage if better arrangements could be
made for the supply of refreshments in the Coffee Room. I have many times
been at the College as early as twenty minutes to seven, and it has been
nearly five minutes to seven before I have been able to get my tea. If in
the interval between 8.15 and 8.25, we could promptly get a cup of coffee
without waiting, it would certainly be a very great advantage. It would give
the students in the class an opportunity of talking with one another. It
would enable us to know our Instructor and our Instructor to know us, and
promote good fellowship and good feeling all round.
This perhaps you may consider a matter worth ventilating through your
valuable JOURNAL. - Yours, etc.,
NORTH LONDON BOAT CLUB,

W.M.C. DEBATING SOCIETY.
ON Tuesday, 8th January, Mr. George F. Shee, M.A., the Secretary of
the National Service League, moved, "That the adoption of Universal
Military Training for National Defence is a just and necessary measure."
Briefly, the scheme of the opener was that instruction in the use of the rifle
and physical training of a military character should form part of the curri-
culum of all schools; and that every able-bodied youth should be compelled
to undergo three months' military training every year between the ages of
18 and 21, at the expense of the State. This, he argued, would free the
standing army from the work of home defence, and would be the best means
of ensuring peace and security for the British Empire, as it would show that
we were prepared for war, and would insure that, should war break out, the
whole national forces might be brought to bear, in order speedily to
re-establish peace. Colonel Keene was in attendance and supported Mr.
Shee. Mr. Torrington, in opposing, tackled the opener's arguments with his
customary thoroughness, and made the fullest use of all the objections to
the scheme. He was supported, amongst others, by a very strong speech
from Mr. C. E. Maurice. The motion produced a warm discussion, and was
ultimately carried by a majority of one; the voting being 25 against 24.
On 15th January, Mr. Fred. Willis, S.D.F., an old member of the
College, proposed, "That Social-Democracy is not only eminently desirable,
but also immediately practicable." Mr. Willis is a fluent speaker, and he
laid his case before the House very clearly and skilfully. He stated that in
his opinion the existing capitalist system was detrimental to the vast body
of the community, that it was the direct cause of unemployment, and that,
while it benefited a few to a great and unnecessary extent, it entailed
considerable waste of labour and hardship on the worker. He urged that, in
place of the capitalist system, the means of production, distribution, and
exchange should be placed in the hands of the people, to be used by them for
the benefit of the whole, instead of for the benefit of the few He looked
forward to the time when the growing desire for a better life for the worker,
and the change from capitalist misery to socialist plenty and happiness,
would be realized. The opposition was in the able hands of Mr. Merriman,
who, while admitting that the present social system was certainly not
satisfactory, opposed Social-Democracy as being altogether inadequate.
Moreover, there was no guarantee whatever that the State would administer
the business of the country more efficiently than private enterprize; and
apart from a host of other practical objections, the root objection to Social-
Democracy was that it overlooked half of human nature altogether. The
discussion which followed was of a most interesting character; and the
motion was ultimately carried by 34 votes to 21.
On 22nd January, Mr. Rigby-Smith opened the discussion by moving,
"That the present literary practice creates monopoly of publicity, buries
information, and thus cripples the student." Apart from the attractive
nature of the subject, the occasion was made particularly interesting by the
presence of Mr. C. E. Maurice to oppose the motion. Mr. Smith sought to

FURNIVALL SCULLING CLUB.
THE month of January was an extremely busy one for us on the river, in
spite of the very changeable nature of its weather. The number of members
joining in the Sunday excursions to the New Inn goes up by leaps and
bounds.
On Sunday, 30th December, two light fours went up, the first having
Munro stroke, West 3, Owen 2, Dr. Furnivall bow, Kate Lock cox; the
second having Peckham stroke, Sammons 3, Lizzie Skinner 2, Dewar bow,
Castell cox. Sunday, 6th January, was a beautiful early spring day, but only
one boat turned out from the Club, a four consisting of Freddie Hogh
stroke, Allen 3, Jack Owen 2, the Doctor bow, Nye cox, for the pull to
Richmond against a sharp tide. The following Sunday was another lovely
day, and the Club had out a sculling eight, two fours, and a pair. January
20th proved a very unfavourable day, for tide and things did not look very
promising, and but few members turned up. After a lot of head-shaking,
these eventually decided that they would at all events get into the boat and
pretend to scull. However, all being College men and therefore having
consciences, when they did start, the boat went up to Richmond in to use
the words of the Doctor-very fair, and of course that means very good
style.
All were looking forward to February 3rd, when the Social in honour of
the Doctor's birthday was held.
JOHN B. WEST, Hon. Secretary.

SATURDAY NIGHT LECTURES.
DIRT, DAMP, AND DISEASE.
On January 19th, a lecture was given at the College under the above
title, by Sir Patrick Manson, medical adviser to the Colonial Office. The
chair was occupied by Major-General Sir J. Frederick Maurice, K.C.B., son
of our Founder.
Sir PATRICK MANSON, in the course of his address, said that it was stated
of Governments, and particularly of the British Government, that they were
slow to encourage scientific research; but his experience was to the contrary,
the Colonial Office having, by sympathy and financial assistance, done much
for the cause of tropical medical study. It was a mistake to regard dirt and
damp as almost synonymous with disease. The relation of the first two to the
last was definite, but not direct. Dirt and damp operated in causing disease,
not because certain places were dirty or damp, but because in places which
were dirty and damp there existed germs which produced disease. Having
referred to the ravages of plague-by which 44 millions of persons had
perished in India since 1898-Sir Patrick said that it was a man's disease only
by accident. Plague was really a rat's disease, as stated in the Bible; and as
dirt encouraged rats, dirt indirectly caused plague. The plague germ could
only affect a body when inoculated into it. The question was-How did the
germ pass from the rats to men? Like human beings, rats were apt to be
attacked by parasites, especially fleas, and when these insects became
impregnated with disease, they conveyed it to human beings. The flea which
sucked the blood of the plague-infested rat also sucked the blood of man.
A recent Commission in India had proved experimentally that horses, dogs,
monkeys, guinea pigs, and rats were all capable of being inoculated with
plague by means of fleas. A clean house was usually a healthy house. Dirt
harboured other things besides rats and rat fleas, and from these other
sources arose diphtheria and typhoid.
Speaking of damp, the lecturer said that influenza and rheumatism were
not due to damp, but to germs which lived in damp surroundings. In tropical
climates people suffered from malaria. How did damp foster malaria? The
answer was that malaria germs lived in damp surroundings-germs had as
much right to live as human beings (laughter) and mosquitoes, which became
impregnated with malaria germs, attacked men and thus infected them with
the germ. Now that the cause of malaria had been discovered, he had not
the slightest doubt that within a reasonable period much of the present
uninhabitable, because insanitary, part of the British dominions would become
healthy. It was now established that the agents of infection were insects-
bugs, fleas, and lice.
The chairman, in proposing a vote of thanks to Sir Patrick Manson for
his lecture, said that the Colonial Office owed the lecturer a debt of gratitude
for his discoveries. When Colonial Secretary, Mr. Chamberlain said that
those who could restore health to great provinces of the Empire did more
than to conquer. The vote was enthusiastically carried. (Standard.)
The Lectures for March are:-

PRICE TWOPENCE.
PROPOSED CLUB RULES.
HE Common Room Committee committed an error
of judgment in drawing up and presenting to the
members of the College Clubs, in the manner in
which they did last month, the proposed fundamental
rules for the government of all clubs in the College.
At all events, if we may judge from the derision with which the
proposed rules and those members of the Committee who
supported them were received at the meeting held on
March 11th, the rules could scarcely have been introduced in a
way less likely to command the respect and adherence of the
members. This is a pity, because the real issue is to some
extent lost sight of, when sarcasm and contumely are provoked
and inveighed against the authors of such a measure, as they
were at the meeting in question. The Coffee Room was filled
with the better known students, who were presided over by
Mr. Pocock. The discussion of the proposed rules was opened
by Mr. H. K. Randall, hon. secretary of the Common Room
Committee, who explained that his Committee had been
requested by the Executive to formulate and present to them a
set of rules, after consulting the members of the clubs upon
them. He spoke in support of the rules, as printed in last month's
JOURNAL, dividing his remarks under three heads,-(i.) the
desirability of having each club's existence formally notified to
the Superintendent and Common Room Committee; (ii.) the
necessity of seeing that each club held a general meeting yearly;
and (iii.) the advisability of a general banker or custodian being
provided for club funds and assets. Mr. Randall was frequently
interrupted during his remarks, and all his supporters shared a
like fate. There appeared to be considerable objection to the
attitude taken up by the Common Room Committee, in proposing
to constitute themselves the authority which should be notified
of the formation of clubs, should have power to convene general
eetings, and should see that the rules were duly carried out.
hough Mr. Randall pointed out that the powers proposed
to be exercised by the Common Room Committee might, by
amendment. be allocated to any Committee which the Clubs


## p. 74 (#66) ##############################################

74
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
might appoint, it was evident that the members present had
their backs up, and that they keenly resented the manner in
which the proposed rules were formulated.
After Mr. Randall's remarks, the chairman suggested that it
should first be settled whether the rules should be taken and
discussed separately or as a whole. Mr. W. C. Jones proposed
that the principle of the rules should first be discussed. Mr.
J. J. Munro (C. R. C.) moved, and Mr. A. Hepburn (C. R. C.)
seconded, that they be discussed in sections, rule I. first, then
rules II. and III., then IV. to VII., and so on. Mr. T. Barnard
asked whether the Shakespeare readers came within the rules;
and Mr. Randall replied that they would not, until they levied
a subscription.
Mr. Castell said the real gist of the matter
lay in rules VIII. and IX., as to custody of club funds and assets.
He objected to the Common Room Committee, however, being
the body appointed to carry out any such rules. The secretary
or one other member of each club should form a committee
to carry them out. Mr. A. E. Homewood, rising to move an
amendment, described the Common Room Committee as an
egregious gang of outrageous swankers," at which there was
much laughter and loud cries of "withdraw." He protested
against the proceedings as a whole. The Committee were a
parcel of students, more or less irresponsible, and he objected
to their having the control of the clubs. He proposed that the
Executive be asked to furnish a statement of the existing rules
of the clubs, and moved that the proposed rules be rejected
by the meeting. This motion was not accepted in that form,
and was altered to an amendment that the rules be discussed
en bloc. Mr. Jones seconded the amendment, and referred to
the previous attempts made, under his guidance, to introduce
fundamental rules for the College clubs, not many years ago.
A set of rules was then agreed to by the secretaries of the clubs,
and approved by the Executive, but when referred to the club
members for their acceptance, they threw them out and declined
to be governed by them. He now urged that the proposed
rules were unnecessary, and that they would fail in their object
to protect club funds. He considered them tactless, and thought
each club must be left to legislate for itself. The amendment
was put, and carried by a large majority.
Mr. J. C. Castell then moved, and Mr. W. C. Jones seconded,
that the rules be rejected en bloc as unnecessary. Mr. Munro,
amidst much interruption, endeavoured to meet Mr. Jones's
statements. Mr. Munro referred to an application made by the
Club and Institute Union for the club rules, and thought this
was a reason for codifying them. Mr. Dent explained that the
Union did not want the rules of the College clubs, but those
of the Common Room, which was affiliated to the Union, whilst
the College clubs were not. Mr. Hepburn quaintly suggested
the Committee should wear badges. Mr. Torrington (C. R. C.)
protested against the affair being treated as a huge joke; he

thought the rules necessary, and that they should be referred to

THE SHAKESPEARE READINGS.
ANOTHER "LADIES" NIGHT.
FEBRUARY 3rd. - "The Taming of the Shrew." There were eighteen
of us and we spent a very pleasant evening. The play, in reading, didn't
cause so much fun as we anticipated. A good deal of the humour is due
to actor's "business" and stage properties." These, of course, were
missing. Some of the descriptive lines made amends for this the pictures
of Petruchio, his horse, and his servant Grumio, for instance.
"
Gates Fowler read the part of Petruchio with the requisite boldness, and
Paterson expressed the Shrew's moods with much skill. The note of sub-
mission in Kate's final speech was touching. It contrasted strangely with
recent utterances on the woman-question. M. K. Field spoke well as
Baptista,
New readers continue to join us. Among recent additions we welcome
Messrs. Buckland, Brett, Manton, E. W. Davis, and Eyres.
February 17th.-"Richard III." A very large audience assembled,
attracted mainly, I think, by a powerful cast. The attendance, numbering
nearly fifty, exceeded any in my recollection.
Our good friend Mrs. Tansley was present, together with Mrs. and
Miss Peck, Miss Steptoe, and Miss L. Walford. Prominent among the
visitors were Mr. and Mrs. Holroyd-Chaplin, introduced by Mr. Peck,
who came with a lengthy experience of Shakespeare Readings in a kindred
Society. Mrs. Holroyd-Chaplin added to our enjoyment by kindly reading
Duchess of York.
Peck, in the title-part, succeeded well in bringing out Richard's
wonderful character-his hypocricies, his ruthfulness, his grim humour.
We were singularly fortunate in our lady readers. All the parts were in
good hands. Mrs. Tansley read Queen Elizabeth; Miss Walford, Queen
Margaret; Miss Steptoe, Lady Anne. The scene with the young princes,
undertaken by Miss Peck and Miss Forsythe, was very pleasing. For Clarence
we were indebted to Paterson, and for the two murderers to A. E. Homewood
and Gates Fowler. Fenton was a vigorous Richmond; Barnett, Hastings;
and Barnard, Buckingham. The rest of a long cast had little to say.
some had nothing at all, as big cuts became imperative near the close of
the meeting.
Indeed
March 3rd.-"As You Like It." A capital attendance, including
one or two readers likely to prove great acquisitions, notably Mayhew, who
read the part of the banished Duke. Paterson was Rosalind; Gates Fowler,
Orlando; and Barnard, Jaques. Hayward, as usual, amused us very much
as Touchstone, which he read at very short notice. To Barnett, Paterson,
and Homewood, we were indebted for songs and music.
Paterson very kindly undertakes the arrangements for the first meeting
of the Shakespeare Readings next season as Barnard is giving up the
Presidency, owing to increased pressure of private work.
For the final College Reading this season, on April 28th, ladies are
invited. In accordance with custom, on this occasion, we forsake Shakespeare
for Sheridan. The play selected is "The School for Scandal."

THE WORKING_MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
W.M.C. CONVALESCENT HOME SOCIETY.
On Monday, March 4th, the annual meeting of this Society was held
in the Coffee Room, Mr. J. J. Dent, President, in the chair. The hon.
secretary, Mr. E. S. Landells, read the report, from which we make the
following extracts:-"Last year there were 3 donations and 58 members'
subscriptions, amounting to £4 3s.; but this year (1906-7) there have been
4 donations and 106 subscriptions, realising £6 9s. The society has
increased its contribution to the Club Union Home from one to two guineas.
The only member of the College who has yet taken advantage of the benefits
of the Society says-'I am writing to thank the Society for the three weeks'
change I was enabled to have at Pegwell Bay. I should also like to say
a word or two in appreciation of the Home, especially as to the freedom
granted to the convalescents. One might almost imagine oneself in a big
hotel or boarding house, there is so little sense of restriction. The bedrooms
are comfortable, with good beds, and the food plentiful and good.
superintendent and his wife I found to be kindness itself.'
The
"As in the case of Friendly Societies and Insurance Companies, so with
our Convalescent Home. It is only by large numbers contributing regularly
a small subscription to the Home that it can be maintained for the benefit
of those of us who may unfortunately fall ill and need a few weeks' residence
in the sea air and pleasant surroundings of Pegwell Bay. The average cost
to the Home, per resident, is nearly £3 10s. for three weeks' stay; and as
this benefit can be obtained, when necessary, by an annual subscription of
one shilling per annum, it is, we venture to say, one of the best investments
a College man can make. Up to the end of last year, the clubs and the
College subscribing to the Home were entitled to nominate a resident for
each guinea subscribed by them to the Home, the resident paying-or having
paid for him by his club-an additional 5s. per week and 5s. for a return
railway ticket. It has been found that it is not possible to efficiently
maintain the Home upon this basis; and with the beginning of this year, a
new method has been adopted, which, while relieving the resident from the
necessity of making any payment whatever beyond his one shilling a year,
will increase the funds annually available for maintenance, and put the home
upon a self-supporting basis. The new plan is that the local clubs and
societies shall send to the Central Fund the whole of their annual subscrip-
tions of one shilling a year per member; and in return the Home Committee
will admit residents without any additional payment, and will supply free
the return railway ticket from London. It will keep a ledger account for
each society or club, crediting it with the shillings sent in annually, and
debiting the account with 15s. per week for each member using the Home.
The balance between the 45s. so debited and the 66s., which is about the
average cost of a three weeks' residence, will be met by the surplus con-
tributions of those clubs whose members are fortunate enough not to require
to use the Home up to the full value of their contributions. By this system
of co-operation, a splendid Home will be at the service, without any charge,
of all members who may need to recuperate after illness, and most of us know
how helpful a three weeks' stay, with good food and pleasant surroundings,
at the seaside, is at such a time. We shall in addition have the great
satisfaction of knowing that, even if we do not need ourselves to take
advantage of it, we are helping many others less fortunate than ourselves, and
this without any resort to charity. The Home is a co-operative institution,
managed upon democratic principles and business lines, by the men who
contribute to its support. No one is asked for financial help outside the
members of the clubs, to whom the Home belongs and who are entitled to
its advantages. It is an institution of which club men are rightly proud, and
the more so in that they themselves provide all the money and management
necessary for its successful maintenance. We hope that every student in the
College will avail himself of the privilege of joining the society and con-
tributing Is. a year to this good work."
Several questions were asked, and Mr. Dent, who wrote the greater
part of the report, addressed the meeting in reply. The following officers
