THE LEICESTER WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE.
We are glad to learn that this College, founded by the Rev. Canon
Vaughan, D.D., a friend of the Rev. J. Llewelyn Davies, in 1862, is still
flourishing and doing good work. For the first six years of its existence,
it was known as the "Working Men's Institute," but in 1868, when there
were 400 students, the title was changed to "The Leicester Working Men's
College." It consists of men, women, and youths, and has a total member-
ship of about 2000. The Committee is going to put up a building suitable
for its new home. "Until this is done," the report says, "the Working
Men's College cannot take its place among the institutions of the town in a
manner commensurate with its tried value."
Tenders for the new College have already been invited, and it is hoped
that building operations will commence early in March. The College will
require about £8000, of which it has already about £6000. The students
themselves are anxious to do their full share of work in the raising of this
amount. Mrs. Vaughan, the widow of Canon Vaughan, has taken her
husband's place in devoting herself to the interests of the College. Two
members of our own College, who were on a flying visit to Leicester on
February 15th, called on Mrs. Vaughan, and she was pleased to see the repre-
sentatives of the London College. She said she had written to the Vice-
Principal, Mr. Lionel Jacob, for information and advice, and had a most
kind letter in reply. She was pleased that the new building would soon be
begun, and said that the aim of the Committee would be to maintain instruc-
tion in the humanities, rather than on the technical side, and they would
endeavour to secure the support and sympathy of the educational authority
for the county. The prospectus concludes by saying that "The Committee
will be glad to have its purely education work co-ordinated with that of the
local educational authority, but there will then remain a field for the College's
humanizing influence. In the view of the Committee, the College has yet
a career before it for the intellectual and moral uplifting of the citizens of
Leicester. They feel that the spirit of brotherhood, which is a mark of its
vigorous life, is yet capable of unmeasured blessings to this and future
generations of our good old town." The Leicester Working Men's College
has the cordial good wishes of the London Working Men's College in its
good work.

THE WORKING MENS COLLEGE JOURNAL.
OBITUARY.
HODGSON PRATT.
ONE of the great workers of the world for the benefit of humanity,
Mr. Hodgson Pratt, passed away on February 26th, at Le Pecq,
in France, at the age of 83.
From the time of his retire-
ment from the service of the East India Company, shortly after the
Mutiny, he devoted his life to at least three great causes-education,
co-operation, and international peace. He was one of the foremost
men in the great co-operative movement, and the founder of the
Working Men's Club and Institute Union. He took a leading part
in the foundation of the International Arbitration and Peace
Association, the furtherance of the objects of which more especially
occupied the later years of his long and active life. He was one of
the most conscientious of men, full of noble thoughts and ideals.
His utterances were remarkable for liberality of view and fair-
mindedness. He strove rather to lead men to think for themselves,
than to persuade them by other means, and the chief object which
he kept in view throughout his many humanitarian efforts was how
to make men better and nobler citizens. Of course, such a man was
attached to, and interested in, this College. He was one of our
Saturday evening lecturers some twenty years ago, and he attended
one or two of the course of lectures in the College on "Co-operative
Life," taking the chair for Mr. M. E. Sadler, and speaking on another
occasion when Mr. Cunningham lectured and Mr. G. J. Holyoake
was chairman. We have also heard him speak at one of the Old
Students' Suppers. Mr. Hodgson Pratt was of an extremely lovable
disposition, possessed of great kindliness of heart and simplicity of
manner. His great courtesy and manliness, and his true nobility of
character, impressed those who came into contact with him. There
was an old-time charm about him, and a certain grandeur of presence
too, that were very pleasing. So far, one of the old school; yet
how marvellously fresh and new, and before their time, were his ideas
and views! His influence for good must have been widespread
indeed.
Mr. Pratt was buried at Highgate Cemetery on March 5th, the
College being represented at the funeral by Messrs. C. Edmund
Maurice, J. J. Dent, T. F. Hobson, R. H. Marks, and L. Pocock.
About sixty delegates from Working Men's Clubs throughout England
attended, and about that number of floral tokens from the clubs
were laid around his grave.
LUBBOCK FIELD CLUB.
FEBRUARY 10th was a dull and misty day, and although at times the sun
seemed likely to clear the air, the conditions were not such as to tempt out
any but the stalwarts. At starting the ground was frozen slightly, but
speedily became particularly soft, except on the roads. We reached Denham
by G. W. R. at 10 o'clock, and striking northward, made our way to Ditton
Marsh Farm. The lanes we traversed were very picturesque, but the
melting hoar frost on the trees interfered sadly with our comfort. After
crossing Oakend Wood, we found ourselves in Chalſont Park, and the
opinion was general that the manner in which we emerged was not a usual
one. Crossing the railway, we reached Gerrard's Cross Common, and then
entered upon a series of pretty paths leading across Bulstrode Park to
Hedgerley. Here we halted for lunch and fared very well, the apples
provided by our host being particularly appreciated. We continued our
route westward across the fields, and emerged on the road just to the north
of Collum Green. Turning south, we followed one of the beautiful roads
just within the border of Burnham Beeches, and on reaching East Burnham


## p. 79 (#71) ##############################################

FURNIVALL CYCLING CLUB,
79
Common turned our faces homeward. The route followed was across and
round Brockhurst Wood, across Stoke Common, and through the pretty
village of Fulmer. We reached the Uxbridge and Beaconsfield Road at the
18th milestone, and after a detour by Denham Mount, regained our starting
place in ample time for the 5.39 train.
Hazel catkins were the chief indications that the winter was wearing on,
but primrose leaves were breaking through in all directions. A remarkable
tree in Bulstrode Park attracted our attention. It had evidently fallen at
some time, after which the trunk had again sought the vertical, while the
prostrate portion had been fortified with masonry. Two large bunches of
mistletoe adorned it, but opinion was divided as to its nature. Curious ice
formations appeared on several ponds, the investigation of which involved wet
feet to one member of the party.

FURNIVALL CYCLING CLUB.
AT this club's annual meeting held on February 23rd, the hon. secretary,
Mr. W. Melzer, read the committee's 12th report, some extracts from which
follow :-The club has 35 ordinary and 12 honorary members. The average
attendance at runs was about 12, and all the 27 runs on the fixture card were
carried out. Miss M. Grellier won the ladies' attendance prize with the large
total of 134 points. The previous best was 76 points, obtained by Miss K.
Adams two years ago. The captain, Mr. W. C. Jones, who has been in the
club since its foundation, secured the men's attendance prize with 140 points,
whilst both Messrs. Lewis and Melzer scored well over 100. The report
referred to the Easter and Whitsun tours, the entertainment provided by the
president of the club, Dr. Furnivall, at Canbury Island on July 22nd, and
the kind hospitality of Mr. and Mrs. Denmead on the visit to their house at
South Mimms, on June 16th.
A supper, admirably prepared by Mrs. Robbie, preceded the meeting,
23 members attending. Dr. Furnivall took the chair, and cigars and
cigarettes having been handed round by Mr. Julius Jacob, the meeting passed
off very pleasantly. After the report and balance sheet had been presented,
Dr. Furnivall was elected president; Messrs. Julius Jacob and W. C. Jones,
vice-presidents; Mr. A. J. Wildey, captain; Mr. C. T. Young, vice-captain;
Mr. A. Haynes, committee-man; and Mr. W. Melzer, hon. secretary. The
latter will he glad to hear of any new members. Subscription, Is. per ann.
At Easter, the club again tours to Brighton. First Sunday run,
April 7th, to Hedgerley; meet at Swiss Cottage. A social run to Pinner
will be held on Saturday, April 13th; meet at Swiss Cottage or Shepherds
Bush Empire at 4.30 p.m. Friends are cordially invited. Other runs are :-
Saturday, April 20th, Sunbury; Sunday, April 28th, Wheathampstead.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
COLLEGE NOTES.
At the Council Meeting held on February 26th, the Vice-
Principal moved that an expression of condolence upon the
death of Sir Godfrey Lushington be sent to Lady Lushington,
and in so doing stated that Mr. Lowes Dickinson wished to be
associated with this vote. Dr. Oswald having seconded, and
Messrs. Forster and Marks having supported the motion, it was
put, and carried unanimously.
The report of the Executive Committee was read. This
document, of which our Superintendent is as usual the author,
makes such excellent reading, that we may perhaps, with
propriety, here give the subjoined extracts from it :-
Student and Class Entries. This time last year the College
had emerged almost entirely from the chaos in which the
building remained during the October term of 1905. The
passages were floored, the windows glazed, the apparatus for
heating and lighting was at work, and the science laboratories
were, if not quite complete, available for two-thirds of their
present accommodation. The result was that a large number of
new members joined in that term, and made the total as large
for the second as it had often been for the first term of former
sessions. Before dealing further with the comparative entries
for the present term, it may be of interest to notice the student
entries for the October term of this session. The number of
individual entries for the first term amounted to 948, or within
fifty of the total for the whole of the preceding year; of these
no less than 556 were new students, leaving 392 as the number
of those who had renewed their membership. This works out
as an eleven per cent. increase on the average of old students
who have rejoined during the past five years in the October
term. Returning to the figures for the present term, as available
up to a week ago, we find that 654 students have joined, as
against 527 at this time last year.
Of these 161 are new
students, who last year numbered 183. It therefore follows that
the percentage of old students, which was a feature of the
October term, has so far risen considerably; the exact figures
being 493 for this term, as against 344 last year. For as large
a number of old students in the January term we have to go
back to 1899, and there the figures relate to the entry for the
whole term, whereas this term has yet another month to run.
Upon analysing the comparative class entries, it appears that of
the thirty-one subjects which are common to the two terms, no
fewer than 21 have improved as compared with last year. Art,
French, German, Greek, Building Construction, Electricity,
Shorthand, Singing, Chemistry, and that most inspiring and
admirable class known as Mr. Scott's class, all show most
substantial increases. At the end of last session some fear was


## p. 81 (#73) ##############################################

COLLEGE NOTES.
81
expressed that the competition provided by the London County
Council Evening Schools might adversely affect our College
classes in Modern Languages. Some thought it would be wise
to lower the fees for these classes, and this suggestion was
debated at length both by the Studies Committee and the
Executive Committee. Finally, it was resolved that no such
reduction should be made, but that students should be given
the option of a sessional fee of 10s. 6d. or of paying the usual
term fee of 5s. The faith of those who deemed it unnecessary
to lower our fees has been justified by the event, the two
languages, French and German, in which competition was most
feared, both show a substantial increase, French of 78, and
German of 55 per cent.
At this time last year, the drop in the class entries for French
and German coincided with a marked increase in Italian and
Spanish. It is curious to note that the position this year is
entirely reversed, Italian and Spanish both having suffered a
decrease, the former more severely, however, than the latter. For
a long time it has seemed impossible to attract to the study of
Economics any but the smallest number of students, and
therefore the fact that Mr. Morison has in his second term no
fewer than sixteen students deserves more than the passing
notice this class would receive when the comparative entries are
read. A course of five lectures on Economics is also being
given on Thursday evenings by Professor A. W. Kirkaldy.
These, up to the present, have been attended by an average of
forty students, so that Economics during this session has been a
distinct success.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
Classes and Teachers.-Two new subjects, Astronomy and
Esperanto, have been added to the programme this term, both at
the request of the students themselves.
Mr. Henkel, who was for four years in charge of Mackree
Observatory, in the North of Ireland, has undertaken to teach the
former, and Mr. G. L. Browne, the latter; both as unpaid
teachers. The singing class, which last term proved so great a
success, again attracted a number of beginners, for whom it
was thought advisable to provide a special class. For this
beginners' class the College has been fortunate in obtaining as
teacher Mr. Mason Tarr, whose brother has been so well known
for years in connection with the musical life of the College, and
under him the class has proved a great success.
The Classical side this term has been a great trouble to its
director, Mr. Lupton. Having obtained with considerable
difficulty Mr. R. N. M. Bailey as teacher for the Beginners'
Greek, and having failed to secure a teacher for the correspond-
ing class in Latin, Mr. Lupton himself undertook the Latin
Class temporarily, and then, after three weeks, found himself
left with the Beginners' Class in Greek, owing to its new teacher
falling ill with scarlet fever. In these circumstances, temporary
assistance was found for the Latin, and Mr. Lupton added to his
other duties that of teaching the Beginners' Greek. Thanks to
Mr. Dent, the College has found a most valuable recruit in Mr.
Strauss, who has put at the College's disposal his one free
evening, and has undertaken a literature and conversation class
for the help of our advanced students in French-a class which
he hopes to run on the same lines as those taken in the old
College with such success by Mr. Jastrzebski. A practice class
for French beginners too being wanted, D. Bardin, a student of
some years' standing, has undertaken the work. In Shorthand,
Mr. Hill and Mr. D. Robson have been obliged to give up their
classes, the former through press of other claims, the latter
through ill-health. Messrs. Randall and Alaway have kindly
filled these vacancies.
Lectures. The lecture lists for this session are most
attractive ones, yet the attendances have not been on the
average at all good. It seems as if the earlier hour of
commencement does not suit the audience as well as the later.
Certainly many more come in late than when the lectures
commenced at 8.30, and the numbers attending are not as large
as in the broken session of last year. Both Thursday and
Saturday lectures have been affected, though the former have
certainly suffered the more. Classes as a rule commence at
7.30, and many end at 8.30, so that an 8 o'clock lecture fails to
get men who would otherwise come, if their classes were not
thus interrupted. The two University Extension series have not

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
At the next meeting of the Old Students' Club, to be held
on Saturday, April 6th, at 7.45, it is intended to do honour to
Mr. R. H. Marks, President of the Club, by making him a
presentation, in recognition of his long and faithful services to
the College, which he joined about fifty years ago Members
of the club will have received notification that they are welcome
to bring their lady friends with them to this meeting.
We have been asked to make special mention of the fact-
and we do it with a great deal of pleasure-that the next
Musical Society's evening will be Saturday, the 20th April, when
a concert will be given by the "Glowworms' Glee Club,"
conducted by Mr. J. F. Budge. The programme will consist of
male voice glees, part songs, etc., and an excellent concert is
promised, so we hope the audience will be large, and come early
-at 8 o'clock.
On March 9th, Mr. A. J. Ashton, K.C., gave an interesting
lecture on "Dr. Johnson." Mr. Ashton, who taught for some time
in the College, and is known to many of the older students,
said that he always had a warm corner in his heart for the place.
Mr. Bros, the Clerkenwell Police Court magistrate, who was
chairman, also said it was a pleasure to him to come again to
the College.
Under date of February 14th, Rev. T. E. S. Catterns, who
is still recuperating at Mentone, writes to the Secretary of the
Old Students' Club-"You have had severe weather in England,
and it has been severe here. Strong winds, heavy seas, and above
all, ice for days in succession. There was a profusion of flowers
up to Christmas, but there are very few now. On February 5th,
the première bataille des fleurs took place, and was the poorest
known. There were only a dozen carriages, fully decorated as
you see them in the illustrations; the three best with white
lilac, red roses, and mimosa bloom. The last probably would
not have been placed but for the occupants-six young and
fairly good-looking English girls, with cream-coloured dresses.
The Carnival procession was on the 7th, and was pretty good.
There was a run on the gigantic, -the king on an enormous
goose and his spouse on a swing. The mounted men were
arrayed in gorgeous Spanish costume, and looked very handsome
There were twelve old maids seven feet high or more; the girls
inside were twelve to fourteen, and in a strong wind found it
difficult to progress. The crowd were largely arrayed in
costumes, masks, and dominos. Plenty of fun, and very little
vulgarity; the rough element is at night, and I did not go out.
The procession was repeated on Sunday, and again on Tuesday,
Mardi Gras, and the figures were burned that night."

COLLEGE NOTES.
85
Mr. F. W. Finn, old student, reports from Calcutta,
February 28th, that the hot season has started about a month
earlier than usual. He longs for some of our cold weather.
We congratulate our friend G. A. Hurcomb and his wife on
their escape with their lives from the Jamaica earthquake; but
we are exceedingly sorry to learn, from the contents of the
following letter addressed to the Secretary of the Old Students'
Club, on February 10th, that he has suffered such a severe loss
of property, and we hope that the insurance companies may
yet make some satisfactory arrangement :-
Both my wife and myself escaped the terrible earthquake of the 14th.
I only got a few bruises-just missing a few tons of falling bricks by an inch
or so, for I ran out in the street. In less time than it takes to tell, the air
became so full of dust from the falling walls that you could see absolutely
nothing. I was in our store at the time, and after groping about trying to find
some others, got into the street, to find the pavement rocking like the deck
of a ship in a heavy sea. When the dust cleared off, the sight was too awful
for words; everywhere men, women, children, horses, and mules covered
with blood, some dead, others with parts of their bodies crushed to pulp,
but still alive, groaning and shrieking. How many were buried under falling
bricks, etc., nobody will ever know. For the past four weeks-to-morrow
will make exactly four weeks-the bodies have been dug out and burnt or
buried. Out of the staff of fifteen in our store, the only one injured was a
man that ran out and got buried. We pulled him out, and he is now
recovering. All the rest stayed in, and luckily the first floor of our building
stood well, and protected those below from that portion of the upper part of
our walls that fell inside. Our stock, too, was intact and undamaged--some
of it only covered with dust. Immediately after the earthquake, most of
our staff pulled themselves together in a wonderful way. One little girl in
particular played an heroic part; alert and active, pulling people from under
bricks, or rather showing the way and getting others to help her take the
bricks off people, bathing and binding up wounds. It is not true, as I have
seen stated, that the earthquake destroyed the water mains, for immediately
after we got plenty out of our pipe, and the pressure was good. I drank
some, for I had a horrible dry choky feeling in the throat. I stayed in the
store for about forty-five minutes after. We put all books in the safe, and
closed and locked all doors before leaving. Misfortunes never come singly.
Fire started some blocks distant, and reached our store some hours afterwards,
completely burning up everything. We are insured in leading English
Companies, but they disclaim liability, although they paid in San Francisco
in an exactly similar case. It is said, however, that their reason for paying
in San Francisco was that they knew that the decision of the United States
Courts would be against them. It was a case of either pay, or clear out of
the United States. But Jamaica is only a small British Colony. I see that
the German Courts have just ordered German Insurance Companies to pay
San Francisco Fire Claims, in spite of the earthquake clause in their policies.
I cannot believe that British justice is inferior to German. If it is, then I say,
so much the worse for the British Empire. One of these same British Companies,
just prior to this fire, was advertising in the Kingston papers that their "losses
in San Francisco, amounting to one million pounds or so sterling, were
promptly paid without touching their capital!" All the policies bristle with
conditions which, if enforced, would enable the Companies to avoid payment
of nearly every claim. And when you questioned the agents about these
conditions they said, "Oh! that's only a matter of form-to protect the
Companies against fraud. It is never enforced in bona fide cases." I must
beg your pardon. I did not start with the intention of writing you this;
but the fact is every business man here will be ruined if fire losses are not
settled on an equitable basis-I say fire losses, not earthquake losses. As for
myself, all I possessed is burnt to ashes, and I now have to start life over again,

THE COFFEE ROOM FUND.
THE fund for the decoration of the Coffee Room has already been
more than half collected, and if to the money now in the treasurers'
hands be added the amounts promised, the total is about £65.
Another £35 is therefore required to be subscribed before the order
can be given for the work. At present all that has been done of a
special nature towards raising the fund has been the holding of the
meeting of February 11th and the issue of a circular to the members.
The Decoration Committee have not found it necessary to work
very hard at collecting, as yet. The chief labour has fallen upon
the hon. secretary, Mr. H. K. Randall, in making out receipts,
acknowledging contributions, and keeping account of the same.
The last £20 will, we suspect, be the hardest to get; but the
Committee is a strong one, and the issue is not to be doubted If
the Common Room Committee come along with the pecuniary
assistance they are able to offer, the contract for the decoration work
may probably be entered into before the end of the current session.

[Under this heading the Editor will be glad to publish letters of interest to
past and present members, but he declines all responsibility for the views
therein expressed.]
COFFEE ROOM DECORATION FUND.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR SIR, -Anon.'s complaint in last month's JOURNAL is, I presume'
unique in the annals of our College, and I trust that the cause of a gentle
grumble I intend to indulge in, Mr. Editor, can also be included in that
category, and that I may enter my earnest protest at the publication of the
amount each individual subscribed towards the redecoration of the Coffee
Room. I do so on the grounds that such a publication defeats the object the
promoters have in view-one that every student must desire-the most success-
ful consummation. It is difficult to write with a due sense of responsibility,
as the whole thing is so obviously insincere. There can be no defence, and
as I trust it will not recur, perhaps I may be forgiven if I attempt to anticipate
the only half-hearted defence which in my opinion may be raised. Can it be
intended to stimulate those who have not subscribed? If so, why not place
the names of those who subscribed the largest amount first. It must be
carelessness, it cannot be design, that some are more prominent than others.
The work at the College of the men that head the list is sufficient refutation
for that suggestion. I firmly believe, Sir, that a great deal of harm has been
done to the fund, and feeling raised, by this ridiculous publication; and as a
humble student who would do anything for the common weal of the College,
I trust you will allow this letter to be published, and that it will not be taken
in the spirit of carping criticism, but in that of a broad-minded interest in a
matter of College history, and a sincere desire for the success of the project.-
Yours faithfully,
EDWARD HAYWARD.
[The publication of the amounts subscribed is not unique in our annals.
It has been the custom, hitherto, to publish such details. One object of
giving the list is, of course, to draw the attention of those likely to contribute,
to the fact that the fund is being raised, pour encourager les autres, as the
saying is. The JOURNAL circulates amongst a number of members who
are likely to give upon seeing such a list, and during the fortnight following
upon the appearance of last month's number, we find that both the number
of receipts issued and the sum collected were more than doubled. Another
reason for printing the sums in the JOURNAL is the ordinary one which
actuates the publication of any accounts of this kind-so that the donors
may have not only the due acknowledgment of their individual donations,
but may see, as a matter of account, how the fund is being raised. The
names are given in the order in which they come in. This must necessarily
be the case until the fund has been closed. To deal with the principle under-
lying Mr. Hayward's criticism, I hope he will believe that no reader of the
COLLEGE JOURNAL thinks ill, or thinks otherwise than well, of a man who
gives a small subscription. Here, so far as our experience goes, every true
College man gives freely of his time and money, to the best of his ability,
for the benefit of his fellow members and of the College, without thought
either of reward or of what other men may think. It is well known, and
often said, in the College, that the gift of a shilling from some men may be
more worthy than the gift of a pound from others. What need then is there
for a man to be ashamed to give a shilling, or even less? None whatever.
So far from it being a "ridiculous publication" to give the donations of
those who can least afford them, we count it as an honourable record.-ED.]

Notices. Report of gifts to the Library. Article on Solitary Chess. Letters

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
MRS. TANSLEY'S CONCERT.
It has been remarked before in these pages, in regard to a Concert given
by Mrs. Tansley, that it was one of the best ever heard in the College. The
Concert of Saturday, March 2nd, however, eclipsed any of its predecessors,
and was on all hands declared to be the best we have ever had. In the
Maurice Hall, we have more space for the Orchestra, and the platform
provides a good vantage ground for the Choir. Both Orchestra and Choir
were most ably conducted by Mrs. Julian Marshall, they performed well
together, and the result was excellent. Soloists-vocal and instrumental-
also played well their part, including Mrs. Eugene Oswald at the piano. The
first part of the programme consisted of a pastoral, entitled "The May-
Queen," written by Henry F. Chorley, and composed by Sir W. Sterndale
Bennett. The soloists who contributed to this piece were Miss Hettie
Stammer, one of the most pleasing sopranos we have ever listened to, who
took the part of the May-Queen; Mr. Stanley Ridout, a capital tenor, as the
Lover; Miss Clutterbuck, who very kindly, in the absence of Mrs. Teasdale
through indisposition, filled and filled well the rôle of Queen; and Mr. W.
Savage Cooper, as Robin Hood, Captain of the Foresters, whose deep bass
voice suited the part admirably. Where all worked so excellently together,
we need say little more, but we think that, by common consent, Miss Hettie
Stamnier won the most delighted applause from the audience. The hardest
worker for our pleasure was Mrs. Julian Marshall.
It was marvellous to
watch her conducting both the large choir, who filled the platform, and the
orchestra at the same time. She evidently took a keen pleasure in doing it ;
her heart was in her work; and consequently the best effect was produced.
Both choir and orchestra contained many of our old friends. Mrs. Tansley
herself was in the former, along with Mr. and Mrs. William Tarr,
Mr. and Mrs. Mason Tarr, Mr. and Mrs Perry, Miss Hutchings, and others
whom we had heard before. We understand that for more than three weeks
constant rehearsals had been going on, which must have meant a great deal of
labour for Mrs. Tansley and her helpers. She and they were accorded a very
hearty vote of thanks, upon the motion of Mr. Lionel Jacob, our Vice-Principal,
when the interval came; and advantage was also taken of the occasion to
recognize both the marriage of Mr. William Tarr and his long, zealous, and
self-sacrificing devotion to College musical work and entertainments, by
presenting him with a choice set of volumes, subscribed for by his many
friends in the College. He was heartily cheered, and made a neat little
speech in acknowledging the gift, which came to him and his wife as a
complete surprise.
The second part of the concert comprised :-Trio and Chorus, "The
prised :
Chough and Crow" (Bishop), Miss Edith Nettleship, Miss Amy Gardner,
and Mr. H. K. Gardner; Violin solo, Swedish Dances (Max Bruch), Miss
Oonah Sumner; Song, "Who is Sylvia?" (Schubert), Miss Clutterbuck;
Three Madrigals by the Choir; "Kathleen Mavourneen," and encore,
"Chloe," Mr. W. Savage Cooper; Song, "Once" (Hervey), and encore,
"Ever so long ago," Miss Hettie Stammer: Valse (Tschaikowsky), the
Orchestra; Song, "Take a pair of sparkling eyes" (Sullivan), Mr. Ridout;
duet, "Spring will bring" (Caryll), Miss Hettie Stammer and Mr. Ridout;
two Irish songs, "I remember meeting you" (Hermann Löhr), and "You'd
better ask me," Mr. C. H. Perry; and Chorus, "Carnovale" (Rossini).
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL is supported partly by

partly by circulation among the Students and Members. Its success
depends upon a regular demand, and to ensure this, the Editor
would be glad if as many readers as can will become Subscribers.

PRICE TWOPENCE.
THE MARKS PRESENTATION MEETING.
JORTUNATE is the College to possess Marks.
Fortunate is Marks to be possessed by the College.
The two seem made the one for the other. It would
appear that the one is the natural outcome, the
natural embodiment of the other. The meeting
held on April 6th to do honour to Marks was unique of its
kind, in the annals of the College. It did not mark any
particular event or turning point in a man's career, such as a
marriage or a leave-taking. It was not to recognize especially
the work of a great College teacher or officer. It was a
co-incidence, not discovered until after the meeting was arranged,
that this is the fiftieth year of Marks's membership of the
College, so that in that particular there was an appropriateness
in the time. But that was not the reason for the meeting being
held now. The feeling was universal-shared by all who knew
him-that now was the time, and now the opportunity, to recognize
with gratitude and thanks the unselfish work which Marks has
for so many years done for the College and its members; to let
him know that the multitude of little acts of kindness and little
deeds of love, standing to his credit here, have made a deep and
lasting impression upon us all; and beyond this, to show him, if
possible, the great affection in which he is held by all his College
friends. The meeting was, above all things, an affectionate one.
The warmth and cordiality of sincere friendship ran through it
all. The leading note was affection and brotherly love. It was
doubtless a trying ordeal for Marks. But each one of us that
was present was filled with a happiness and a satisfaction that
could not be concealed, at being enabled to take part in telling
Marks what we thought of him, how much we admired and
respected his character, and how much we loved him personally.
It was to Lucas that the idea first occurred, of making the
presentation. Many thanks to him for it. Eagerly was the idea
seized upon, and quickly was it taken up and spread. No other
thought could have found readier response. Like spark in
tinder, like flame in autumn prairie grass, it flashed throughout
our community at home and abroad; and the answer came back
alike from all, supporting the proposition, without a dissentient


## p. 90 (#84) ##############################################

90
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
voice, but with unanimous approval. The committee formed for
the purpose of arranging the affair had a most excellent secretary
in Reglar, who spared no pains or time to make it a success,
whilst the Vice-Principal, as chairman, guided, and plarmed, and
otherwise took active part, with Lucas, Mure, and others on the
committee, in bringing it to a happy conclusion.
An Old Students' Club Meeting was to be held on April 6th
-the last meeting of the session-and Mr. Lucas was to open
on the subject of "Historic Centres in the United Kingdom."
It was decided to take advantage of this occasion to make the
presentation, combining it with the club meeting. Mr. Lucas
accordingly gave his paper, which was an exposition of a method
adopted by the Empire League to spread a knowledge of one
part of the Empire to another, through the children, by means
of lantern-illustrated lectures intended to be delivered in the
colonies. Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, and Hong Kong had
each given £300, with the aid of which, under the direction of
Mr. Mackinder, of the London School of Economics, a book of
seven lectures had been written and about 350 slides had been
collected. One of these lectures, dealing with Historic Centres
in the United Kingdom, Mr. Lucas proceeded to read to us,
showing us on the screen, at the same time, the slides introduced,
which included British, Roman, Saxon, Norman, and later
erections and buildings of historic interest, besides many abbeys
and cathedrals, and scenes of university life.
An interval then took place for refreshments, after which we
re-assembled in the Maurice Hall, and Professor A. V. DICEV,
K.C., the Principal of the College, took the chair, and called
upon Mr. LIONEL JACOB, the Vice Principal, to address us.
Mr. JACOB said it sometimes happened to us to be at the sea-side,
and we felt ever so much better for the change, and put it down to
something in the air. People who affected to be scientific thought
it was the ozone. Probably many ingredients in the air made one
feel better. In the atmosphere of this College there were a good
many ingredients; and one of them which we took as a matter of
course, and which was yet our special delight, was the ingredient or
ozone that we called Marks. We had taken it as a matter of course,
till Lucas usefully gave us a hint, and the result was this meeting.
We wanted to tell Marks just a little what we thought of him, so we
had a committee, with an excellent secretary, Mr. Reglar, who wrote
and told all the people we knew that we proposed to say to Mr.
Marks that we remembered something of what we owed to him.
The response was universal. Everybody was most delighted. The
response came, in odd ways, from all parts of the world. Messages
of the greatest respect and admiration for Marks came from Naughty
in Dingwall, from Finn in Alipore, from Denham in Mysore, from
Upperton in Johannesburg, from old friends in Jamaica, from
Macdonald in Topeka, Kansas-suddenly we found the fame of Mr.
Marks was world-wide. One of those distant ones was Mr. Hastings
Hughes, brother of one of our founders, Tom Hughes; and many other
well-known names would be found in the list of contributors to the
Address. Those of the founders unable to be present, Professor


## p. 91 (#85) ##############################################

THE MARKS PRESENTATION MEETING.
91
Westlake, Mr. Llewelyn Davies, and Mr. Ludlow, had written their
hearty concurrence in the objects of the meeting, as also had Mrs.
Tom Hughes, Miss May Hughes, Mrs. Winkworth, Sir Robert
Mowbray, Mr. Cornford, Mr. Caröe, Mr. J H. Collins, Mr. R. C.
Taylor, Mr. Trevelyan, Mr. Sonnenschein, Mr. Fotheringham, the
Misses Buckie, Mr. E. Bown, Mr. J. C. Bailey, Mr. Gerald Ritchie,
Miss Corfield, Mr. Goldsworthy Lowes Dickinson, the late Sir Godfrey
Lushington, Mr. Vernon Lushington, Major General Maurice and
Mr. C. Edmund Maurice, the two sons of our Founder, and many
others-such a collection of letters as any man might well be proud
to read; but Marks had not been allowed to read them, for fear it
should make him proud. (Laughter.) There was one letter, from a
dear friend of ours who was with us that night, Mr. Lowes Dickinson
(cheers), which he would like to read. In it, he said: "Let us try to
emulate Marks's qualities, his faithful work, his readiness to help all
who need it, his indifference to what is called position in the world,
in one word-his character. His moral idea of Life is, whether he
knows it or not, to follow the great tradition of his Founder."
(Cheers.) We were sorry Mr. Marks's son was not well enough to
be present to see the honour and affection we had for his father, and
were very delighted to see Mrs. Pocock there, and that for once it
was she who had brought Pocock to the College, and not he who
had brought her. For all the people anxious to do honour to Marks,
there was only one recalcitrant, Marks himself. It seemed a most
cruel thing to order him to the photographer's to have his portrait
taken (laughter); but we were all happy to have it on our walls to tell
those who come after us what manner of man he was. It had been
decided to let our tribute take a variety of forms. We wanted to
tell him what we thought of him, as we had done in the address ;
we wished to give him some present, and chose books, knowing his
love of reading, and his love of French, German, and other
languages; we wanted to have a special memorial of him on our
walls-his portrait; and finally we had founded a prize bearing his
name and remaining in perpetuity in the College-we thought it
would be an honour for any student to gain such a prize and thus
to be associated with his name. (Cheers.) It was fifty years this
year since Marks joined the College, though we did not know it when
we began; and the fifty years of faithful service he had given us was
the service of pretty well a life-time. The College had always been
rich in men of devotion and self-sacrifice, but a record like Marks's
could not be matched for length of time and faithfulness of service.
We all knew what the service had been. We knew that when any
work had to be done, Marks was always ready to take off his coat
and set to at it. The only time he had had any recognition was
when we were moving from the old College, and he was as usual
working with his coat off, when an outsider, appreciating the
assistance he was rendering, offered him a tip-sixpence. (Laughter.)
Whether he took it or not, was not known. We knew his service
had been quietly given all through the years. In one connection
only had Marks been known to be grasping, and that was the Old
Students' Club. He was treasurer and secretary, when, like
Cerberus, the three-headed, he took on the presidency. But he went
beyond that, for he took on a fourth head, and became the auditor
(laughter). Besides having three or four heads, he seemed to have
been born with quite an unusual number of hearts. If he had not
three or four hearts as well as heads, at all events his heart had the
capacity of three or four other men's. Everyone there felt that


## p. 92 (#86) ##############################################

92
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
Marks was a personal friend, and all those not present, who had
written, had the same feeling. He (Mr. Jacob) bore witness to
many years of kindnesses by Marks-acts, thoughts, and deeds--to
him and his; and he had seen by chance, here and there, kindnesses
to old men and young, to old students faded out of recollection from
everyone but Marks, who had ministered to them in trouble and had
attended to them in sickness, and when they had died, had looked
after their families. That sort of thing one only found out by chance.
Therefore, beyond all others we had with us, the Old Student
Marks was to be honoured for having kept up the human and the
humane side of our work. (Cheers.)
Mr. MURE said it was his pleasant duty to present the Address.
It gave him great pleasure to take part in that reception, so
deservedly given to Marks by members of the College and especially
of the Old Students' Club. It was fifty years since Marks came as
a student, and we had gained a great deal from him. We owed
him for many acts of kindness, besides his general influence. He
(Mr. Mure) did not know whether we owed to Marks, directly or
indirectly, the introduction of Pocock, or whether it was unconscious
premonitory instinct which led Pocock to become his son-in-law.
Both played parts in the College for which it would be difficult to
find understudies. The principal part lately taken by Marks was the
presidentship of the Old Students' Club, and his genial chairmanship
at the Suppers and when presiding at any other social functions was
well known. The chief thing that had struck him in Marks's
character was a sort of mental and moral sunshine, which illuminated
the place wherever he might be. If the College could produce men
like Marks, it could do most things. (Cheers.) Mr. Mure then read
the Address, which was handsomely and suitably illuminated, and
bound in album form, and presented it to Marks amidst cheering.
The Address runs thus :-
WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE.
TO ROBERT HENRY MARKS,
We, the undersigned, being past or present Members of the
Working Men's College, or otherwise connected with it, are happy to express
to you our gratitude for your long, faithful, and loving service to this College,
and for your friendship to us one and all individually.
It is a delight to us to think that one so deservedly beloved as yourself
should be the first recipient within the walls of our new home of such
affectionate recognition as a College Address can give.
It is now fifty years since you became a student of the College. That
you loved learning, and spared no pains to acquire it, is proved by the range
of your attainments. Throughout your life you have remained a student at
heart, and have always recognized the paramount claim of education on your
fellow students. As years have gone on you have taken an increasingly
active part in the administration of the College. Its interests, we all know
well, have ever been near your heart; and in devising and working out plans
to make it more useful and more efficient, you have spared neither labour
nor money nor thought. At times of stress you have taken on yourself
large part of the burden; at no time and under no circumstances have your
advice, your assistance, and your sympathy been wanting.
a
It is, however, as Secretary, and in succession to your and our dear
friend, George Tansley, as President of the Old Students' Club, that your
most characteristic work has been done. You have bound to the College
many men who would otherwise have drifted away. You have been an
unfailing friend to old and new students alike. There is scarcely one of us
who cannot tell of kindnesses received at your hands. How many more there
are, of which we know nothing, we can only conjecture.


## p. 93 (#87) ##############################################

THE MARKS PRESENTATION MEETING.
93
We ask your acceptance of the Gift that accompanies this Address, as
a token of the very warm regard and affection which we one and all feel
for you. At the same time we desire that the College shall possess a visible
sign to remind its members of all that you have been and all that you have
done here. We have therefore had your portrait taken to hang in the room
to which your presence has always brought happiness; and we are founding
a prize to bear your name, in the hope that it may stimulate younger men to
follow so fruitful an example.
If this College can secure a succession of students, as true to knowledge,
as mindful of others, as forgetful of themselves, as you have been and are,
it will have fulfilled its highest aim, and trained citizens whose kindly strength
and gentle sympathy will bless the coming time.
Signed on behalf of the Contributors,
6th April, 1907.
A. V. DICEY, Principal.
LIONEL JACOB, Vice-Principal.
REGINALD J. MURE, Bursar.
Mr. ALFRED GRUGEON spoke of Marks's work for the Old
Students' Club. The Club was much indebted to him, because he
had made it his special business to strengthen and enlarge it. His
wide experience and knowledge of College men, past and present,
had enabled him to draw in every available person who could be a
member. As a result, the Old Students' Club was strong
numerically, strong socially, and strong financially, all owing to
Marks, and we felt proud of it. The mantle of George Tansley
had fallen upon Marks, and he wore it most gracefully. We were
all as grateful as it was possible to be, and this was our mode of
expressing it. Going outside the Old Students' Club, and taking
College life in general, he might say Marks was a very old friend of
his own, of forty-six years' standing; but as he was also a friend of
every other person present, he did not put forward his claim as
anything special. He had known Marks as the warm friend of
every College student, and recognized him as the College comforter.
Many a student had been grateful for his presence when on a bed
of sickness, and on many occasions he had been the last person
that student had shaken hands with. Formerly Marks had a
co-worker with him, Jamie Dougall. He had known an instance of
a lonely man passing away with those two at the bed side, and
thinking he was in the presence of angels, and he wasn't far wrong.
He (Grugeon) had known Marks about forty-six years and wished he
had known him longer. He would like to have gone to school with
him; if he had done so, he might have grown up a better man
than he was ever likely to be. (Cheers.)
Mr. FORSTER said he felt it a privilege to be allowed to tell us
something about his very dear old friend Marks. It was, he believed,
forty-six years ago that week that he joined the College, then quite a
youngster, as a student of the French class, and the first man there
with whom he made acquaintance was Robert Marks. Marks had
been there some year or two before, and seeing him a stranger
coming to the class, he set to work at once to make him at home.
This was a help he could never forget, and the friendship then begun
had continued from that day to this. He had seen Marks holding
out the hand of friendship, in the same way, to many another since
that time. Wherever help was wanted, or work had to be done in
the College, Marks was there. Many were helped by him, without
knowing whence the assistance came, for Marks had the faculty of
hiding his light under a bushel. He was also wanting in the
capacity to make enemies. We never heard anyone say a hard or
unkind word about Marks. He (Mr. Forster) did not think anyone


## p. 94 (#88) ##############################################

94
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
could, nor could the mind of man imagine any justification for saying
an unkind word about Marks. He possessed the remarkable
capacity, in a degree unequalled in the speaker's experience, for
remembering his friends. In that respect his work had been most
valuable in the College, keeping together the men, and frequently
bringing back those who would not otherwise have returned. It was
Marks who knew where all our old students were and what had
become of them. He had kept in touch with them, and consequently
he made an ideal president of the Old Students' Club. Marks had
carried on the ideal and traditions laid down by our Founder. He
was an example of the men that our Founder founded this College
to produce; and so long as the College could produce men of his
stamp, so long would the College exist and do a great work in
England, and hold its own among our institutions. (Cheers.)
Mr. TORRINGTON, speaking on behalf of the younger generation
in the College, bore witness that all that had been said by the older
members about Marks was equally true of him in the present time.
He must have begun very quietly indeed, for he had been very
successful. He did not wait to be emulated. He went along
quietly and did things, and made us emulate him. When there was
a job, he set the example, by getting on with it, and showing others
the way. He always made people feel at home. If you met a
College man who had been away awhile, the first man he asked
about was Marks. Everyone knew Marks, and what was more to the
point still, Marks knew them as well as they knew him. The first
man he (Torrington) got to know after Mr. Jennings, his old teacher,
was Marks. He lent men books, brought foreigners along to help
them learn languages, and encouraged others to help in the same
way. He had the right College spirit, as we all knew. (Cheers.)

Dr. EUGENE OSWALD spoke of the early days, in the sixties,
when Marks entered his French class, eager to learn then, as
afterwards and now, faithful to that class and later to the German
one. The relationship of student and teacher soon became closer
and a very great friendship sprang up between them.
impression of him, as a good, kind, intelligent, and excellent man,
had never altered or been modified. There was present another old
student and teacher of the French classes, Mr. R. A. Reed, and he
could not help linking his name with that of Mr. Marks, as College
friends and fellow-workers of his. (Cheers.)
Mr. LUCAS:-At other times and in lighter vein some of us have
ventured to joke with Marks, never I hope with impertinence, and
always I am sure with affection. To-night we are here for another
purpose to tell him, severely, what we think of him. We do this
for our pleasure, not for his; for Marks, as you will observe, pro-
foundly disapproves of the whole proceedings. It has been the glory
of this College to produce a race of men, who one after another have
shunned such advertisement as is dear to those of coarser grain.
Among them the most modest and most retiring of all has been our
friend whom we have met to honour to-night. But an inveterate
habit of doing good in secret is sure, sooner or later, to be found out,
and you cannot have a Marks without re-marks. (Laughter.)
cannot speak of Marks as Grugeon has spoken, for I am not one of
his oldest friends, and did not know the little cherub in his infancy.
Nor can I speak of him as Torrington has spoken on behalf of the
newer men, to whom he is a kind of father of the College. Mine is a
voice from the middle ages. The Middle Ages were the days of
chivalry, and, had Marks lived then, none would have been more
I


## p. 95 (#89) ##############################################

95
chivalrous than he. He would have been to the forefront in fighting
or working. But I am quite certain that he would never have
become a knight. He would always have remained a squire, for he
would have allowed some one else to carry off the prize; and if he
had taken a prisoner, he would have insisted on paying the ransom
himself, and would have wound up with asking one and all of his
foes to an Old Squires' Supper. (Laughter.) As long as men of his
type survive, the age of chivalry is not yet past. Marks is a man of
many friends; some are human and some are bound in calf; and
the love and sympathy which he has so warmly given to the friends
of both kinds have been as warmly returned. He is the type of
citizen whom we are here to train, and whom we honour for ever in
the memory of George Tansley. The money which Reglar has so
well collected has been laid out, over and above the Address, first in
giving Marks some of those old friends of his, books, wisely selected
by that good judge of books, our Vice-Principal; secondly, in giving
the College a photograph of a face which has brought brightness
and happiness wherever it has been seen, and copies of which may
be obtained from the secretary for two shillings, with an extra charge
if they are signed by Marks himself (laughter); thirdly, it has been
laid out in founding a prize bearing his name, to be given year after
year, appropriately to the student who has got the most Marks.
(Laughter.) But our debt of gratitude to Marks is not only for what
he has done and is doing, but because he is the father-in-law of
Mr. Pocock. All men in this room or outside it have a high opinion
of the intelligence of ladies, but few ladies have shown such delicate
intuition and such exceptionally good taste as the lady who selected
to be the daughter of Mr. Marks, the wife of Mr. Pocock, and the
mother of the future President of the Old Students' Club. (Cheers
and Laughter.) I have taken part now in a good many testimonials
in this College, but I hardly remember any occasion of the kind on
which there has been embodied so much real affection as has been
shown to our friend here. Great are-great will be-Mr. Marks's
services to the College, but it is not so much on account of them that
we are here to-night. We are here to pay a simple and heartfelt
tribute to a true, a trusted, a loving, and a well-loved friend.
(Cheers.)
Professor DICEY said :--I cannot claim, on the one hand, such a
life-long acquaintance with Mr. Marks as his older friends, nor, on
the other, the close and intimate knowledge of his kindness which
is possessed by our younger students. All I can claim is a true
friendship with our friend Marks, and a high appreciation of the fine
qualities of his character. This meeting suggests to me three things
which I wish to say, but I must pause before I enter upon them. I
must perform a duty which it would be unpardonable to forget, and
convey to you a message from one of our friends who would so like
to have been present with us. Mrs. Litchfield begs me to say how
sincerely she regrets her inability to come here. She has been kept
in the country solely by her having to entertain friends there, whom,
as a hostess, she could not leave. I have performed my duty, and
have given you a message which on no account would I have
omitted. I have sacrificed a good deal to friendship, and have spoilt
the logical sequence of my speech. Allow me to take up again my
three points. First, - Mr. Marks has been an ideal student of the
Working Men's College. These books before us are the testimony
to one great feature in his career. He has done more than study.
Many of us have done that for a time and in our youth, but he has


## p. 96 (#90) ##############################################

96
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
done more. He has done what all of us might have done; he has
through life kept up, and not only kept up but also improved, the
knowledge which he gained when young. Many of us have tried as
students to learn something and have succeeded; but it is only one
here and there who in later life has remembered the danger of
forgetfulness, and has reflected that it is as much a duty to retain
and improve as to acquire knowledge. It is because he has
remembered this that our friend is an example to all members of
our College. The Working Men's College has one advantage which
more famous, more ancient, and more wealthy institutions lack.
The undergraduates and graduates of our Universities, who have
really learned something of value, more often than not forget
the results of creditable study. Nor is it entirely their fault.
They go away from Oxford or from Cambridge, and their place
knows them no more. With our College it is otherwise. Many of
our students can, and some of them do, stick to the College
for years. They can go on learning for years. They can preserve
and even brighten the treasures gained by youthful energy in a way
which is impossible to most graduates of our great Universities. In
this, Marks has set them a noble example, which I trust they may
follow. Secondly, our friend has combined in himself and in his
career the two sides of our College life. He has cultivated not only
learning, but also genial sociability. These two qualities are not always
combined. It has been my good fortune to know some few men
of profound learning, but I cannot say they were always genial
companions. I have known many thoroughly good fellows, but
it would be impossible for me, in some instances at least, to
guarantee their erudition. Robert Marks has been the best of
students and the best of triends. Thirdly, we are often told that
it is wrong and tasteless to praise a man to his face. This maxim
has been so dinned into our ears that I have not the boldness to
question its general correctness, yet sometimes I have found it
impossible not to question its absolute truth. We lost, a year or
two ago, at Oxford a man of great learning, and whose knowledge
was the more valuable because of that ardent love of truth which
made him avoid, with something of Quaker-like zeal, any kind of
inaccuracy. He was one whose conversation was delightful,
whose quiet naturalness and sense of humour gave to intercourse
with him a special charm. When he died it was well said of him,
and with a truth which no human being could dispute, that he was
the best-loved man in Oxford. He was with his learning and his
social attractiveness, so modest and unassuming that I have
sometimes doubted whether he himself knew how much affection
he had gained. The thought has sometimes passed through my
mind that it might after all not have been amiss, if some among
us had told our friend whilst he was still with us, how much he
was beloved. This thought at any rate emboldens me to defy at
this moment the validity of the well-worn maxim I have quoted.
I will not deny to our friend here a possible satisfaction, or to
ourselves an absolutely certain pleasure. I will venture in your
name to tell Mr. Marks to his face that he is more-no, comparisons
are in such things odious, and are also almost untrue-that he is
as much loved by us all as any man among either the students,
or the teachers, or the officers of the Working Men's College.
(Cheers.)

our dear friend Mr. Marks. It gave her extreme pleasure, partly

When the cheering had subsided, Mr. MARKS said: -Mr. Principal,
ladies, and gentlemen, -I don't think I know the Mr. Marks you have been
speaking about to-night. I should like to know him as such. I should like
to recognize him. When I told the Vice-Principal that I should be very
much embarrassed as to what I should say on this occasion, he said, with
his usual kindness, you need only say, "Thank you!" which I heartily do,
but I felt that I ought to say something more. I am reminded of what our
dear friend Charles Crawley said, when he found himself in a similar position
to my present one. He said. "Is there not a cellar somewhere in which I
can hide myself?" I felt like that also. (Laughter.) As there is no candid
friend here to take the part of the devil's advocate, I will venture to suggest
what he would probably say, if he were here: "This fellow has no initiative,
no judgment, no talent, no imagination. He is only a plodder-a hewer of
wood and a drawer of water. He has been in the College for fifty years, and
has only taken ane certificate, while his friend Castell in a dozen years, and
with less opportunity, has taken them by the score. He is president of the
Old Students' Club, where speeches are made, and he can't make one; he
is president of the Musical Society, and he can neither play a tune nor sing
a song; he is president of the Swimming Club, and can't swim a stroke."
I joined the College as an apprentice. In those days, in order to appear
desperately studious, I cultivated long hair and the habit of reading in the
street. Attendance at the College led to less obtrusive methods of reading,
and a visit to Paris, to the shortening of the hair. Since those days, in a
very humble way, the pleasure of seeking knowledge for its own sake, a love
of nature, and the congenial and stimulating companionship afforded by the
College, have made life worth living. The working-man of to-day, who has
certainly more advantages than he had fifty years ago, if he seeks pleasure
in study, in nature, and in such surroundings as we have here, will have as
good a chance of leading a useful life as any man in the community. I
believe that the best things in life are within the reach of most of us, and
they are not costly. To serve the College and to follow in the footsteps of
the men who have worked for it so strenuously and so unselfishly in the past
is a privilege. I call to mind such men as Thomas Dunman, Leopold Owen,
and Alfred Grugeon, who devoted themselves to the teaching of science
when equipments and funds were scarce. I am mindful of the life-long
services of Hughes, Litchfield, and Tansley; nor do I forget the many years
devoted to the College by its Secretary, H. R. Jennings, nor all the Vice-
Principals who have done so much for it. It is a satisfaction to recognize
that many of the men who have been most prominent in the social life have
not been so on account of position or rank, but simply by force of character,
which we endeavour to make our standard; we try to ignore class distinctions,
and to meet together as man and man. No one familiar with the social life
of the College, and with the elements of which it is composed at the present
time, need have any misgivings as to the maintenance in the future of its best
traditions for unselfish work and enthusiasm. The teachers and students of
the present time are well qualified to safeguard the best interests of the
College in the spirit of its Founder. My friends in the College date from the
earliest days to the most recent ones. Of the oldest not a few are still with
us. They include Dr. Furnivall, Dr. Oswald, Forster, Bromhall, Roebuck,


## p. 98 (#92) ##############################################

98
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
Taylor, Philip Read, Ebenezer Cooke, Colonel Bolton, Fotheringham,
Rosenthal, Rigby Smith, Sonnenschein, Catterns, Grugeon, Murphy, and
many others. I have said before in the College that I am not ambitious. I
was unknown in the College till Lucas made me Secretary of the Old
Students' Club, and a little later on I got a further lift up by becoming
Pocock's father-in-law. Had I been ambitious, I could have had no higher
ambition than to have attained the honour of presiding at the College Supper
and to have gained the esteem and affection of the College friends whom
I see around me. I am greatly indebted to the Vice-Principal and Lucas for
their kindness to me for many years past. Indeed, I have always received
the greatest kindness and consideration from every one in the College. I
am deeply touched by all you have done for me on this occasion, for which I
am now and shall always be most grateful, and the memory of which
I shall ever cherish. (Hearty cheering.)
Dr. FURNIVALL here interposed with a thoroughly characteristic remark
with regard to the portrait of Mr. Marks exhibited on the platform. "Have
we," he asked "ever seen Bobbie Marks with a pair of stiff white cuffs on?"
-as depicted in the photograph. He proceeded to explain that he had
ascertained that Marks had no cuffs on when he went to have his photo taken,
but the photographer insisted upon them, and sent out there and then and
bought a pair, and "put 'em on Bobbie." (Great delight and much laughter
from the audience).

Mr. Sydney Presburg has sent a guinea towards the Main-

The Common Room Committee have decorated the Club
Room and covered the floor of that room with linoleum, at a
cost of about £13 5s. They have also purchased a handsome
English bracket clock for the Common Room, with a very plain
dial, which may be easily read from any part of the room.
Mr. Cornford of Trinity has again kindly invited about forty
College men to spend a week-end at Cambridge with him and
his friends, on May 25th, 26th, and 27th. Names of students
and teachers desirous of participating in this deservedly popular
excursion should be given in at once to the Superintendent.
Mr. James Anderson, a College student, who has left London
for Glasgow, feels the want of the College there, but says "the
JOURNAL helps materially to restore the old atmosphere." Do
any of our readers know any former members resident in Glasgow ?
The emigration wave has extended to the College.
Con-
sequently we have lost four most useful men. Mr. H. Trott,
having worked very hard at German during the past year, has
gone to the land "where they speaks the lingo." He has written
home saying that so far he has experienced nothing but kindness
and encouragement on his travels. He thanks, not only his
teachers, but those German gentlemen who frequent the
Common Room and who gave him introductions and "tips," so
that his visit might be made as pleasant as possible. So diligent
a student as Trott is bound to succeed, wherever he finds himself
located.
Canada and the lands thereabout have attracted Mons.
Jean Waller, so well-known to the "Linguists," A. E. King,
of the German classes and our Cinderellas, and that fine athlete
and student of Spanish, S. H. Spry. Of the latter, Señor
Victoria, who is disconsolate, says "one of my very best
students."

Spry and King are en route, and will write on their arrival.
Both are leaving England because of the un-English "hustling,"

men, admirably fitted for the rough Colonial life they have
elected to follow. They have our very best wishes.
We wish to correct a mistake in the March JOURNAL, in the
Old Students' Club report. It was Mr. Hepburn who made the
point, attributed to Mr. Gümpel, as to the taxation of land values,
even to extinction, being in his opinion perfectly logical and just.
Writing from Johannesburg on February 21st, Mr. H. V.
Birrell, old student, says that Mr. Richard Feetham, a one time
teacher in the College, "has been nominated to our local House
of Lords, the personnel of which has excited the scorn and
derision of the majority of folk here. Perhaps they are intended
to emulate Gilbert's House of Peers, and do 'nothing in
particular.' For better or worse our legislative assembly was
elected yesterday, a job lot they are too; the expected happened,
a Het Volk majority is secured. The general impression, usually
held in a more or less indifferent spirit, is that the predominant
party cannot do much harm, even if they do no good, and it is
hardly possible for things to be made worse than they are and
have been under the Eckstein régime. I am getting rather tired
of ups and downs, and have struck a long streak of bad luck,
but still go on hoping for good times again. It hurt me to have
to sell my horses and dogs, and now I wish I'd never had them.
I was very glad to learn of the continued advance and prosperity
of the dear old College, and would like to take part in its affairs
again."
Mr. J. B. Upperton, old student, also writing from
Johannesburg, on February 25th, says:--"Our weather here,
for summer, has been wretched-storms and cold rain-possibly
a reflex of the climatic and atmospheric disturbances all over
the planet; and we now read that an Italian astronomer has
predicted that a comet is fast and furiously approaching the
Earth, with the idea of a collision. Well, the sooner the better,
as far as I am concerned, as my pains and aches from
rheumatism and cramp have been awful. Kindest regards to all
members of the Old Students' Club."

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
Mr. Thomas Denham, old student, writes from Mysore,
February 18th. After referring to the loss of his savings in the
Macfadyen and Arbuthnot failure, he says he is worried, too,
with the plague, which is making its reappearance in a virulent
form there. Two children of his servants have just died from it.
This means endless trouble, such as disinfection of the servants
quarters, the erection of temporary buildings for them, etc.
With great regret, we have to record the death of another
son of the Rev. J. Llewelyn Davies, one of the founders of this
College. Mr. Arthur Llewelyn Davies, who had been very
seriously ill for several months, died on April 19th, at Egerton
House, Berkhamsted, at the age of 44. He was a man of great
ability and promise, by profession a barrister, and had read for
the bar with Mr. Justice Walton. His knowledge and attain-
ments were such that it appeared likely he would have had a
great career before him. He married Miss Sylvia du Maurier,
daughter of the well-known artist, and leaves a family of five
sons. Much sympathy is felt for his widow, children, and father
in their sad loss. The funeral service took place at Golder's
Green Crematorium on April 23rd.
LEICESTER WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE. - Mrs. Margaret
Vaughan, in writing to the Vice-Principal recently as to the
future of the Leicester Working Men's College (founded by
Canon Vaughan in 1862), says:-"We have told the local
authority that we wish to work on the old lines next session,
and be independent of them. We have, however, to submit our
programme of classes for their approval, so as not to compete
with the town's "continuation schools," but we shall appoint
our own teachers, and receive grants from the Board of Education.
I am afraid we may have some difficulty in getting the funds,
but we are going to try what rigid economy and the interest of
the students in collecting the subscriptions will do. The new
building will, we hope, be ready for use in October. We all
much wish that the Local Education Authority would make us
a grant, as the London County Council does in your case, but
it will not hear of such a thing. We had your first letter copied
and distributed amongst the members of the Town Council
Committees, that they might see what London does, but in vain.
We could throw ourselves upon the rates, but should lose the
entire management, if we did; we are therefore going to run the
financial risk next session. There is much enthusiasm amongst
the students, and I believe the social work will go on prosperously
as soon as the new buildings are ready for it. That, of course,
is entirely independent of the Town Council Committee. The
educational work is hampered by our being obliged to co-operate
with the town authority." We in the London Working Men's
College heartily wish our Leicester friends every success in an
undertaking so kindred in nature to our own.

THE WORKING MENS COLLEGE JOURNAL.
GARIBALDI'S DEFENCE OF THE
ROMAN REPUBLIC.
BY GEORGE MACAULAY TREVELYAN, Μ.Α.
The above book was published on April 8th (Longmans, Ios. 6d., net)
on which day an excellent and sympathetic review of it by Henry W
Nevinson appeared in the Daily Chronicle, from which we take the
following:-
"Garibaldi was not a great poet like Byron, not a great thinker like
Mazzini. 'Heart of gold, and brain of ox,' his own people once called him
in their haste. But no more irresistible theme could be found for all heroic
minds than the career of that fair-haired, sea-blue-eyed Italian, who was born
just a hundred years ago, and Mr. George Trevelyan was just the right man
to tell it. A true Liberal, in the sense of regarding liberty as the watchword
of politics; a devoted student, who has not let his learning blunt his sense of
action or his sense of humanity; an enthusiast free from rhetoric; a minutely
careful historian still capable of wide outlook and grandeur of expression, he
has presented us with an inspiring and memorable chapter of heroic life.
The only fault one could find with a work so genuine, and sustained at so
high a level of achievement, is the very rare fault that it is too short. It
deals with only one chapter of a life that had two chapters of glory, and four
of extraordinary interest. Our hope is that Mr. Trevelyan will not rest
satisfied within the strict limit he has laid on himself, but within the next few
years will proceed to the later and even grander story, so as to give the world
a modern epic of heroism complete. He could hardly discover a finer theme,
or one better suited for his power."
Referring to Garibaldi as a "Man of Destiny," Mr. Nevinson quotes
the author's description of him, which he describes as being "as excellent as
it is brief." Mr. Trevelyan says:-
"He had all the distinctive qualities of the hero in their highest possible
degree, and in their very simplest form. Courage and endurance without
limit; tenderness to man and to all living things, which was never blunted
by a life-time of war in two hemispheres among combatants often but half-
civilized; the power to fill men with ardour by his presence and to stir
them by his voice to great deeds; but, above all, the passion to be striking
a blow for the oppressed, a passion which could not be quenched by failure,
nor checked by reason, nor sated by success, old age, and the worship of the
world."
Lengthy and appreciative notices of the book have also appeared in the
Daily News, Tribune, and several other papers. Mr. Trevelyan has kindly
presented a copy to the College Library.
LUBBOCK FIELD CLUB.
A PARTY of eleven turned out on March 10th, in which we were pleased
to see some new faces. The weather was inclined to be showery, and the
ground was unpleasantly yielding at times. A round of about twenty miles
was covered, which, considering the uneven nature of the country visited,
was not at all bad. An early start was made, Purley being reached about
9.45. We crossed Riddlesdown by Hamsey Green, and after passing
Warlingham, spent some time on Worm's Heath examining and discussing
Hutcircles and Dewponds. We then turned southwest, but before reaching
Woldingham, climbed up the long track leading to Flint House Farm. On
reaching the escarpment over Oxted chalkpit, we were driven by the pangs of
hunger, and a sharp shower, down the hill and into the village. After lunch,
we turned our faces northward, leaving however one man, who declined to
negotiate any more hills, preferring to wait an uncertain number of hours for
the next train. We followed the track past the lake and tumulus at Barrow
Green, and were soon in difficulties with the mud at the geologically
interesting point where the Gault Clay crops out on the hillside. On reaching
the chalk we fared better, but it was a struggle at

we entered Marden Park, where one of our favorite tracks was marked "no

hand, it was decided to walk on to Kenley, but we took things too easily,
with the result we reached the station just as the train began to move.
Consequently there was nothing for it but to return to Purley, where we
caught the 6.12 train.
Primroses were found in bloom, but otherwise the signs of the times
were to be read only in the leaves of arums, bluebells, lls, dog's mercury,
celandine, and wood violets. There was, however, a fine show of snowdrops
in Marden Park.

FURNIVALL SCULLING CLUB.
For some weeks prior to the glorious 7th of April, the day of the
General Meeting, it had been remarked that some proportion of the members,
and more particularly the College men, seemed somewhat distracted and
more deep in thought than is wont even in College men, and, to the uni-
nitiated, without any apparent reason. The cause of their trouble, however,
was the fear that the General Meeting would pass off quietly, as has been the
case during the last year or two; and the wretched people in question,
having degenerated through attending meetings of a noisy nature at the
College-one refrains from particularizing-could not tolerate the idea of a
quiet reunion for business purposes, without some element of disturbance.
However, they seemed later to be satisfied.
The usual delightful Sunday was spent by many of the members on the
River, three fours, in one of which was of course the Doctor, going to Richmond
and back.
The meeting started shortly after tea, the Doctor being in the chair.
The secretary's cash account was very satisfactory, there being some £16
in hand, though that of course was already swamped by Mr. Biffen's bill for
repairs to boats, etc., estimated at £20, repairs necessary to raft, and cost of
new box and gangway. The members then re-elected the president and
vice-presidents (adding Mr. Radford, M.P., and Mr. Munday), Miss Moulden
as captain, and Mr. Fisher as captain of the boats. Votes of thanks were
passed to everybody in a particularly hearty manner. Mr. Howard was
unanimously elected hon. secretary in place of West, who was resigning.
The following were elected and re-elected on the committee; the Misses
Adams, Appleby, Deane, Dewar, Munro, and Skinner, and Messrs. Clark,
Gillies, Munro, Owen, Richardson, and West. The question of cleaning the
boats having been discussed and settled, Charles Richardson presented
statement of the catering committee, and showed a most successful financial
half-year. He was able to hand over £3 to the funds of the Club, keeping
£2 odd in hand as capital. Upon the Committee then putting forward the
suggestion that a levy of 2s. 6d. per member be made to meet the expense of
the new ran-dan, it was thought by Mr. Reglar that the sum necessary could
be raised by private subscription, which he forthwith proceeded to do, having
a good start with £2 generously given by a popular member of both Club and
College. It was, however, decided, to meet future expenses of boats, etc.,
to raise the men's subscription 6d., making it 3s. per month. The most
successful meeting ended by the usual hearty vote of thanks to the Doctor.
J. B. W.
