THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
CORRESPONDENCE.
[Under this heading the Editor will be glad to publish letters of interest to
past and present members, but he declines all responsibility for the views
therein expressed.]
THE PROPOSED GENERAL RULES FOR THE GUIDANCE
OF THE COLLEGE CLUBS.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
SIR,-May we trespass on your space to address to you a few words on
the above subject? The meeting of the Clubs on March 11th, at which the
proposed rules were rejected by a large majority, appears to have laboured
under a misapprehension regarding the scope and object of the proposal,
which unfortunately the spokesmen of the Common Room Committee did
not succeed in dispelling. The meeting seems to have been under the
impression that the scheme was an insidious plot on the part of the Common
Room Committee to obtain a controlling voice in the management of the
clubs. Nothing could be further from the truth. In bringing forward the
rules, the Committee were-as they thought-voicing the desire of many
thinking men in the College that there should be laid down certain definite
and well-established rules to which, for the maintenance of that high standard
of efficiency which is vital to the existence of the College, all clubs should
be obliged to conform.
The Common Room Committee merely made the first move in the
matter, because they seemed to be the natural body to do so; but their
proposal was nothing more than a draft designed to serve as a basis of
discussion. They are perfectly ready to eliminate themselves from the
scheme entirely, if the clubs are of opinion that they have arrogated to
themselves too important a position. All that they desire to do is to obtain
from the Clubs a serious and considered opinion on the principle involved in
the proposal, and this they do not think was done at the meeting of
March 11th.
H. K. RANDALL, Hon. Secretary, C.R.C.
T. M. BALSON, Chairman, C.R.C.
"ANON.'S" GRIEVANCE.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR MR. EDITOR, -I have read "Anon.'s" letter carefully, and with
the exception of knowing our instructor, have quite failed to observe any
good fellowship existing between the students, and I most entirely agree with
the student who stood up, referred to by Anon. I have personally made
attempts to fraternize, but was met with a frigid reception in the style of
"What does he want?" It seems to me that if a student who had attended
the College for some time and had been fortunate enough to make a few
acquaintances were to take the new member in hand, such as is usual in
Volunteer Corps or Clubs, it would tend to make matters much more
comfortable for the fresh student, and bring about that spirit of good
fellowship talked about by "Anon.," but which I have failed to notice, and
which would have the effect of increasing the membership.
With regard to the concluding portion of the letter, it does not to my
mind call for any reply, but the break between the two classes strikes me as
an excellent idea. - Yours, etc.,
ANOTHER STUDENT,

SOLITARY CHESS.
SOLITARY CHESS.
107
ADVANCING years cut a man off from society by the unwillingness
to travel in the evening, and to some extent from the solace of books
by the weakening of the eyesight.
Some pleasing solitary amuse-
ment becomes desirable. Many try solitary chess for the purpose,
but in the form of solving problems. This practice is rather irritating
than soothing to me, and very few make it a daily resource. I have
adopted another form of solitary chess, which I have now used with
great pleasure for years, and which I will describe for the benefit of
persons in similar circumstances to myself.
I cut out and play over the games published in the newspaper.
I do not merely put the pieces on the board and follow the moves
as a spectator, but I take a hand in the game. I take the winning
side, and endeavour to anticipate the text move. Sometimes there is
an editorial note: "This move is very ingenious and ensures an
early win." If this happens to be the move independently decided
on by me, the selection is a gratifying score. I find it convenient to
cover the text with a card, which I shift line by line so as not to see
the text move until I have made my own decision. A folded card is
convenient for cuttings; if you play white, the fold should be at the
side-you can then pull the cutting out line by line; if you play
black, the fold should be at the bottom, and the cutting should
protrude on the left so that the card only covers black's moves.
I keep the games of unusual interest in a classified order based
on Staunton. Very popular openings I subdivide, e.g., the Ruy
Lopez divides into three: the white king's pawn is often left
unsupported; this gives three cases, (1) offered and taken, (2) offered,
not taken, (3) not offered. The queen's pawn game can be similarly
divided.
I use a white note sheet with a blue half-sheet for every division,
and I file the games in the order of the number of moves, so that I
get a numbered register to which I can readily refer. I put all the
white victories before the blue sheet, and black victories after. I
keep notes to special games, sometimes under the name of the player
and sometimes under the peculiarity of the game, e.g., clever sacrifice.
Ruy L. p. not k. Wh. 43.
I find this practice very interesting and also improving for play.
I have a weekly opponent, on whom I try the novelties I pick up in
my solitary practice.
COLL. FELL.
A MID-DAY COLLEGE MEAL.
THAT College men are mostly gregarious, omnivorous animals, and
generally feed shortly after noon, is widely known; but it was only to the
resourceful mind of Citizen Edward Hayward (he objects to be called
"Mister") that the brilliant idea occurred to take advantage of the fact, by
instituting a periodical College lunch or dinner, to be eaten at an agreed
hostelry within a definite radius of the Bank, on a given day each month.
Quite a number of members have been carried away with enthusiasm and
the thoughts of a good dinner cheap-on hearing of the suggestion, and all
it now wants is a guiding hand, Hayward's for example. It would be
nice to meet, say, at one o'clock on the first Thursday in each month, at the
same board with our friends. Intending diners could drop a card to the
caterer:-"Shall be dining with the Citizens on Thursday." A score of such
cards would encourage mine host to provide accordingly, and we all know the
advantages of co-operation.

THE GLOWWORMS' CONCERT.
ON Saturday, April 20th, the Glowworms Glee and Musical Society,
conducted by Mr. F. Budge, gave a concert in the Maurice Hall. It was their
first appearance in the College, as a society, but we had often previously had
the pleasure of hearing some of their members, including Mr. William Tarr,
Mr. Mason Tarr, Mr. C. F. Marshall, and Mr. Thurgood. On this occasion
they gave their audience so much pleasure, with their glees and part-songs,
that we hope often to hear them again in the College. The chair was taken
by Mr. de Jastrzebski, during the first half of the performance, and by
Mr. R. H. Marks during the second. Mr. William Tarr acted as accompanist
and musical director. The Society's choir was about two dozen strong, and
they sang well together, and were ably conducted by Mr. Budge, who, as
everyone knows, is the father-in-law of Mr. Tarr. The glees comprised
"Fill the shining goblet" (John Parry), "If music be the food of love"
(Benson), "Queen of the night" (Smart), "Come, silent evening" (Cummings),
"Bold Turpin" (Bridge), “Away, away, to the summer woods" (Coward),
"Venetian boat song" (Cusins), "Is it the roar of Teviot's tide?" (Dr. Clarke),
and "Song of the Northmen" (Maunder). These were interspersed with
songs, "Ailsa mine" (Newton), and encore, "Very good company," sung by
Mr. Dudley Ward, who showed great command and delicacy of voice
manipulation; "Out on the deep" (Löhr), by our old friend Mr. Thurgood,
excellent as usual; "A soldier's song" (Mascheroni), and "Tell her I love
her so (de Kaye), by Mr. A. A. Speer; "The maid of Malabar" (Stephen
Adams), and encore, "Alice, where art thou?" by Mr. F. Wentworth;

Mr. Wentworth and Mr. Thurgood also sung solos in one of the glees,
"Is it the roar of Teviot's tide?" in which we thought Mr. Tarr's accompani-
ment a real treat to listen to. Mr. de Jastrzebski proposed a hearty vote of
thanks, which was given to the society, just before the interval for refreshments,
and was afterwards acknowledged by Mr. Budge, whilst Mr. Tarr's efforts
were also recognized in like manner, on the motion of Mr. Marks.

FURNIVALL CYCLING CLUB.
THE COLLEGIANS' DANCE.
109
ONE never appreciates the saying "that you may take a horse to the
water, but you can't make him drink," so much as when M.C.-ing a dance.
If you ask the men if they enjoyed themselves on March 23rd, at the
22nd Collegians' Dance, they will probably vote it a huge success, and from
their point of view it undoubtedly was. Many a man is prepared to purchase
a ticket, he will even favour you with his presence, but it is another matter
to get him to dance, and this was our trouble on the occasion of our last
dance. From the attitude of some of the men, one would imagine that
dancing was the last idea they had in their minds, and it was with great
difficulty they were persuaded to book up with our lady friends. They do
not appear to realize the additional pleasure it will give to a lady to find her
programme filled up after the first three or four dances; the knowledge that
she will not be dependent on the efforts of the M.C. for each separate dance,
and will not be compelled to sit out, is calculated to increase her enjoyment
considerably, and to give her a much more cheerful view of the proceedings
and a greater appreciation of her partners.
"
As regards the actual dance, although it did not seem to have quite the
same 'go" in it as the previous one had, we believe everyone had a good
time on the whole. The majority of ladies went through every dance, and
we can assure those few ladies who were compelled to miss a dance or two
that it was not through lack of men or of effort on the part of the M.C's and
stewards, but solely because of our inability to get some of the men to dance.
We have to thank the Misses Randall and also the Misses Reglar and
their brother for the valuable assistance and suggestions given the committee
in the decoration of the hall, and we acknowledge our indebtedness to Flint
for the ready help he gave us on the night.
This is the last dance we shall have this season, but we look forward
to the Executive granting us the Hall again next season for a renewal of these
pleasant social re-unions. The dances have been a financial success, and this
has enabled us to hand £1 6s. 2d. to the Coffee Room Decoration Fund.
H. K. RANDALL,
Hon. Secretary, Dance Committee.
FURNIVALL CYCLING CLUB.
ONCE again the Easter tour to Brighton has been an immense success.
Twenty-four members took part in it. For other particulars, I must refer
to the captain's report of the trip. [To appear next month.-ED.]
On Sunday, April 7th, it rained very hard during the early part of the
morning, and consequently very few members ventured out. The captain,
sub-captain, and secretary had a most enjoyable run. The roads were in a
fairly good condition. We made our way through the lanes to Perivale,
Greenford, Ruislip, crossed the main at Uxbridge, and had lunch at Fulmer,
after which we reached Hedgerley, a beautifully situated little village, well
worth a visit. In approaching it you have to pass through some magnificent
woods, reminding one of the New Forest. From Hedgerley, we went to
Burnham Beeches, Slough, and had tea at Windsor. Altogether it was a
charming run, and no doubt the "fair weather" cyclists of the club regretted
missing it.
The Social Run to Pinner, held on Saturday, April 13th, was attended
by 37 members, although the weather early in the morning was not at all
promising. After tea and a walk round the country lanes, we returned to the
"Cocoa Tree," and spent a pleasant social evening. The thanks of the club
are due to the Misses Reglar and Messrs. Haynes and Young, who played the
piano, and to Miss Toyé and Messrs. Lawrence, Nye, Nield, and Reglar for
providing the vocal part of the entertainment. The runs for the current
month are Saturday, 4th, Harrow Weald; Sunday, 12th, Virginia Water;
Saturday, 18th, Whitsun Tour; Saturday, 25th, Eltham.
W. MELZER, Hon, Secretary.

110 THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
W.M.C. DEBATING SOCIETY.
ON Tuesday, 29th January, Mr. G. P. Gooch, M.P., moved a vote of
confidence in the Liberal Government. In quite a perfect Parliamentary
speech, Mr. Gooch dealt with the work accomplished by the Government,
and foreshadowed the measures intended to be introduced during the coming
session, which included an Irish Devolution Bill, Licensing and Housing
reforms, a small Holdings Bill, and a warning note to the House of Lords.
Mr. A. E. HOMEWOOD was extremely happy in opposition, and his humorous
coruscations were much enjoyed. A keen discussion followed on a very high
level, and the motion was ultimately carried, amid enthusiasm, by 56 votes
to 22.
On February 5th, Mr. E. M. Forster, M.A., moved :-"That the sense
of humour should be cultivated with caution." Mr. Forster, in a delightfully
humorous speech, argued that it was pernicious that the sense of humour
should be made to direct our lives; it was not capable of performing such a
task; the tendency was for the sense of humour to be cultivated in fields
where it had never been sown before, and he believed the crop would be
disastrous. In opposing the proposition, Mr. HEPBURN gave his capacious
wit the fullest scope. He kept the House in a continual roar of laughter,
and was ultimately successful in beating the opener by 18 votes to 12.
February 12th.-Mr. FRANK SAMUEL, M.A., moved, with much good
humour, "That Music Halls are demoralizing." Mr. A. E. HOMEWOOD
defended the Music Halls, and was supported by the majority of the speakers
who took part in the very animated discussion. Chief among the opener's
supporters was Mr. Starling, who made some exceedingly good points in
the course of a characteristic speech. Mr. Samuel shone distinctly in his
reply, and eventually secured 30 out of the 61 votes, the motion being lost
by the narrow margin of I vote.
February 19th.-Mr. SYDNEY PRESBURG moved: "That London is
best governed by a Progressive County Council," and the motion was
productive of a spirited and well-sustained discussion, although the element
of opposition was not strong. Mr. Presburg, who spoke with a thorough
mastery of his subject, urged that the good work done during the Progressive
term of office justified them in asking for the continued confidence of the
electorate. Mr. W. PARRY JONES opposed, and dealt chiefly with the
proposed electrical scheme, which he contended would be too great a specu-
lation for the ratepayers to be asked to undertake.
February 26th.-Mr. G. K. CHESTERTON, who had promised to come
and move "That the ideal of Nationalism is superior to Imperialism or
Cosmopolitanism," telegraphed that he much regretted his inability to be
with us, but at the last moment he had been called into the country on urgent
political business. Our president, Mr. LUPTON, who had arranged to oppose,
kindly consented to fill the gap, and opened the discussion by moving, "That
the ideal of Nationalism is inferior to Cosmopolitanism. Mr. Lupton's
arguments in favour of Cosmopolitanism were very telling, and his speech
was thought to be one of the best ever heard in our Debating Hall. Mr.
RIGBY SMITH supported the National State, but was opposed by most of
the speakers, Mr. Lupton's motion being carried by 40 votes to 7.
March 5th.-Mr. W. H. BERRY moved:- "That the conduct of the
Police and the appointment of unpaid Magistrates are grave social evils,
menaces to individual liberty, and urgently need reform" Mr. Berry
subjected the conduct of the Police to a severe criticism in respect of the
general corruption which existed in the force. He further maintained that
mis directions of justice were of frequent occurrence, in consequence of the
appointment of men with no legal training or qualification whatever as
Magistrates. Mr. M. W. STARLING was briefed on behalf of the police, and
advanced an admirable defence to the charges made against them, at the
same time urging that the courage and tact with which they performed their
very trying duties called forth the strongest commendation. He was, however,
unable to convince the majority of the jury, and the police were convicted
by 24 against 8.

DR. FURNIVALL'S CHILDREN'S TEA.
III
On March 12th, Dr. JERNEGAN, an American friend of Dr. Furnivall,
supported a motion in favour of Co-education. Dr. Jernegan, in a most
lucid and interesting address, told how satisfactorily the system worked in the
United States; that it produced men of a more tolerant and appreciative
type, and more dignified and self-possessed women; that considerable economy
was secured, and discipline had improved continually. Dr. Furnivall was
present and supported in a characteristic fighting speech. Mr. C. D.
ROBERTSON, M.A., attacked the proposition more particularly from the
theoretical standpoint, and most of the speakers supported him, but the
motion was ultimately carried by 23 votes to 19.
C. F. W. MEAD, Hon. Secretary.
DR. FURNIVALL'S CHILDREN'S TEA.
IN dealing with this function we feel that an apology is due to the
members of the College for the delay in presenting our report and balance
sheet; but owing to the difficulty of getting in accounts and other matters, we
have been compelled to hold over the record of our stewardship until the
present.
On Saturday, December 22nd last, the members of the College gave the
annual tea to the poor children of the neighbourhood, and some 280 to 300
children were entertained. As a result of our appeals for clothing in the
November and December numbers of the JOURNAL, the Committee are
pleased to acknowledge parcels of clothing from the following:-Misses
Estall, Hamilton, Munro, J. and G. Sutton, Chandler, Vinters, and Lidington,
Mrs. Fox, Mrs. Pocoek, Mrs. Tutte, Mrs. Lionel Jacob, and Mrs. and Miss
Taylor, and the large number of articles sent may be estimated when it is
mentioned that each child received one or more garments. Our application for
toys was also responded to splendidly, the Misses Sewell, Skinner, kinner, Murray,
Rogers, Ellis, Dyer, D. Dyer, D. and V. Smith, and Miss Moulden, the Hammersmith
skipper, kindly contributing. Sweets and biscuits were sent by Messrs.
Evans, Hawes, and W. R. Emslie, and Miss Dyer. Several parcels arrived
without names attached, and to the ladies and gentlemen who contributed
these anonymous gifts we tender our warmest thanks. Hepburn at the last
moment treated us to a most agreeable surprise by bringing 630 bright
pennies, collected from the counting house staff of Messrs. McCorquodale
and Co. To the gentlemen who contributed this splendid gift, most sincere
thanks are due. To Mrs. Butcher we owe hearty thanks for the loan of cups,
saucers, and plates to make up the number required. Following the wise
policy of Colesby, we have purchased some more crockery for use on future
occasions; and we hope this will place the "Children's Fund" upon a better
and more secure basis, and save the trouble and expense of hiring or borrowing
the necessary utensils.
As to our helpers, it seems a pity perhaps to individualize, as all were
good enough to place themselves at our absolute disposal and each did his or
her share most willingly We feel, however, that we owe a deep debt of
gratitude to our old friend "Bobby" Marks for the hard work done by him.
Mrs. Martin, Mrs. Hopkins, and Miss Hamilton also put in most excellent
work, sorting and parcelling the garments, and picking out the children who
were in the most apparent need of the clothes at their disposal. I should
like also to mention Mrs. Robbie, Munro, and his sister, who worked hard
the whole day. All these and Mr. Levinsohn arrived early in the morning,
and at once set to work, and we managed to keep them busy until the
children left at 10 o'clock in the evening.
Owing to the generous support afforded to us, we were able to provide
18 pairs of boots for the boys, Jackman purchasing them at a low figure, and
seeing that we got a good quality boot.
Finally we must thank all who assisted for their kind and sympathetic
help. Their names would make a very long list, our thanks are not the less
warm because they are not all mentioned.
H. K. RANDALL,
on behalf of the Committee of the "Children's Tea Fund."

THE SHAKESPEARE READINGS.
MRS. JACOB ENTERTAINS THE READERS.
April 7th.-" As you Like It" was read under very happy conditions
at the house of our worthy Vice-Principal. By kind invitation of Mrs. Jacob,
there assembled a large company, including Mrs. Tansley, Mr., Mrs. and
Miss Peck, and Mr. Levinsohn. Mr. Sidney Lee was unavoidably absent. A
pleasant surprise came in the shape of a song, "Under the Greenwood Tree,"
given before the play, by Miss Green. We had a splendid welcome from
Mr. and Mrs. Jacob, whose keen personal interest in our comfort quickly
put us at ease.
The reading had many points of interest. A new Rosalind to us, Miss
Steptoe, gave us much delight in the well-known speeches. Mrs. Tansley,
as Celia, again charmed us with her splendid delivery, restrained, but most
effectual. Paterson, as Touchstone, gave us of his drollery, and added to our
enjoyment by singing the songs in the text set down for Amiens. Peck, with
his forceful and impressive delivery, made a deep impression as Jacques.
Orlando was taken by Barnard, and the rest of the characters were main-
tained at a high level.
A brief acknowledgment of our gratitude for a delightful evening, with a
suggestion that Mrs. Jacob's experiment if repeated by other friends of the
College Readers would be much appreciated, brought the proceedings to a
close. We then passed into another room where refreshments were being
dispensed with the assistance of our hostess' two charming little girls. With
literary chat and social gossip and peeps at rare old volumes, the time passed
pleasantly enough. My only inducement to leave at all was the prospect of a
five miles' walk home.

VOL. X.-NO. 172.
JUNE, 1907.
PRICE TWOPENCE.
SHORT STUDIES IN SHAKESPEARE.
I. THE INVISIBLE SUPERNATURAL, AND THE RELATION
OF "ARIEL" TO THE SAME.
HE element of the supernatural in Shakespeare's plays
furnishes an interesting subject of study. It is a
feature frequently met with, and is used for the
purpose of furnishing a plot or of giving life or colour
to the same; of creating an atmosphere, or as a
means of diversion; of marking a situation, or giving prevalence
to an idea.
We find it in its grosser or material aspects in
witches and hags, and other abortions of the flesh or something
worse; in unsubstantial forms as ghosts or apparitions; as airy
shapes and elemental forces, with but shadowy personifications;
or as an influence working secretly but effectually in the minds
of men.
In this paper we are concerned only with what has been
called the "Invisible Supernatural." But, although the range
of our inquiry is necessarily narrowed, there is yet ample scope
for the exercise of bent and skill, for the idea itself opens out
a splendid field for study and speculation. It has been pointed
out that in the play of Richard II., there is an undercurrent
of the Invisible Supernatural. Thus, at some time previous to
the actual period of the play, the Duke of Gloster, an uncle
of the King, had been murdered. As the Duke had been
prominent among a party which had for some time thwarted
Richard in his vicious pursuits, there were many who thought
that the murder was an act of vengeance on his part. This
unnatural act was, then, the origin of the "Invisible Supernatural"
element referred to. Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, was supposed
to have been Richard's tool in getting rid of Gloster, and at
the opening of the play we see Bolingbroke charging Norfolk
with having plotted the crime. This is our first acquaintance
with the prevalent feeling of repulsion thus engendered; and
all through the play we find it welling up, now here and now
there, resulting in that general falling away from allegiance to
the King which led to his rapid downfall.


## p. 114 (#110) ############################################

114
THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
But it is a significant fact that we get no hint that this ghostly
successor to Richard's alleged crime made any subjective appeal
to him. There are no exclamations of terror or words of self-
reproach in connection with it; through all the scenes, there is
nothing more than a passing allusion to his "weaved-up follies."
Are we to assume from this that Shakespeare withheld his
sanction from the grave charge, or are we to infer that he intended
to represent Richard as being so morally degraded as to be
unable to realize the nature of his offence?
In dealing with the question of the relation of Ariel in
The Tempest to the Invisible Supernatural, we are brought into
contact with an entirely different set of conditions. There is
much in this play that appears incredible to us. But this need
not detract from our interest in or appreciation of it. For a
work may be true to life, and yet appear incongruous in its
presentation of facts, as well as in the means and methods by
which they are brought about; and The Tempest is a case in
point. Thus, if we regard it as an allegory, it has a significance
for us quite apart from the nature of its machinery or the
credibility of its facts. We find in it that which accords with
our highest aspirations respecting the destiny of man; that is,
Nemesis working in conjunction with the Spirit of Mercy,
bringing to a happy issue the dire events which have made such
a powerful appeal to us. It is this beneficent blending of forces,
which can be readily identified as the "Law of Compensation,"
that constitutes the Invisible Supernatural in the play. Having
reached this conclusion, it now remains for us to trace out the
particular relation we are in search of. In doing this, a brief
reference must be made to Prospero and Caliban, as well as to
Ariel. The character of Prospero is undoubtedly one of
Shakespeare's finest creations. It is in fact the embodiment of
the highest type of mind and will and spirit in an individual,
who had, however, a defect of the qualities, which, while it does
not detract from his essential merits, had painful consequences
upon his own life and that of his daughter, and gave occasion
for the set of circumstances with which the play is concerned.
This character may be taken to represent the moral and motive
forces which, in the last resort, operate upon mundane affairs to
right the wrong, and conduce to that ultimate fitness of things
which makes possible the onward progress of the world. With
Prospero are two subordinate agents-the one Ariel, a spirit of
the air, and the instrument whereby Prospero gives effect to his
beneficent purposes; and the other Caliban, a half-devil, who
would rob the world of its benefactor, and bring back the horrors
of unmitigated savagery into the lives of men.
Undoubtedly, Ariel occupies a position of honour and
usefulness, and its achievements are marvellous. But yet it is
a kind of mechanical service that it renders, and that for
immediate reward only, and not for love of the work. In the
same way that the intellect in man depends for its possibilities


## p. 115 (#111) ############################################

THE SHAKESPEARE READINGS.
115
for usefulness upon its association with character, so Ariel
depended upon Prospero: apart from its master it is helpless,
and fit only to live a life of vegetative dalliance. What then
is this shadowy entity-if entity it can be called, which is so
nearly allied to the insensate-intended to stand for? Is it not
for the refined and subtle mental powers in man, which, if
governed by an intelligent will and rightly employed in practical
pursuits, may give a world of added power to the individual,
making him an effective co-worker with destiny in beneficently
moulding human affairs? In conclusion, then, we may infer that
the relationship of Ariel to our assumed Invisible Supernatural.
is in a sense that of cause to effect; the former in its sub-
ordinate and material aspect, being strictly conditioned and
subject to constraint; the latter universal, unerring, and sublime.
G. S.
THE SHAKESPEARE READINGS.
OUR final Reading this season was "The School for Scandal." on
April 28th. Surely it was the liveliest one of the whole series: a large
number of listeners; Readers revelling in their parts; and to crown all,
Paterson singing in his inimitable way, "Here's to the maiden of bashful
fifteen." Of course we joined in the chorus. Of course we chaffed him
on his tender sentiments; and of course we made pretence to bang tables
and clink glasses, as if we were toasting Marks at a Club Supper. This
concord of sweet sounds would have stirred the most apathetic listener.
Our Readers turned up in full force. Miss Steptoe as Lady Teazle,
and Barnard as Sir Peter, in their quarrels caused much amusement.
Mrs. Tansley made Mrs. Candour so natural as to obscure all traces of
effort. Her reading was truly described as a little gem."
Miss
Lady Sneerwell was in the capable hands of Miss Walford.
F. Reglar undertook the rather colourless Maria; and Miss Peck gained
our thanks for the unthankful part of a Servant, who jumped up at intervals
to announce visitors, and as suddenly retired.
Chief honours among the men fell to Wallace Davis, Fenton, Gates
Fowler, and Hayward. Moses was a splendid characterization, and Crabtree,
also by Davis, no less amusing. Fenton was happily cast as Joseph Surface.
The part is unsympathetic, but Fenton scored every dramatic point.
Gates Fowler was a gay and reckless Charles enough, and Hayward seemed
as fond of his part as the audience was of him. The rest of the cast had
little to do; but it is apparent what a good effect generally the season has
produced in our reading. We have all improved.
The prospects of a strong company of Readers next season are most
promising.

know if they will be joining the party.

PROPERLY constituted College men are gregarious animals: they
carry their fellowship beyond class times, and take their holidays
together. That is why Munro and I were tramping together in
Normandy.
Straight and white and dusty, the route nationale stretched
away in front of us. For miles we had followed it through the solemn
aisles of pine forests and through lighter woods where the ground
was white with anemones; past steep downs and sunny banks where
primroses and violets ran riot. Now it led past great orchards
where the white blossom covered the branches overhead, and drifted
petals scattered the road under foot; now through broad fields,
where the rough peasant men and women paused to stare at us.
Evidently they thought us mad, to trudge about the country on foot :
but then obviously we were English
The sun was sinking behind the downs, so that they stood as a
purple bar between the glowing sky and glowing river, as we reached
Jumièges. We were very dusty and very hungry, and the pleasant
old lady who took us in was like a ministering angel in a Norman
cap, which latter is the happy mean between the head-gear of a nun
and of a nursemaid.
We had dinner by the yellow light of one candle-a sumptuous
and most excellent dinner. In an adjoining room we saw, through
the glass door, a table with an oilcloth cover, laid out with coarse
cutlery, round which sat big countrymen in blue blouses and queer
peaked caps. This was the real table d'hôte in its elementary form,
for there our hostess dined with her company.
It was quite night now, and we threw wide the casements to the
brilliant moon. We were under the very shadow of the Abbey, and
we gazed at its great towers and ruined arches, standing out grey
and ghostly under the dark blue sky; so dim and so misty that they
seemed a phantom, an unreal thing that a breeze might blow away. On
such a night as this the monks who during thirteen centuries had
lived in those grey walls, might well return to glide in silence about
them again; they are indeed such stuff as dreams are made of, those
long forgotten brethren; yet once they were real enough, real as we
two, who young, strong, and sunburnt, gazed at those shadowy
arches.
We tried to explore Jumièges some more, and we went through
the silent little street, and through the orchards, glimmering silvery
in the moon. But all the dogs in the countryside seemed to wake at
our steps, so we went back. Our hostess suggested that it was
bedtime-everyone else had gone to bed. So we went too: it was
only 9.15, but there was no help for it.
The bed was small, and Munro is large, so it was a tight fit.
Still-
"Frère Jacques, frère Jacques, dormez vous, dormez-vous?
Sonnez les matines, ding din-don!"
We nearly slept the clock round!

DRAMATIC PERFORMANCE.
117
So we had a breakfast which, for the country, was unusually
large; and paid our bill, which was unusually small-four francs
each. We visited the Abbey, which contained no ghostly monks,
only countless primroses; and the glamour of the night was still on
us, so we grossly overtipped the gardien. Then it was "Forward"
for Candebec. The river shone broad and blue in the early sun; in
front of us, white and endless, stretched the route nationale.
A. E. HOMEWOOD.
MISS LOWES DICKINSON'S DRAMATIC
PERFORMANCE.
ON May Ist, Miss Lowes Dickinson and her friends delighted a large
audience in the Maurice Hall at the College with their representation of
W. S. Gilbert's Farcial Comedy Engaged. There was not too much time
allowed for preparation beforehand, yet the performance was a great
success in every way. Personally, we enjoyed it immensely. The stage was
properly fitted up with appropriate scenery, the first scene, that of the garden
of a cottage near Gretna, on the border between England and Scotland,
being very pretty and well painted. It was the work of members of the
College Art class, working under the direction of their teacher, Mr. Ralph
Wilkinson. They were much pressed for time, but by working hard to a
late hour every night for a week or more before the event, they got it ready,
and it was much admired.
The dramatis persone were as follows:-
Cheviot Hill (a man of property)
Belvawney (his friend)
Mr. Symperson
Angus Macalister (a Lowland peasant lad)
Major Macgillicuddy
Belinda Treherne
Minnie (Symperson's daughter)
Mrs. Macfarlane (a Lowland widow)
Maggie (her daughter)
Parker (Minnie's maid)
Mr. Gilbert Cannan.
Mr. Grosvenor Berry.
Mr. Levien.
Mr. Sheppard.
Mr. R. Mayor.
Miss Lowes Dickinson.
Miss Flora Mayor.
Miss Alice Mayor.
Miss Garcia.
Miss Christie.
All the points of the cleverly written farce were admirably. brought out,
and the piece went well from start to finish. The most difficult parts, we
thought, were those taken by Mr. Cannan and Miss Lowes Dickinson, and
both acted them splendidly. They were well supported, too, by all their
friends, with the result that, during the three acts, much pleasure and amuse-
ment were afforded to the audience, as was shown by their hearty laughter
and frequent applause.
The College is much indebted to Miss Lowes Dickinson for her kindness
in arranging to give the performance for the entertainment of members and
friends, and also for the addition to the Maintenance Fund of the sum
of £44 6s. Id. net, realised by the sale of tickets. The best thanks of the
College are also due to Mr. Wilkinson and his students for their welcome help.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
CYCLING CLUB'S EASTER TOUR.
AMONGST my many embarrassing duties as captain, the writing of this
report is to my mind the most embarrassing, following, as I do, one whose
facile pen has charmed and amused the students and their friends by racy
elaboration of the doings of the Cycling Club whilst on tour. However,
with humble apologies, allons à nos moutons.
This was the third successive Easter tour to Brighton, and it was blessed
with even better weather than the last one. After many anxious days and
sleepless nights for our estimable secretary, arrangements were finally
concluded with the Misses Buckie at least ten days before Good Friday.
Contrary to all precedent with College functions, the members definitely.
gave in their names as intending participants in the tour long before the
final date fixed by the committee, and much to the latter's regret and the
Secretary's dismay, many applications had to be refused, including one from
that sturdy cyclist and jovial friend, Davis, whose absence was lamented by
more than one of the party, but who, torn by conflicting emotions and
unable to decide between his dog, the Zoo, Harrow Weald, and Brighton, had
perforce to content himself with the three former, a decision largely
influenced, no doubt, by the anticipated pleasure of a visit to the Zoo.
Some of the ladies of the party went by train on Thursday and Friday,
and one or two of the aristocracy rode to Dorking on Thursday night, taking
it easy on the way and arriving at Brighton about 2 o'clock on Friday
afternoon. Our old friend Hoppy got kicked out of bed at an early hour,
leaving home at 7 o'clock, to be greeted on arrival by his wife, his sister-in-
law, and lunch. The few faithfuls who met at Hammersmith Bridge to be
guided by the captain to their destination were Melzer, Young, Lewis,
Poulteney, Lawrence, and Walters. They started at 10.10, to the accom-
paniment of expressions of good-will from Davis, who had turned up with
his canine friend to see them off.
We went via Barnes Common, Putney Heath, Wimbledon Common, and
through the pleasant rural lanes to Worcester Park, there to be greeted by
a breeze on the Ewell Road, which, with the heat, subsequently worried us
considerably. We rode merrily through Ewell, climbed to Burgh Heath, and
so on to Reigate Hill, where the party refreshed themselves. Here Lawrence
left us, having had enough of it. The others pushed on steadily until
lunch, which we had in the pleasant lanes between Redhill and East
Grinstead. After lunch we rode on through the lanes, lost our way, retraced
it, and rode through Horne to Blindly Heath and East Grinstead, after
passing through which we had our first free-wheel, 1½ miles, to be followed
immediately by the long and anxiously anticipated 24 miles ascent at Forest
Row. On reaching the summit, we rested, but Melzer, to show his
superiority to fatigue, took off his tyre to discover an imaginary puncture.
After admiring the scenery in many languages, our devoted, toil-worn band
resumed their pilgrimage to the shrine of the Queen of the South Coast.
We wheeled along with smiling faces and flashing feet, for now we had
reached the easy stage of our journey. Leaving the Ashdown Forest and the
open moor-like country with its glorious views, we gradually descended
between smiling meadows, by a tree-fringed road, which we had almost to
ourselves for five miles, until we reached Sheffield Park, famous in the annals
of Australian Cricket, and so on to Chailey, where we had a cup of tea and
an interesting conversation with a tramp, who made all sorts of mysterious
promises to one of our party, and invited him to Chailey early in July.
Then on again, through Lewes, we rode without another pause to Brighton,
to be greeted by the rest of the party and la gentil donna, amata da tutti.
As a matter of record, our mileage was 68 miles from Hammersmith Bridge,
and in the writer's humble opinion, we went by far the nicest way to
Brighton, by solitary roads and fine scenery, albeit not adapted to fast going.
All the cyclists found the ride to Brighton a very trying one, Peckham
having his cycle carried in for him, but one young lady, who had ridden from
Reigate, treated the whole thing as a mere bagatelle, and wanted to ride back

to look for the club. Castell did the journey most quickly, reaching Brighton
quite fresh and as perky as ever in about two hours.
After dinner and a song or two, we all strolled by the sad sea waves,

and Lewis is strongly recommended to pay great attention to his method of
procedure. After dinner, certain members sought seclusion in the smoking
room and the conservatory, until tea time. Over the portals of the smoking
room may be seen these words, Lasciate ogni speranza di entrare, voi, che lo
volete, for it is always engaged. But the door opens not all' Inferno, but
al Paradiso. Our officials will supply all information required.
In the evening we split up again, some going on the Pier, and others
seeking peace and quietness, to admire the beautiful night and the moon-
light sparkling on the incoming tide. After supper an interesting function
took place, Castell proposing a vote of thanks to the secretary, and calling
upon Hoppy to second it, but before the latter could rise, sa chère dame
threw her wifely arms around his neck, saying she would not allow him to
make a fool of himself. However, Melzer suitably responded, and becoming
emboldened by his verbosity, read extracts from Byron, chosen by Castell,
in a voice rendered clear by a cold. The ladies having retired, their guardian
angels hied themselves heavenwards only to find that their beds were sewn
up and various articles placed thereupon in a medley of confusion. Melzer
went into hysterics and rolled upon the floor, compelling us to shut the door
and thrust a pillow into his mouth, but, being unable to quite get it in, we
became anxious lest he should wake the house up.
This little episode
accounted for the weary angels getting to bed at 3.30.
After Melzer had struggled with mathematics for about an hour on
Monday morning, the Club, composed of the Misses Grellier and Miss
Martin, Jones, Lewis, Young, Walters, and Wildey, started punctually at the
time fixed by the latter, 11 o'clock, leaving Melzer behind to settle accounts,
et pour l'occasion de faire ses adieux. He, Nye and Peckham caught us up at
Dorking, and after a pleasant day, we reached the Sculling Club headquarters
at Hammersmith at 9.30, and there partook of the club's usual bountiful
hospitality to its guests, seeking our respective homes at 11 p.m.
I am sure all those who took part in the tour will join with me in
heartily thanking the Misses Buckie and Norah for their kindness and
attention, and also Melzer for the arrangements made and the trouble taken
by him to make the tour successful.
A. J. WILDEY, Captain.

COLLEGE NOTES.
COLLEGE men were very sorry to learn in the early part of
last month that Mr. Cornford was suddenly taken ill with
appendicitis. The excursion to Cambridge, for which he had as
usual kindly invited forty of our members, had in consequence
to be cancelled. We shall all hope to hear of Mr. Cornford's
speedy return to convalescence.
Early in July will be held the Senior Student Examination.
As may be learned from the Calendar, the College grade of
"Senior Student" can be gained either by taking three first
stage certificates, one in each subject in the Lower Division,
within three years-or by taking two advanced stage certificates,
one of them being for Arithmetic-or by passing the "Senior
Student Examination," in all three subjects. It is hoped that
there may be several students this year who will avail themselves
of this examination, to qualify for the honour.
At the Shorthand Examination held by Mr. E. H. Carter, on
27th March, the following students passed :-R. W. Alaway
(excellent) at 80 words; and S. Goodwin, H. W. Hughes, and
Thomas Martin, in Theory. Fifteen sat. This was a poor
result, and it is hoped that at the next examination, to be held on
July 1st, a better-equipped lot of men will present themselves.
The Marks Committee have met and deliberated upon the
foundation of the "Marks" Prize, and they have been assisted
in their deliberations by Marks himself. With his approval, the
Prize will consist of books, and will be offered each year as a
prize in Literature.
The portrait of Mr. Marks presented with this number of the
JOURNAL is taken from the photograph, from which was made
the enlargement forming part of the Marks Testimonial,
and now adorning the wall of the Coffee Room.
The names of Mr. James A. Marks and Miss Elsie Marks
were accidentally omitted from the list, given in the May
JOURNAL, of those present at the Marks Presentation Meeting on
April 6th. We apologize for this slip.
It is a very attractive list of Outings that the Common Room
Committee have arranged for Saturday afternoons during June
and July; and as there will probably be a great desire to
participate in them, members are recommended to put down
their names early for the parties they intend to join. Particulars
may be obtained by consulting the notice boards in the Common
Room.

COLLEGE NOTES.
121
Mr. S. J. Hertford, a member of Mr. Wilkinson's Art Class
and of the Sketching Club, has a picture in this year's Academy,
a water-colour, 14 by 10, representing Hemingford Gray Mill,
on the Ouse, near St. Ives, Hunts. We heartily congratulate
him on his success, and think the College ought to be proud, as
doubtless it is, of the fact.
We see it announced in the Daily News that Major-General
Sir J. Frederick Maurice, K.C.B., has been awarded the Chesney
gold medal, in consideration of his valuable contributions to
military literature. Incidentally, it is mentioned that during the
war in South Africa, General Maurice wrote many articles for the
Daily News on the progress of the campaign.
When the L.C.C. put up a tablet on the house Frederick
Denison Maurice once occupied in Queen's Square, Bloomsbury,
and thereon described him as a "Theologian," many of us in
the College considered the description inadequate, as we regard
him more in the light of a social reformer, to whom our College,
Queen's College for Women, and the Boys' Home, Regent's
Park, principally owe their existence. A passage in the preface
to Mr. Maurice's "Friendship of Books," written by his and our
friend Tom Hughes, seems, however, to justify the LC.C. in
describing our Founder, from his own point of view at all events,
as a theologian. Mr. Hughes says-" Mr. Maurice was always
careful to remind his readers and his hearers, that he felt as a
theologian, thought as a theologian, and wrote as a theologian';
and, as in his last published work he again declares, 'all other
subjects are to my mind connected with theology, and
subordinate to it."
Mr. E. M. Forster has written another book, "The Longest
Journey" (Blackwood, 6s.), which has been well noticed in the
press. Mr. C. F. G. Masterman, in the Daily News, speaking
of the work as "this amazingly clever book," tells us that the
promise of "Where Angels Fear to Tread" is more than
fulfilled in this volume, and thus continues :-
It is difficult, elusive, exasperating, with something of the cleverness of
the young in it, and something of the cruelty. The influence of Meredith
is there, especially of such a work as "Rhoda Fleming," with the strong
acknowledgment in both of the strange impalpable influences which the
earth exercises over her children. There is little story; when Mr. Forster
wishes to get rid of his characters, he murders them ruthlessly with sudden
death on a railway crossing or in the football field. There is a cold satire
upon the normal respectable life, the revolt against convention and routine,
and the hypocrisies which make up the world of every day, combined with
a kind of quality of elusiveness and suggestion which opens the vision of
far horizons even in the suburban street or the school playing-field.
"The Longest Journey" is not a great novel; but it has embedded in it
many of the ingredients of greatness. Its author will go far.

THE WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
We regret to report that Mr. William Hastings Hughes, the
brother of our founder Tom Hughes, died at Milton,
Massachusetts, on April 20th, at the age of 73. Mr. Hastings
Hughes was much interested in the doings and progress of the
College, and was an intimate friend of the oldest of our Fellows,
Mr. John Roebuck, a sympathetic letter from whom appears on
another page, referring to the death of Mr. Hughes.
With much sorrow, we have to record the death from
drowning, of Frank Colton, aged 28, a member of the College
and of the Furnivall Sculling Club, who lost his life in a boat
accident at Hammersmith, on Saturday, May 4th. He was out
with two other men in one of the club skiffs, sailing between
Putney and Hammersmith Bridges. The afternoon was some-
what rough and squally, and a strong tide was running up,
when the wind suddenly dropped, the boat lost way, and before
they could get the sculls out, drifted under the stern of a moored
barge, was upset and threw the men into the water.
The two
others had narrow escapes, and Colton, who evidently received a
blow on the head, failed to come to the surface. His body was
recovered by the river police twenty minutes afterwards, but their
attempts to restore animation proved fruitless. At the inquest
subsequently held, a verdict of accidental death was returned,
and a few of poor Colton's College friends attended the funeral
at Nunhead, on May 9th. He was of a quiet, retiring disposition,
but had many friends in the College and Club, all of whom were
much shocked at his sudden and untimely death; and all
sympathized deeply with the sad loss sustained by his mother,
who lost in him her only child. Flint has written the appended
notice for the JOURNAL.
Frank Colton, whose tragic death is recorded above, was not
what one would call a thoroughly representative College man.
Joining as far back as January, 1900, he took up French as a
study. From French he drifted to Ambulance, and on to
literature and other English subjects, finally settling down to
Book-keeping. He was more constant to this than to any of his
other studies, and under Mr. Bride he made rapid progress.
That Colton's name was seldom seen on the Honours List may
be accounted for by the fact that his health was never good for
any length of time, his studies having to be constantly given up.
No one regretted this more than himself, and when examination
time came round, he invariably found himself unable to sit.
But it was on the social side of College life that Colton found
himself quite at home. Endowed with a most entertaining
manner, he was just the man for the work of "breaking the ice"
with a new student. His anecdotes frequently caused the
Common Room to resound with laughter. No man was more
ready to tell of his own mistakes than he was, and the
humorous side of them was invariably brought out in the telling.


## p. 123 (#121) ############################################

FURNIVALL SCULLING CLUB.
123
The story of how he dealt with the dissatisfied cabman will live
long in the minds of those who were fortunate enough to have
heard it. His experiences of the "Bloomsbury Landlady" were
as unique as they were varied, and told in Frank's own quaint
fashion, added to the pleasure of many an evening's talk.
At the Furnivall Sculling Club, he was a great favourite.
Always obliging and kind, he was ever ready to do anything
which he thought would give pleasure to others-the true College
spirit. His light weight made him a desirable man to have in
a boat as cox, and his steering was rarely at fault. Whether he
had had sufficient experience to manage a craft such as the one
he was sailing, at the time he met his death, it is useless to
discuss. It is so easy to moralize after the event. What he did
was what a great many more men had done before with success.
He tried and failed, and we know to our deep grief the penalty
he paid.
FURNIVALL SCULLING CLUB.
R. R. F.
ON May 4th occurred the first fatal accident in the history of the Club.
Three members, Colton, Hoad, and Watson, went out in a double-sculler
under sail. On returning, and almost within sight of the Club, the boat
drifted under a barge and capsized, Colton being drowned. Hoad managed
to reach the overturned boat, and Watson was rescued with difficulty while
in the water. Poor Colton was held in great esteem by all of us here, and
the sad event has cast a gloom over the Club which only time can dispel.
To prevent any similar accident occurring in future, the Committee have now
forbidden the use of sails in any of the Club boats.
The Club Regatta, originally fixed for 11th May, has been postponed
till the 8th June, the race with the Polytechnic rowing four taking place on
the 15th June.
H. S. HOWARD, Hon. Secretary.
FURNIVALL CYCLING CLUB.
At last old times have come back! The attendances on the runs
during the past month have considerably increased, and les demoiselles are
turning out more. Never in my time, do I remember such good feeling
in the Club as prevails, and I hope it may continue. On the Sunbury
run, eighteen members attended. We had a good tea at the "Flower Pot
Hotel, and after a little music, returned in the rain. Eight members
attended the Wheathampstead run, including our vice-president, Mr.
J. Jacob, who pioneered us through the lanes. On May 4th, sixteen
members went to Harrow Weald. We had tea at "The Case is altered,"
and a pleasant walk on the common. On Sunday, May 12th, on the occasion
of the favourite run to Virginia Water, twenty-five members were present.
This is the largest number we have had for some time on a Sunday run.
At Whitsun the Club went to Henley. Although it was rather cold, eighteen
members participated in this tour, of which our Captain will no doubt give
an account. On Saturday, May 25th, Mr. Pocock invited the Club to spend
the evening at his house at Blackheath. We had a very enjoyable soirée,
though not more than nine members took advantage of the invitation. The
runs for the current month are: -Sunday, June 2nd, Chobham Common;
Saturday, June 8th, Ruislip3 Sunday, June 16th, Surprise Run, meet at
Hammersmith Bridge; Saturday, June 22nd, Claygate; Sunday, June 30th,
Chipperfield. For Saturday, July 6th, Mr. Denmead has kindly invited the
Club to tea at his house at South Mimms, and I shall be glad to hear from
those members who intend to be present. W. MELZER, Hon. Secretary.

THE LATE MR. W. HASTINGS HUGHES.
To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR SIR, You will probably have been advised before this reaches
you of the death of the last of the brothers of that one of our founders,
who was the immediate successor of our first Principal, Mr. Maurice-
Mr. W. Hastings Hughes.
Mr. Hughes died at his home "Orchard Knoll," Milton, Mass., on the
20th day of April last, after a very brief illness, of which the known
seriousness must have been apparent less than a week.
On the 15th April, I received a letter from him (the first and only one
since his leaving this side for his English visit with his family) beginning
"Dear John,—
"Putting away a letter, which I got last February from E. J. H.
Reglar at the Working Men's College, reminded me of you and all I
intended to do last summer over there, and didn't do !
I
had to miss most of the things I had intended doing, including a visit
to the new quarters of the Working Men's College
The
rest of us here [his letter refers to his son Walter] are fairly well, except
that Dorothy [his daughter, Miss Hughes] and I are in our several rooms
laid up with colds which caught us last week. It is a good opportunity
to talk with one's friends and to ask you, one of these days, to let me
have news of the Senora and yourself.
"Ever yours,
"W. H. HUGHES."
To my great surprise and sorrow, I saw an announcement in the
New York Sun of Sunday, April 21st, of the death the day before of my
dear friend.
In acknowledgment of a few lines of the sympathy of myself and wife,
I received the following from Mrs. Hughes :-
""Orchard Knoll,' Milton, Mass.
"April 23rd, 1907.
"My Dear Mr. Roebuck,-
"Mr. Hughes died quite without pain and happy. His illness
was indeed little painful. He had been wonderfully happy and content-
Let all his friends be so too. My kind regards to your wife.
"Yours very sincerely,
"S. F. HUGHES."
Such, dear Mr. Editor, was the peaceful ending of the life of one of
the best of men, whether regarded as son, brother, husband, parent or friend.
JOHN ROEBUCK.
Yours always,

To the Editor of the WORKING MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
DEAR MR. EDITOR, -The complaints made in these columns by
"Anon." and "Another Student," supported as they have been, by verbal
expressions of discontent on the part of new-or comparatively new-students,
call for the immediate attention of all those really interested in the

new-comer. At once the blame is laid on the shoulders of those whose
business it is to make new men feel at home. That one new student comes
into the Common Room without at least receiving courteous attention,
let it be said to their shame. But we may be too ready with our censure,

they are"?
It was Sir Richard Steele, amongst other thoughtful men, who said
as far back as the end of the seventeenth century, "Man is said to be a
sociable animal, and as an instance of it, we may observe, that we take all
occasions and pretences of forming ourselves into those little nocturnal
assemblies which are commonly known by the name of Clubs." This is just
what happens in the Common Room. Men, having tastes in common, meet
two or three times a week to discuss, amongst other things, those matters
which are dear to their hearts. The new-comer sees groups of men in
conversation, and, if he is not taken in hand, by some good-natured soul, in
the early stages of his membership, goes away saying petulantly-"There's
a room full of 'cliques!" Now, Sir, this has actually happened. This ugly
word has been used by men who did not know that "Exclusiveness finds no
place in the Working Men's College." A new-comer is likely to form a
hasty judgment upon the meagre evidence he has at his disposal. But it
is unkind to say that there is an absence of good-fellowship in the College.
Because a few men have been missed, it does not follow that there is not
a warm welcome extended to strangers.
In the Common Room, all men are equal, and, if a new student addresses
himself to anyone, or makes himself known to any group of men he finds
there, he may be sure of cordial treatment. But he must do his part. He
must show that he desires to make friends. If he hides himself in a corner,
and speaks in whispers, how can he expect to make friends? He must
"spread himself out." Modesty can be carried too far. The best advice a
man of experience can offer to a new man is that he should take part in
everything that is going on in the social life of the place. Let him go to the
debates, concerts, dances, and Student and Teachers' Meetings on every
available occasion. Let him air his views on all subjects, no matter how
crude they may be. The season of Pilgrimages and Field Club Walks is
at hand, and he is invited to take part in these.
If by following this advice he makes less than a hundred friends during
the present term, then the writer of this letter has lived, during the past
seventeen years, in a Fool's Paradise, and should no longer be able to sign
himself
AN OLD STUDENT.

THE WORKING_MEN'S COLLEGE JOURNAL.
LUBBOCK FIELD CLUB.
APRIL 14th was a dull, cold day, and consequently the party was smaller
than usual. We reached Great Missenden at 10.30, and proceeded south-
west to Atkin's Farm, where we turned towards Prestwood. A series of
tempting paths, hovering near the edge of the map, conducted us westward,
and when we next recognized our whereabouts we were in Monkton Wood.
At Redland End, an unexpected but welcome inn was found, and we
settled down to lunch. Resuming our journey, the next point of interest
was Windsor Hill, whence, in spite of the haze, a fine view was obtained.
Only a short halt was allowed, as our objective, Whiteleaf Cross, was in
view. This cliff monument, SO striking from a distance, is very
disappointing viewed close at hand, and some of the party appeared dubious
as to whether it had been reached. A stiff climb ensued up Pulpit Hill, and
as the weather became at this point very threatening, we contented ourselves
with a distant view of Coombe Hill and its monument, and struck through
the woods back to the road. Rain now began to fall, and we kept to the
road until we reached a track leading by Hampden House to Great Hampden
Church and thence to the Rectory at Hampden Row. The associations of
this historic neighbourhood were not allowed to detain us, as we decided to
make a dash for the 4.21 train from Missenden. On reaching Prestwood,
however, it was found to be too big a task, and we accordingly slowed up,
and were able to obtain tea in the village before returning by the 5.29 train.
In spite of the far from favourable conditions, the views from the hills were
very fine; but from a natural history point of view, the country was most
disappointingly backward. Still, good displays of oxalis, violets, gorse, and
primroses were seen, together with a few cowslips and pansies. The
blackthorn was just showing for blossom. A large hawk attracted our
attention at one point, while at our lunch place we were able to inspect the
contents of an old beehive. The distance covered was about seventeen
miles, including a fair amount of hill climbing.
Eleven men set out on May 12th.
The weather was perfect, the
summerlike heat being tempered by a delightful breeze. An early start was
made, Hayes being reached shortly after 10 o'clock. We started at a steady
pace across the Common, reaching the road at the "Fox." After a short
spell of road work, we entered upon Keston Common, and continued across
Holwood Park, with the customary halt at Wilberforce's tree. On reaching
the road, after some hesitation we struck a path leading to Downe, on
reaching which village the majority of the party refreshed. We then
continued south, and soon passed over the edge of the only map in the
possession of the party. On reaching Cudham, we turned southwest, and
ultimately reached the Westerham Road just above the "Fox and Hounds."
Here we halted for lunch, which, owing doubtless to the heat, was a long and
interesting meal. With some difficulty the guides persuaded the party to
resume the march, which however only extended a mile or so in the direction
of Tatsfield, when another halt took place on the edge of a long strip of
wood. Here some members botanized, while others, it is said, slept. From
this spot to Rickett's Hill is a very short distance, but we contrived to do a
fair share of unauthorized wandering before reaching the "Wym," a
delightful spot, where we were welcomed by Miss Jacob and her friends, who
had prepared for us a sumptuous tea. In spite of the lazy day we had had,
we did ample justice to the tea, and then accompanied our hostesses to a
picturesque view spot, where several valleys meet, and from whence we
could see the alterations that “week-enders" were effecting in the landscape.
All too soon it became necessary to start on our homeward journey, which
was by an extremely picturesque route into Westerham. Our grateful thanks
are due to our kind entertainers for an extremely pleasant ending to a
particularly pleasant day, as well as for the floral trophies with which some of
our men returned.
One result of the cold spring is that all the spring flowers appear to have
rushed into bloom together. Consequently we found hawthorn, primroses,
violets, bluebells, early purple and meadow orchids, cowslips, apple and

recently killed blind worm was also seen.

W.M.C. DEBATING SOCIETY.
REPORT, 1906-1907.*
IN presenting the Annual Report of this Society, it is gratifying to
reflect on the work of the season which is now drawing to a close, and to
recall the happy events which have made this perhaps the most successful
year in the annals of the Debating Society.
It may be remembered that the successful launching, last May, of a
Parliament in the College, and the enthusiasm with which it was maintained
till the approach of the Summer Vacation, caused some to think that it
should take the permanent place of the Debating Society, as it was less formal
and presented facilities for the making of an orator which did not obtain in
the latter. It was, however, ultimately thought that the Debating Society
was the more useful; and as its work had become such a feature of the social
and educational life of the College, it would be unwise to allow its place
to be taken by a political institution, in which matters of a literary and
general character would scarcely find entry. It is thought that we have all
good reason to congratulate ourselves upon this conclusion being arrived at,
for the debates have gone right merrily along; success has attended the
Society's every meeting; and a very high level of debating has been
maintained.
There have been 24 meetings, and as Cowper once wrote, "Variety
being the very spice of life that gives it all its flavor," a very wide and
diverse range of subjects has been discussed, as for instance: Land
Nationalization, Municipal Trading Trusts, Modern Civilization, Spelling
Reform, the County Council, Conscription, Social Democracy, Imperialism,
and Women's Suffrage. It was unfortunate that the happy suggestion of
Dr. Furnivall, that a representative of the female sex should open this latter
debate, did not meet with favour, but the Doctor himself attended and gave
the opener his most vigorous support; and it is considered a serious reflection
on the magnanimity of the College debater that this motion was not carried.
The particularly brilliant discussions which followed the openings of
Mr. Hyder, "Land Nationalization"; Mr. Gooch, M.P., "Vote of confidence
in Liberal Government"; Dr. Jernegan, "Co-education"; and Sir Vincent
Caillard, "Tariff Reform," are deserving of special mention. By common
consent the last mentioned debate was protracted until within a quarter of an
hour of midnight, when the motion was rejected amid enthusiasm.
Individual achievements at the meetings are altogether too numerous to
mention, but this report would be lamentably deficient without the specific
mention of such names as Hepburn, A. E. Homewood, and Cash. Hepburn,
our genial Scot, a contributor to every discussion, goes down to posterity as
*
Read at the Annual General Meeting, 23rd April, 1907.

a wag of remarkable skill and dexterity. His witty sallies and the ingenuity
of his arguments will be long remembered by those who had the pleasure of
listening to them. Homewood, a Tory, but an accomplished debater, ever
ready to step into any breach where others might fear to tread, and, although
not always identified with the winning side, yet invariably scoring an
individual victory. Lastly, the illuminating oratory of Cash, whose
remarkable powers of rhetoric hold his audiences spell-bound; when he
panegyrises, they are contented and happy; when he condemns, they are
reduced to a condition of chaotic despondency. Surely the eloquence of
Cash would grace the debating halls of a Utopian world.
The Society has added to its roll twenty-six new members, most of whom
have taken part in the discussions, and their maiden efforts were received
with that kindliness which is one of the proudest traditions of the Debating-
Society.
Financially we still flourish, and as appears from the Cash Statement,
a credit balance is carried forward of £1 2s. 6d. Only once did the writer
feel some apprehension that the Society might end the year in the sphere of
bankruptcy, due, apparently, to the wisdom displayed in the selection of
tobacco, the use of which is quite free to members, but the mysterious
breaking of the churchwarden pipes speedily reduced the consumption of
the tobacco within moderate bounds. It is, of course, unnecessary to say
that the veiled suggestion that the secretary was the culprit had no founda-
tion in fact.
For the rest it is desired most cordially to thank those who have con-
tributed to the remarkable success of the Debates, and to express the hope
that the Society will continue, as it is to-day, a very real feature in the
life of the College; and that all new men will join us in the intermingling
of minds and the clashing of ideas; and as a means to ensuring what
Milton thought to be a complete and generous education: "That which fits
a man to perform, justly, skilfully, and magnanimously, all the offices of life
both private and public, of peace and war.
C. F. W. MEAD, Hon. Secretary.
TANSLEY SWIMMING CLUB.
On Tuesday, May 7th, our Club met the Aldenham Institute Swimming
Club in a friendly team race of 232 yards. Gay lost about two yards on the
first man; J. Hagerty was going well, but missed his turn, which enabled
the Aldenham Institute man to increase the lead by about eight yards;
Barclay was overhauling his man when he, too, missed his turn, so the
Aldenham Institute increased their lead still further. When our last man,
R. Hagerty, started, he was about fifteen yards behind his competitor, but he
managed to decrease their lead to about eight yards. Result: Aldenham
Institute Swimming Club Ist (time 3. min. 73 secs.); Tansley Swimming
Club 2nd (tinie 3 min. 20 secs.)
Tansley Team, Messrs. Gay, J. Hagerty, Barclay, and R. Hagerty (Capt.)
Aldenham Team, Messrs. Underwood, Allen, Hughes, and Newman.
W. H. BARNETT, Hon. Secretary.
